virtual

Especially:

Animal animal = new Dog();
animal.Speak();

and why override behaves differently from new.

Microsoft's C# documentation specifically identifies runtime polymorphism and virtual/override behavior as core OOP concepts. Microsoft Learn

2. Interfaces

You should be very comfortable with:

  • Interface definition
  • Implementation

This becomes especially important because interfaces are commonly used as abstractions for DI in .NET. Microsoft Learn

3. SOLID

For your experience level, do not just memorize definitions.

Be able to explain:

SRP → one responsibility
OCP → extend without modifying
LSP → derived type should substitute base
ISP → small focused interfaces
DIP → depend on abstractions

And give a practical example from a Web API/service architecture.

Microsoft's .NET architecture guidance explicitly describes SOLID as important for modern application/microservice design. Microsoft Learn

4. Dependency Injection

This is probably one of the most important .NET-specific OOP/design topics for you.

Know:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

and:

  • Constructor injection
  • Transient
  • Scoped
  • Singleton
  • IoC
  • IServiceCollection
  • IServiceProvider
  • Lifetime mismatch
  • Singleton → scoped problem
  • DI vs DIP
  • DI vs Service Locator
  • Why DI improves testing

.NET has built-in DI support and Microsoft recommends avoiding direct instantiation of dependencies inside services because it increases coupling. Microsoft Learn

1. Class & Object

We'll start with the first topic in our fixed sequence. For interviews, you should be able to explain class, object, their differences, object creation, instance members, and how they relate to memory/reference behavior.

Common Questions

Q1. What is a class in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A class is a blueprint or template for creating objects. It defines the data and behavior that objects of that class will have. Data is represented using fields or properties, and behavior is represented using methods.

Real-World Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee is working");
    }
}

Here, Employee is the class. It defines the Name property and Work() method, but it is not an actual employee object yet.

Follow-up:

What is the difference between a class and an object?

Q2. What is an object in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer:

An object is an instance of a class. It represents an actual entity created from the class and contains its own state while having access to the behavior defined by the class.

Real-World Example:

Employee employee = new Employee();

employee.Name = "Saurabh";
employee.Work();

Here:

Employee → Class
employee → Object

employee is an actual instance of the Employee class.

Follow-up:

How do you create an object in C#?

Q3. What is the difference between a class and an object?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A class is a blueprint that defines properties and behavior, while an object is an actual instance created from that class. A class defines what an object can have and do, whereas an object represents the actual data and state.

Real-World Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

Employee is the blueprint.

Employee emp1 = new Employee();
Employee emp2 = new Employee();

emp1.Name = "Saurabh";
emp2.Name = "Rahul";

Here emp1 and emp2 are two different objects created from the same class.

             Employee Class
                  │
          ┌───────┴───────┐
          ↓               ↓
       emp1 Object     emp2 Object
       Name = Saurabh  Name = Rahul

Q4. How do you create an object in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer:

We normally create an object using the new keyword, which creates an instance of the class and invokes its constructor.

Example:

Employee employee = new Employee();

There are three important parts:

Employee employee = new Employee();
   ↑        ↑          ↑
  Type    Variable   Object creation

new Employee() creates the object.

Q5. Can a class have multiple objects?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. A single class can be used to create multiple objects. Each object has its own instance state, while the class defines the common structure and behavior.

Example:

Employee emp1 = new Employee();
Employee emp2 = new Employee();

emp1.Name = "Saurabh";
emp2.Name = "Amit";

Both objects are based on the same Employee class, but their Name values are independent.

Q6. Can two objects of the same class have different values?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. Each object has its own instance state. So two objects created from the same class can contain different values for their instance fields and properties.

Example:

Employee emp1 = new Employee();
Employee emp2 = new Employee();

emp1.Name = "Saurabh";
emp2.Name = "Rahul";
emp1 → Name = Saurabh
emp2 → Name = Rahul

The class is the same, but the objects maintain separate instance state.

Q7. What are instance members of a class?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Instance members are members that belong to a particular object rather than the class itself. Each object gets its own instance state. Fields, properties, and methods can be instance members.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} is working");
    }
}

Here Name and Work() are instance members.

We access them through an object:

Employee emp = new Employee();

emp.Name = "Saurabh";
emp.Work();

Q8. What is the difference between instance members and static members?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Instance members belong to an individual object, so we access them using an object reference. Static members belong to the class itself and can be accessed using the class name without creating an object.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }  // Instance member

    public static string Company = "ABC"; // Static member
}

Usage:

Employee emp = new Employee();

emp.Name = "Saurabh";       // Instance member

Employee.Company;           // Static member

Think:

Instance → Object-specific
Static   → Class-level

Q9. Does creating a class create an object?

Interview-Ready Answer:

No. Defining a class only creates the type definition or blueprint. An object is created when we instantiate that class, normally using the new keyword.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

At this point, we have defined the class but haven't created an Employee object.

Object creation happens here:

Employee emp = new Employee();

Q10. Where is an object stored in memory?

Interview-Ready Answer:

For a typical class instance, the object is allocated on the managed heap, while the variable holding the reference can be stored separately depending on its context. The .NET Garbage Collector manages the object's lifetime on the managed heap.

For an interview, avoid saying simply:

"The object is always on the heap and the reference is always on the stack."

That's an oversimplification. The exact storage behavior depends on context and runtime optimizations.

Example:

Employee emp = new Employee();

Conceptually:

emp
 │
 │ reference
 ↓
Managed Heap
┌─────────────────┐
│ Employee Object │
│ Name            │
└─────────────────┘

This becomes more important when we reach Value vs Reference Types and Runtime / Memory later in our roadmap.

Q11. What happens when you create an object using new?

Interview-Ready Answer:

When we use new for a class, memory is allocated for the object, its instance members are initialized, and the appropriate constructor is executed. The resulting reference is then assigned to the variable.

Example:

Employee emp = new Employee();

Conceptually:

new Employee()
      ↓
Object allocated
      ↓
Members initialized
      ↓
Constructor executes
      ↓
Reference returned
      ↓
emp stores the reference

Q12. Can a class exist without creating an object?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. A class can be defined without creating any objects from it. Also, classes containing only static members can be used without creating instances.

Example:

public class MathHelper
{
    public static int Add(int a, int b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }
}

We can call:

int result = MathHelper.Add(10, 20);

No object is required because Add() is static.

Q13. Can one object reference another object?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. A class can contain a reference to another object. This is a fundamental concept behind composition and relationships between objects.

Example:

public class Engine
{
    public void Start()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Engine started");
    }
}

public class Car
{
    private Engine engine = new Engine();

    public void StartCar()
    {
        engine.Start();
    }
}

Here:

Car Object
   │
   └── Engine Object

This leads directly into our later topic Composition.

🔥 Most Important Interview Differences

Class vs Object

ClassObject
Blueprint/templateInstance of a class
Defines structure and behaviorContains actual state
Doesn't represent a specific entityRepresents a specific entity
Used to create objectsCreated from a class

Instance vs Static

InstanceStatic
Belongs to an objectBelongs to the type
Requires an object to accessUsually accessed using class name
Each object has its own instance stateOne class-level member
emp.NameEmployee.Company

🎯 Questions You Should Be Able to Answer Now

For interviews, make sure you can answer these naturally:

  1. What is a class?
  1. What is an object?
  1. Class vs object?
  1. How do you create an object in C#?
  1. Can one class have multiple objects?
  1. Can objects of the same class have different state?
  1. What are instance members?
  1. Instance vs static members?
  1. Does defining a class create an object?
  1. What happens when new is used?
  1. Where is a class object stored?
  1. Can you use a class without creating an object?
  1. Can an object contain another object?

⭐ Interviewer's likely deeper chain

A typical interviewer could take you from:

Class & Object

→ What is an object?

→ How is it created?

→ What happens internally when new is used?

→ Where is it stored?

→ What is a reference?

→ Class vs struct?

→ Value type vs reference type?

→ What happens when you copy an object reference?

→ How is the object eventually removed from memory?

We'll cover those deeper concepts later in the exact sequence you've defined, so don't worry about memorizing the runtime/memory details yet.

2. Fields & Properties

This topic is very important because interviewers often use it to test whether you understand how C# objects store and expose data, not just the syntax.

Common Questions

Q1. What is a field in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A field is a variable declared inside a class or struct that is used to store the state or data of an object. Fields can have access modifiers such as private, public, or protected.

Real-World Example:

public class Employee
{
    private string name;
    private int age;
}

Here, name and age are fields that represent the employee's internal state.

In real applications, fields are commonly kept private and accessed through properties.

Q2. What is a property in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A property provides controlled access to data. It uses get and set accessors to read or modify a value, and unlike a simple public field, it allows us to add validation or custom logic.

Real-World Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

We can use it like:

Employee employee = new Employee();

employee.Name = "Saurabh";

Console.WriteLine(employee.Name);

The property provides a controlled way to access the employee's name.

Q3. What is the difference between a field and a property?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A field directly stores data, whereas a property provides an abstraction over data access. Properties can contain logic inside their get and set accessors, while fields cannot have accessor logic.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    private int age;             // Field

    public int Age               // Property
    {
        get { return age; }
        set
        {
            if (value >= 18)
                age = value;
        }
    }
}

Here:

Field     → stores the actual value
Property  → controls access to the value

Interview tip

Don't say:

"A property is just a method."

A property is a member with accessors and has property semantics in C#. Its accessors are implemented as methods at the IL/runtime level, but you should distinguish the language feature from an ordinary method.

Q4. Why do we generally prefer properties over public fields?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Properties provide encapsulation and flexibility. We can control whether a value is readable or writable, add validation, change the implementation later, and expose only the access that is required.

Real-World Example:

Instead of:

public int Age;

we can use:

public int Age
{
    get { return age; }
    set
    {
        if (value >= 18)
            age = value;
    }
}

Now the class can control invalid values.

For example, an Employee object shouldn't allow:

employee.Age = -10;

The property gives us a place to enforce the rule.

Q5. What are auto-implemented properties?

Interview-Ready Answer:

An auto-implemented property is a property where C# automatically provides the backing storage, so we don't need to explicitly declare a field.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public int Age { get; set; }
}

We don't explicitly write:

private string name;
private int age;

The compiler provides the necessary backing storage for these auto-properties.

Real-world usage

DTOs and request/response models commonly use auto-properties:

public class EmployeeDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

Q6. What is a backing field?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A backing field is a field used internally to store the value exposed through a property. We use it when the property needs custom logic.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    private string name;

    public string Name
    {
        get
        {
            return name;
        }
        set
        {
            if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
                name = value;
        }
    }
}

Here:

Name property
     ↓
private name field
     ↓
actual stored value

Q7. Can a property have only a getter?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. A property can be read-only by exposing only a get accessor.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; }

    public Employee(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }
}

Outside the class:

employee.Name = "Rahul"; // ❌ Not allowed

Real-World Example

An employee's EmployeeId might be assigned when the object is created and should not be changed afterward.

public int EmployeeId { get; }

This supports controlled and potentially immutable state.

Q8. What is a property with private set?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A property with a private setter can be read from outside the class, but its value can only be changed from within the class.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; private set; }

    public Employee(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }

    public void ChangeName(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }
}

Outside:

employee.Name;             // ✅ Read

employee.Name = "Rahul";   // ❌ Cannot set directly

Real-world scenario

This is useful when the class needs to control how its state changes.

For example:

public OrderStatus Status { get; private set; }

Only the Order class should decide how the status changes.

Q9. What is an init property?

Interview-Ready Answer:

An init accessor allows a property to be assigned during object initialization, but it cannot normally be changed afterward.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; init; }
}

We can initialize it:

var employee = new Employee
{
    Name = "Saurabh"
};

But later:

employee.Name = "Rahul"; // ❌

Real-World Scenario

init is useful for objects whose configuration should be fixed after creation, such as configuration or immutable-style data models.

Q10. What is the difference between get; set;, get; private set;, and get; init;?

Interview-Ready Answer:

get; set; allows both reading and writing from accessible code. get; private set; allows reading publicly but restricts modification to the containing type. get; init; allows assignment during object initialization but prevents normal modification afterward.
PropertyRead outsideSet outsideSet during initialization
get; set;✅✅✅
get; private set;✅❌Constructor/class controlled
get; init;✅❌ after initialization✅

Example:

public string Name { get; set; }

public string Email { get; private set; }

public int EmployeeId { get; init; }

This is a very useful interview question because it connects properties with encapsulation.

Q11. Can a property contain logic?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. A property can contain custom logic in its get and set accessors. This is useful for validation, transformation, or calculated values.

Example:

private decimal salary;

public decimal Salary
{
    get
    {
        return salary;
    }
    set
    {
        if (value < 0)
            throw new ArgumentException("Salary cannot be negative");

        salary = value;
    }
}

Real-world scenario

In an employee-management system, we can prevent an invalid salary from being assigned.

Q12. What is a read-only property?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A read-only property exposes only a getter, so callers can read its value but cannot normally assign a new value through that property.

Example:

public int EmployeeId { get; }

It can be assigned inside the constructor:

public Employee(int id)
{
    EmployeeId = id;
}

This is useful when a value should remain fixed after object construction.

Q13. What is a calculated property?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A calculated property doesn't need to store its own value. Instead, it calculates and returns a value based on other data.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public decimal Salary { get; set; }

    public decimal AnnualSalary
    {
        get
        {
            return Salary * 12;
        }
    }
}

Usage:

employee.AnnualSalary;

There doesn't need to be a separate field for AnnualSalary.

Real-world scenario

In an employee system:

Monthly Salary → ₹50,000
Annual Salary  → ₹6,00,000

AnnualSalary can be calculated from Salary.

Q14. What is the difference between a field and an auto-property internally?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A field directly represents storage declared by the programmer. An auto-property is a language feature where the compiler generates a hidden backing field to store the property's value.

Example:

public string Name { get; set; }

Conceptually, the compiler provides backing storage for the property.

You don't normally need to manage that field yourself.

Q15. Can properties be static?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. Properties can be static, in which case they belong to the type rather than a particular object.

Example:

public class Application
{
    public static string Version { get; set; }
}

Usage:

Application.Version = "1.0";

No Application object is required.

Q16. Can properties be virtual or abstract?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. Properties can be virtual, override, or abstract, just like methods.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public virtual string Role { get; set; }
}

A derived class can override it:

public class Manager : Employee
{
    public override string Role
    {
        get { return "Manager"; }
        set { }
    }
}

This becomes especially important when we study Inheritance and Polymorphism.

Q17. What is an expression-bodied property?

Interview-Ready Answer:

An expression-bodied property is a concise syntax for a read-only calculated property.

Example:

public decimal AnnualSalary => Salary * 12;

Instead of:

public decimal AnnualSalary
{
    get
    {
        return Salary * 12;
    }
}

Both express the same basic idea; the first is simply more concise.

Q18. What is the difference between a field and a property in terms of encapsulation?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A field directly exposes storage, while a property allows us to control access to that state. Therefore, properties are generally preferred for exposing an object's data because they provide better encapsulation.

Real-world scenario:

Instead of exposing:

public decimal Balance;

use:

public decimal Balance { get; private set; }

Now external code can read the balance but cannot directly modify it.

The class can control changes through methods such as:

public void Deposit(decimal amount)
{
    // validation
    Balance += amount;
}

This is a practical example of encapsulation through properties.

🔥 Most Important Interview Questions

If you're short on time, make sure you can confidently answer these:

  1. What is a field?
  1. What is a property?
  1. Field vs Property?
  1. Why prefer properties over public fields?
  1. What is an auto-implemented property?
  1. What is a backing field?
  1. get; set; vs get; private set;
  1. What is init?
  1. private set vs init
  1. Can properties contain logic?
  1. What is a read-only property?
  1. What is a calculated property?
  1. Can properties be static/virtual/abstract?
  1. How do properties support encapsulation?

🎯 Interview Mental Model

Remember this simple chain:

Field
  ↓
Stores state
  ↓
Property
  ↓
Controls access to state
  ↓
Getter / Setter
  ↓
Validation / Business Rules
  ↓
Encapsulation

One interview-ready statement to remember

"Fields are primarily used for internal storage, while properties provide controlled access to an object's data. In C#, I generally keep fields private and expose properties when I need to provide controlled access, validation, or abstraction over the underlying state."

That is a strong, concise answer for a .NET interview.

3. Constructors

Constructors are a high-priority C# interview topic because they connect directly to object creation, initialization, inheritance, dependency injection, and object lifetime.

We'll cover the questions most likely to come up in a 3+ YOE .NET interview.

Common Questions

Q1. What is a constructor in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A constructor is a special member of a class that is automatically called when an object is created. It is mainly used to initialize the object's state and ensure that the object starts in a valid state.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; }

    public Employee(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }
}

Creating the object:

Employee employee = new Employee("Saurabh");

The constructor runs automatically when new Employee() is executed.

Real-world scenario

In an employee-management application, an employee shouldn't exist without a valid name or ID. The constructor can ensure these required values are provided when the object is created.

Q2. Why do we use constructors?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Constructors are used to initialize an object's required data and establish a valid initial state. They are also commonly used to initialize dependencies and configuration required by the object.

Example:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        this.repository = repository;
    }
}

Here the constructor ensures that OrderService receives the repository it needs.

This is also how constructor dependency injection works in ASP.NET Core.

Q3. What are the different types of constructors in C#?

For interviews, know these:

  1. Default / parameterless constructor
  1. Parameterized constructor
  1. Constructor overloading
  1. Copy-constructor pattern
  1. Static constructor
  1. Private constructor
  1. Constructor chaining
  1. Primary constructor

Interview-Ready Answer

C# supports parameterless and parameterized constructors, and we can overload constructors. It also supports static and private constructors. Constructors can be chained using this or base, and modern C# also supports primary constructors.

Q4. What is a parameterless constructor?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A parameterless constructor is a constructor that doesn't take any parameters. It initializes an object without requiring input values.
public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public Employee()
    {
        Name = "Unknown";
    }
}

Usage:

Employee employee = new Employee();

Important interview point

If you don't explicitly declare any instance constructor, C# generally provides an implicit public parameterless constructor for a class.

But once you declare an instance constructor yourself, the compiler doesn't automatically add that constructor for you.

Q5. What is a parameterized constructor?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A parameterized constructor accepts parameters and uses them to initialize the object's required state.
public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; }
    public string Name { get; }

    public Employee(int id, string name)
    {
        Id = id;
        Name = name;
    }
}

Usage:

Employee employee = new Employee(101, "Saurabh");

Real-world scenario

For an Order object:

public Order(int orderId, int customerId)
{
    OrderId = orderId;
    CustomerId = customerId;
}

The constructor guarantees that an order is created with its required identifiers.

Q6. What is constructor overloading?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Constructor overloading means defining multiple constructors in the same class with different parameter lists. It allows objects to be initialized in different ways.
public class Employee
{
    public Employee()
    {
    }

    public Employee(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }

    public Employee(int id, string name)
    {
        Id = id;
        Name = name;
    }

    public int Id { get; }
    public string Name { get; }
}

Now we can create the object in different ways:

var e1 = new Employee();

var e2 = new Employee("Saurabh");

var e3 = new Employee(101, "Saurabh");

Real-world scenario

An application might allow creating an employee with minimal information or with complete employee information.

Q7. What is constructor chaining?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Constructor chaining means one constructor calls another constructor in the same class using this, or a base-class constructor using base. It helps avoid duplicate initialization logic.

Using this

public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; }
    public string Name { get; }

    public Employee()
        : this(0, "Unknown")
    {
    }

    public Employee(int id, string name)
    {
        Id = id;
        Name = name;
    }
}

Here:

Employee()
    ↓
this(0, "Unknown")
    ↓
Employee(int, string)

Real-world benefit

If multiple constructors contain the same initialization logic, chaining allows us to keep that logic in one place.

Q8. What is the difference between this and base in constructors?

Interview-Ready Answer:

this is used to call another constructor in the same class, while base is used to call a constructor of the base class.

this

public Employee()
    : this(0, "Unknown")
{
}

Calls another constructor in the same class.

base

public class Employee : Person
{
    public Employee(string name)
        : base(name)
    {
    }
}

Calls the constructor of Person.

Easy way to remember

this → same class
base → parent/base class

Q9. Which constructor executes first in inheritance?

Interview-Ready Answer:

When a derived-class object is created, the base-class constructor executes before the derived-class constructor.

Example:

public class Person
{
    public Person()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Person constructor");
    }
}

public class Employee : Person
{
    public Employee()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee constructor");
    }
}
Employee employee = new Employee();

Output:

Person constructor
Employee constructor

Real-world explanation

The base part of the object needs to be initialized before the derived class can initialize its own state.

Q10. Can constructors be inherited?

Interview-Ready Answer:

No. Constructors are not inherited by derived classes. However, a derived-class constructor can explicitly call a base-class constructor using the base keyword.
public class Person
{
    public Person(string name)
    {
    }
}

public class Employee : Person
{
    public Employee(string name)
        : base(name)
    {
    }
}

The Employee constructor isn't inherited from Person; it explicitly invokes the Person constructor.

Q11. Can a constructor be private?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. A constructor can be private. This prevents other classes from directly creating instances using that constructor.
public class Singleton
{
    private Singleton()
    {
    }
}

Real-world use

Private constructors are commonly seen in patterns such as Singleton, factory-based object creation, or classes that expose only static behavior.

For example:

public class Configuration
{
    private Configuration()
    {
    }

    public static Configuration Create()
    {
        return new Configuration();
    }
}

The class controls how instances are created.

Q12. What is a static constructor?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A static constructor is used to initialize static data or perform one-time initialization for a type. It has no access modifier and takes no parameters.
public class Application
{
    public static string Version;

    static Application()
    {
        Version = "1.0";
    }
}

Important points

A static constructor:

  • Has the same name as the class.
  • Has no parameters.
  • Cannot have an access modifier.
  • Cannot be called directly.
  • Runs automatically before the type is first used in a way that requires static initialization.

Real-world scenario

Suppose an application has static configuration:

public static string ApplicationName;

static Application()
{
    ApplicationName = "Order Management System";
}

The initialization can happen automatically when the type is first used.

Q13. Can a class have both static and instance constructors?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. A class can have a static constructor for type-level initialization and one or more instance constructors for initializing individual objects.
public class Employee
{
    static Employee()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Static constructor");
    }

    public Employee()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Instance constructor");
    }
}

Conceptually:

Type initialization
       ↓
Static constructor
       ↓
Object creation
       ↓
Instance constructor

Q14. Can a static class have a constructor?

Interview-Ready Answer:

Yes. A static class can have a static constructor, but it cannot have an instance constructor because you cannot create instances of a static class.
public static class Logger
{
    static Logger()
    {
        // Static initialization
    }
}

Q15. Can constructors be virtual, abstract, or override?

Interview-Ready Answer:

No. Constructors cannot be virtual, abstract, or overridden because constructors are responsible for creating and initializing an object, while virtual dispatch applies to instance member behavior after the object is being constructed.

Invalid:

public virtual Employee() // ❌
{
}

Interview follow-up

Why can't constructors be virtual?

Because the derived object must first be initialized through its construction chain. Virtual dispatch is not used to select constructors.

Q16. Can a constructor return a value?

Interview-Ready Answer:

No. A constructor doesn't have a return type, not even void. Its purpose is to initialize the object rather than return a value.

Correct:

public Employee()
{
}

Incorrect:

public void Employee() // This is a method, not a constructor
{
}

Q17. What happens if I declare a method with the same name as the class but give it a return type?

Interview-Ready Answer:

It is treated as a method, not a constructor. A constructor must have exactly the same name as the class and must not specify a return type.
public class Employee
{
    public Employee()
    {
        // Constructor
    }

    public void Employee()
    {
        // Method
    }
}

Q18. What happens if I don't define a constructor?

Interview-Ready Answer:

If a class has no instance constructors declared, the compiler generally provides an implicit public parameterless constructor.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

Conceptually, you can use:

Employee employee = new Employee();

But if you define:

public Employee(string name)
{
    Name = name;
}

the compiler will no longer provide the implicit parameterless constructor.

Therefore:

new Employee(); // ❌

unless you explicitly define a parameterless constructor.

Q19. What is the difference between constructor and method?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A constructor initializes an object and is automatically invoked during object creation. A method represents an operation or behavior and is explicitly called after the object exists.
ConstructorMethod
Initializes an objectPerforms an operation
Called during object creationCalled explicitly
No return typeCan have a return type
Same name as classCan have any valid name
Cannot be inheritedMethods can be inherited
Cannot be virtualCan be virtual

Real-world example

Employee employee = new Employee("Saurabh");

The constructor initializes the employee.

employee.CalculateSalary();

The method performs an operation on the already-created object.

Q20. What is a primary constructor?

Interview-Ready Answer:

A primary constructor provides a concise way to declare constructor parameters directly in the class or struct declaration. Those parameters can then be used by the type's members.

Example:

public class Employee(string name, int id)
{
    public string Name => name;
    public int Id => id;
}

This reduces boilerplate compared with a traditional constructor.

Real-world scenario

It can be useful for small services or immutable-style objects where constructor parameters directly represent required dependencies or state.

For example:

public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
{
    public void CreateOrder()
    {
        repository.Save();
    }
}

This syntax is particularly relevant to modern C# interviews.

🔥 Most Important Constructor Questions

For your interview preparation, prioritize these:

Must Know

  1. What is a constructor?
  1. Why do we use constructors?
  1. Parameterless vs parameterized constructor
  1. Constructor overloading
  1. Constructor chaining
  1. this vs base
  1. Constructor execution order in inheritance
  1. Can constructors be inherited?
  1. Can constructors be private?
  1. Static constructor
  1. What happens if no constructor is defined?
  1. Constructor vs method

Strong Interview Level

  1. Can constructors be virtual/abstract/override?
  1. Can a static class have a constructor?
  1. Can a class have static and instance constructors?
  1. Why can't constructors have return types?
  1. Primary constructors

🎯 Important Interview Scenario

An interviewer may give you this:

public class Person
{
    public Person()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Person");
    }
}

public class Employee : Person
{
    public Employee()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee");
    }
}

Employee emp = new Employee();

Expected answer:

Person
Employee

Because the base-class constructor executes first, followed by the derived-class constructor.

⭐ One answer worth memorizing

If the interviewer asks:

"Explain constructors in C#."

You can say:

"A constructor is a special member of a class that is automatically called when an object is created. I use constructors mainly to initialize required state and dependencies and ensure the object starts in a valid state. C# supports parameterless, parameterized, overloaded, static, and private constructors, and constructors can be chained using this or base. In inheritance, the base constructor executes before the derived constructor."

That's concise enough for an interview while giving the interviewer several directions for follow-up questions.

4. Access Modifiers in C#

Access modifiers are very common interview questions, especially for 3+ YOE .NET roles.

We’ll cover them in interview order:

  1. What are access modifiers?
  1. public
  1. private
  1. protected
  1. internal
  1. protected internal
  1. private protected
  1. Default access modifiers
  1. Class vs member access
  1. private vs protected
  1. protected internal vs private protected
  1. Can an interface member be private?
  1. Can a constructor be private?
  1. Can a class be private?
  1. Real-world usage
  1. Common tricky interview questions

1. What are access modifiers in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer

Access modifiers define the visibility and accessibility of classes, methods, properties, fields, and other members in C#.

They help implement encapsulation and control how much of a class or component is exposed to other parts of the application.

Main access modifiers

ModifierAccessible from
publicAnywhere
privateSame class/struct
protectedSame class + derived classes
internalSame assembly
protected internalSame assembly OR derived class
private protectedSame assembly AND derived class

Easy memory trick

public            → Everyone
private           → Same class
protected         → Child classes
internal          → Same assembly
protected internal → Same assembly OR child class
private protected → Same assembly AND child class

2. What is public?

Interview-Ready Answer

public members can be accessed from anywhere, as long as the containing type itself is accessible.

Example

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Display()
    {
        Console.WriteLine(Name);
    }
}
Employee employee = new Employee();

employee.Name = "Saurabh";
employee.Display();

Both Name and Display() are accessible from outside the class.

Real-world example

A service method that should be called by a controller:

public class EmployeeService
{
    public Employee GetEmployee(int id)
    {
        // Business logic
    }
}

The controller can call:

var employee = employeeService.GetEmployee(10);

Follow-up

Q: Should every member be public?

No. We should expose only what consumers need. Internal implementation details should generally remain private or protected.

3. What is private?

Interview-Ready Answer

private members can be accessed only within the containing type. They cannot be directly accessed from outside the class or by derived classes.

Example

public class BankAccount
{
    private decimal balance;

    public void Deposit(decimal amount)
    {
        balance += amount;
    }
}

This is not allowed:

BankAccount account = new BankAccount();

account.balance = 10000; // ❌

But this is allowed:

account.Deposit(10000);

Why use private?

To hide implementation details and protect object state.

Real-world example

public class Order
{
    private decimal totalAmount;

    public void AddItem(decimal price)
    {
        totalAmount += price;
    }

    public decimal GetTotal()
    {
        return totalAmount;
    }
}

The caller cannot directly modify totalAmount.

4. What is protected?

Interview-Ready Answer

protected members are accessible inside the containing class and inside classes derived from it.

Example

public class Vehicle
{
    protected string brand = "Toyota";
}

public class Car : Vehicle
{
    public void DisplayBrand()
    {
        Console.WriteLine(brand);
    }
}

Car can access brand because it inherits from Vehicle.

But:

Vehicle vehicle = new Vehicle();

vehicle.brand; // ❌

A normal external class cannot access it directly.

Real-world example

A base service can expose reusable state to derived services:

public class BaseService
{
    protected readonly ILogger logger;
}

public class OrderService : BaseService
{
    public void ProcessOrder()
    {
        logger.LogInformation("Processing order");
    }
}

5. What is internal?

Interview-Ready Answer

internal means the member or type can be accessed from anywhere within the same assembly, but not directly from another assembly.

An assembly is typically a compiled .dll or .exe.

Example

internal class PaymentHelper
{
    internal void ProcessPayment()
    {
    }
}

Another project referencing this DLL cannot directly access PaymentHelper.

Real-world example

Suppose you have:

MyApplication
│
├── Controllers
├── Services
├── Repositories
└── InternalHelpers

You may keep implementation-specific classes internal so other projects cannot use them.

6. What is protected internal?

This is a very common tricky interview question.

Interview-Ready Answer

protected internal means a member can be accessed either from the same assembly or from a derived class, even if that derived class is in another assembly.

The key word is OR.

Same assembly
      OR
Derived class

Example

public class BaseClass
{
    protected internal void Display()
    {
    }
}

Accessible:

Same assembly                  → Yes
Derived class same assembly    → Yes
Derived class different assembly → Yes
Unrelated class different assembly → No

Memory trick

protected internal = protected OR internal

7. What is private protected?

Interview-Ready Answer

private protected means the member can be accessed only by derived classes within the same assembly.

The key word is AND.

Same assembly
      AND
Derived class

Example

public class BaseClass
{
    private protected void Display()
    {
    }
}

A derived class in the same assembly can access it.

A derived class in another assembly cannot.

Memory trick

protected internal → OR
private protected   → AND

This distinction is frequently tested.

8. protected internal vs private protected

Featureprotected internalprivate protected
Same assembly✅✅
Derived class same assembly✅✅
Derived class different assembly✅❌
Unrelated class same assembly✅❌
LogicORAND

Interview answer

protected internal provides access when either the caller is in the same assembly or is a derived class. private protected is more restrictive because both conditions must be satisfied.

9. What are the default access modifiers in C#?

Very important interview question.

Class

If you don't specify an access modifier for a top-level class:

class Employee
{
}

It is:

internal

So:

internal class Employee
{
}

Class members

For members:

class Employee
{
    string name;
    void Display()
    {
    }
}

name and Display() are:

private

by default.

Important table

DeclarationDefault
Top-level classinternal
Class memberprivate
Struct memberprivate
Interface memberGenerally public for declared interface members, subject to modern C# rules

For interviews, remember:

Top-level class → internal; class members → private.

10. What is the difference between private and protected?

Interview-Ready Answer

private restricts access to the containing class only, whereas protected also allows derived classes to access the member.

Example

class Parent
{
    private int a;
    protected int b;
}

class Child : Parent
{
    void Test()
    {
        // a = 10; // ❌
        b = 20;    // ✅
    }
}

Easy way to remember

private   → Me only
protected → Me + my children

11. Can a derived class access a private member of the base class?

Answer

No, not directly.
class Parent
{
    private int value = 10;
}

class Child : Parent
{
    void Test()
    {
        // value = 20; // ❌
    }
}

If the base class wants derived classes to access it, use protected.

class Parent
{
    protected int value = 10;
}

12. Can a private member be accessed through a public method?

Yes.

This is actually a common encapsulation pattern.

public class BankAccount
{
    private decimal balance;

    public decimal GetBalance()
    {
        return balance;
    }
}

The field is private, but its value is exposed through a public method.

Interview answer

Yes. A private member cannot be accessed directly from outside, but a public method or property inside the class can provide controlled access to it.

This is one of the foundations of encapsulation.

13. Can a constructor be private?

Yes.

public class Singleton
{
    private Singleton()
    {
    }
}

Now external code cannot do:

var obj = new Singleton(); // ❌

Why use a private constructor?

Common reasons include:

  • Singleton pattern
  • Factory pattern
  • Preventing direct object creation
  • Utility/static-style classes

Real-world example

public class Configuration
{
    private Configuration()
    {
    }

    public static Configuration Create()
    {
        return new Configuration();
    }
}

Objects must be created through the controlled method.

14. Can a class be private?

Top-level class

❌ No.

This is invalid:

private class Employee
{
}

A top-level class can generally be:

public
internal

Nested class

A nested class can be private:

public class Outer
{
    private class Inner
    {
    }
}

Interview answer

A top-level class cannot be private, but a nested class can be private because its accessibility is relative to the containing type.

15. Can an interface be private?

For a top-level interface, you cannot declare it private.

private interface IEmployee // ❌
{
}

But a nested interface can have restricted accessibility.

Modern C# also allows more nuanced accessibility for individual interface members in specific cases, but for interviews, the key point is:

A top-level interface cannot be private; nested interfaces can have access modifiers.

16. Can an abstract class have private members?

Yes.

public abstract class Animal
{
    private string name;

    public void SetName(string name)
    {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

Abstract classes can contain:

  • private members
  • protected members
  • public members
  • fields
  • properties
  • methods
  • constructors

17. Can an interface have private methods?

Modern C#

Yes, modern C# supports private interface members, mainly for sharing implementation between default interface methods.

Example:

public interface ILogger
{
    void Log()
    {
        WriteMessage();
    }

    private void WriteMessage()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Logging...");
    }
}

However, for interviews:

Historically interface members were primarily public contracts, but modern C# allows private interface members for internal implementation support.

Don't confuse this with the traditional interview rule that interface contract members are public.

18. Why are access modifiers important?

Interview-Ready Answer

Access modifiers provide controlled visibility. They help us hide implementation details, protect object state, reduce coupling, and expose only the APIs that consumers actually need.

Real-world example

Consider:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly OrderRepository repository;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository repository)
    {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    public Order GetOrder(int id)
    {
        return repository.GetById(id);
    }

    private void ValidateOrder(Order order)
    {
        // Internal implementation
    }
}

A controller only needs:

GetOrder()

It doesn't need direct access to:

repository
ValidateOrder()

So we keep those private.

19. Access Modifiers and Encapsulation

This is a likely follow-up because your next topic is Encapsulation.

Interview answer

Access modifiers are one of the mechanisms used to achieve encapsulation. They allow us to control which parts of an object are exposed and which implementation details remain hidden.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    private decimal salary;

    public decimal GetSalary()
    {
        return salary;
    }

    public void IncreaseSalary(decimal amount)
    {
        if (amount > 0)
        {
            salary += amount;
        }
    }
}

Instead of:

employee.salary = -50000; // ❌

we control modification through:

employee.IncreaseSalary(5000);

20. Most Important Interview Question: Explain all C# access modifiers

Interview-Ready Answer

C# has six main access levels: public, private, protected, internal, protected internal, and private protected.

public is accessible everywhere. private is accessible only within the containing type. protected is accessible within the type and derived types. internal is accessible within the same assembly. protected internal allows access from the same assembly or from derived types. private protected allows access only from derived types within the same assembly.

That's a very good 30-second interview answer.

⭐ Priority for Your Interviews

For your 3+ YOE / Senior .NET interviews, prioritize these:

🔴 Must Know

  1. public
  1. private
  1. protected
  1. internal
  1. protected internal
  1. private protected
  1. private vs protected
  1. protected internal vs private protected
  1. Default access modifiers
  1. Access modifiers + encapsulation

🟡 Good to Know

  1. Private constructor
  1. Nested class accessibility
  1. Interface accessibility
  1. Modern interface member accessibility

🧠 One-Line Memory Trick

public              → Everyone
private             → Same class
protected           → Class + derived class
internal            → Same assembly
protected internal  → Same assembly OR derived class
private protected   → Same assembly AND derived class

The two tricky ones

protected internal = OR
private protected   = AND

5. Encapsulation in C#

Encapsulation is one of the most important OOP concepts and is frequently asked in .NET interviews.

For your interview level, focus on:

  1. What is encapsulation?
  1. Why do we need encapsulation?
  1. How is encapsulation achieved in C#?
  1. Encapsulation vs data hiding
  1. Fields vs properties
  1. Private fields + public properties
  1. Validation through encapsulation
  1. Real-world example
  1. Encapsulation vs abstraction
  1. Common interview scenarios

1. What is Encapsulation?

Interview-Ready Answer

Encapsulation is the process of bundling data and the methods that operate on that data inside a class, while controlling access to the internal state.

In C#, we commonly achieve encapsulation using classes, access modifiers, properties, and methods.

Simple example

public class BankAccount
{
    private decimal balance;

    public void Deposit(decimal amount)
    {
        if (amount > 0)
        {
            balance += amount;
        }
    }

    public decimal GetBalance()
    {
        return balance;
    }
}

Here:

  • balance → hidden from outside
  • Deposit() → controlled way to modify it
  • GetBalance() → controlled way to read it

2. Why do we need Encapsulation?

Interview-Ready Answer

Encapsulation protects an object's internal state from uncontrolled modification and allows us to expose only the operations that are required.

It improves security, maintainability, validation, and control over data.

Without encapsulation:

public class BankAccount
{
    public decimal Balance;
}

Anyone could do:

account.Balance = -50000;

With encapsulation:

public class BankAccount
{
    private decimal balance;

    public void Deposit(decimal amount)
    {
        if (amount <= 0)
            throw new ArgumentException("Invalid amount");

        balance += amount;
    }
}

Now the class controls how its state changes.

3. How do you achieve Encapsulation in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer

In C#, encapsulation is commonly achieved by using access modifiers, private fields, properties, and methods.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    private decimal salary;

    public decimal Salary
    {
        get { return salary; }
        private set { salary = value; }
    }

    public void IncreaseSalary(decimal amount)
    {
        if (amount > 0)
        {
            Salary += amount;
        }
    }
}

Outside code can read Salary, but cannot directly set it.

4. Is private alone enough for Encapsulation?

Interview-Ready Answer

No. private provides access control, but encapsulation is broader. Encapsulation combines data and behavior inside a type and provides controlled access to that data.

For example:

private decimal balance;

is data hiding.

But:

public void Deposit(decimal amount)
{
    if (amount > 0)
        balance += amount;
}

provides controlled behavior around that data.

Together they provide effective encapsulation.

5. Encapsulation vs Data Hiding

This is a common interview follow-up.

EncapsulationData Hiding
Bundles data and behaviorRestricts direct access to data
Broader OOP conceptPart of encapsulation
Uses classes, methods, properties, access modifiersPrimarily uses access restrictions
Focuses on controlled interactionFocuses on hiding implementation/state

Interview answer

Data hiding is about restricting direct access to internal data, while encapsulation is the broader concept of combining data and behavior and controlling how they are accessed.

6. How do Properties help with Encapsulation?

Interview-Ready Answer

Properties allow us to expose controlled access to private fields instead of exposing the fields directly.

Example:

public class Employee
{
    private decimal salary;

    public decimal Salary
    {
        get
        {
            return salary;
        }
        set
        {
            if (value >= 0)
                salary = value;
        }
    }
}

Now:

employee.Salary = 50000; // ✅
employee.Salary = -1000; // ❌ validation prevents it

The class controls how the value is changed.

7. Why not make fields public?

Interview-Ready Answer

Public fields expose the internal state directly and don't provide much control over how the value is accessed or modified. Properties allow us to add validation, logging, calculations, access restrictions, and other behavior without changing the public API.

Bad design

public class Employee
{
    public decimal salary;
}

Anyone can do:

employee.salary = -10000;

Better design

public class Employee
{
    private decimal salary;

    public decimal Salary
    {
        get => salary;
        set
        {
            if (value >= 0)
                salary = value;
        }
    }
}

8. What is the difference between private set and public set?

Public setter

public decimal Salary { get; set; }

Anyone can modify it.

employee.Salary = 50000;

Private setter

public decimal Salary { get; private set; }

Anyone can read it, but only the class can modify it.

Console.WriteLine(employee.Salary); // ✅

// employee.Salary = 50000; // ❌

Interview answer

private set is useful when the object should expose a value for reading but should control when and how that value changes.

9. Real-world example: Bank Account

This is a very good example to explain encapsulation in an interview.

public class BankAccount
{
    private decimal balance;

    public decimal Balance => balance;

    public void Deposit(decimal amount)
    {
        if (amount <= 0)
            throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive.");

        balance += amount;
    }

    public void Withdraw(decimal amount)
    {
        if (amount <= 0)
            throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive.");

        if (amount > balance)
            throw new InvalidOperationException("Insufficient balance.");

        balance -= amount;
    }
}

Usage:

var account = new BankAccount();

account.Deposit(10000);
account.Withdraw(2000);

Console.WriteLine(account.Balance);

The outside code cannot directly modify:

balance

Instead, it must use:

Deposit()
Withdraw()

The class therefore maintains control over its state.

10. Can Encapsulation be achieved without properties?

Yes.

Properties are common, but they aren't mandatory.

You can use methods:

public class Account
{
    private decimal balance;

    public decimal GetBalance()
    {
        return balance;
    }

    public void Deposit(decimal amount)
    {
        balance += amount;
    }
}

Interview answer

Yes. Encapsulation can be implemented using private fields and public methods. Properties are another convenient mechanism for controlled access.

11. Can Encapsulation be achieved using only properties?

Technically, properties can provide access control, but good encapsulation is about more than simply using properties.

For example:

public decimal Balance { get; private set; }

provides controlled mutation.

But a richer domain model might expose behavior:

public void Withdraw(decimal amount)
{
    if (amount > Balance)
        throw new InvalidOperationException();

    Balance -= amount;
}

This is generally stronger because the object's rules are kept inside the object.

Good interview statement

Encapsulation isn't just about hiding fields; it's about keeping the object's state and the rules that govern that state together and controlling how consumers interact with them.

12. Encapsulation in a .NET Web API

This is especially useful for your .NET interviews.

Imagine an Order domain object:

public class Order
{
    private readonly List<OrderItem> items = new();

    public IReadOnlyCollection<OrderItem> Items => items;

    public void AddItem(OrderItem item)
    {
        if (item == null)
            throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(item));

        items.Add(item);
    }
}

Instead of exposing:

public List<OrderItem> Items { get; set; }

we prevent external code from freely replacing or modifying the collection.

The object controls how items are added.

This is particularly useful when implementing business rules.

13. What is the benefit of Encapsulation in large applications?

Interview-Ready Answer

Encapsulation reduces the number of places that can directly modify internal state. This makes business rules easier to maintain and reduces unintended side effects when the application grows.

For example:

Without encapsulation:

Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Repository
   ↓
Anyone can modify object state

With encapsulation:

Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Domain Object
   ↓
Controlled business operations

The object's rules stay inside the object.

14. Encapsulation vs Abstraction

This is a very common interview question.

Encapsulation

Focuses on:

How do we protect and control data/state?

Example:

private decimal balance;

Abstraction

Focuses on:

What should the consumer know/use while hiding unnecessary implementation details?

Example:

public interface IPaymentService
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

The consumer knows:

Pay()

but doesn't need to know how payment processing works internally.

Comparison

EncapsulationAbstraction
Protects internal stateHides unnecessary implementation details
Controls accessDefines essential behavior
Uses access modifiers/properties/methodsUses interfaces/abstract classes and APIs
Focus: How data is accessedFocus: What is exposed

Strong interview answer

Encapsulation is mainly about protecting and controlling an object's state, while abstraction is about exposing essential behavior and hiding implementation complexity.

15. Is Encapsulation the same as making everything private?

No.

This is a common trap.

Bad answer:

"Encapsulation means making all fields private."

Better answer:

Encapsulation doesn't mean making everything private. It means controlling access to an object's state and behavior and exposing only what consumers need.

For example:

public void Withdraw(decimal amount)

should be public because consumers need that operation.

But:

private decimal balance;

should remain private because consumers shouldn't directly modify it.

16. Can a class expose a public field and still be encapsulated?

Technically, a class can still encapsulate some other state/behavior, but a public field itself provides no access control over that field.

For interview purposes:

A public field weakens encapsulation because external code can directly modify the object's state.

Prefer:

private decimal balance;

public decimal Balance => balance;

over:

public decimal Balance;

17. What happens if encapsulation is poor?

Suppose:

public class Employee
{
    public decimal Salary;
    public int Age;
    public string Department;
}

Any code can do:

employee.Salary = -50000;
employee.Age = -10;
employee.Department = null;

The class has little control over its state.

With encapsulation:

public class Employee
{
    public decimal Salary { get; private set; }

    public void UpdateSalary(decimal salary)
    {
        if (salary < 0)
            throw new ArgumentException();

        Salary = salary;
    }
}

Now business rules are centralized.

18. Most Common Interview Question

"Explain encapsulation with a real-world example."

Strong 30-second answer

Encapsulation means bundling data and the operations that work on that data inside a class and controlling how the internal state can be accessed.

For example, in a BankAccount class, I would keep balance private and expose methods like Deposit() and Withdraw(). These methods can validate the amount and enforce business rules. This prevents external code from directly setting an invalid balance and keeps the object's state consistent.

That's a very interview-friendly answer.

⭐ Priority for Your 3+ YOE Interviews

🔴 Must Know

  • Definition of encapsulation
  • Why encapsulation is required
  • Private fields + public properties
  • private set
  • Encapsulation using methods
  • Encapsulation vs data hiding
  • Encapsulation vs abstraction
  • Real-world example
  • How encapsulation protects business rules

🟡 Strong Interview Level

  • Encapsulation in domain models
  • IReadOnlyCollection
  • Controlling collection mutation
  • Why public fields are generally avoided
  • Encapsulation in Web API/service architecture

🧠 One-line memory trick

Encapsulation = Keep state + behavior together, hide internal state, and expose controlled ways to interact with the object.

6. Abstraction in C#

Abstraction is one of the four core OOP concepts and is very frequently asked in .NET interviews.

For your 3+ YOE interviews, you should be able to explain it using both real-world examples and C# interfaces/abstract classes.

1. What is Abstraction?

Interview-Ready Answer

Abstraction means exposing only the essential functionality to the consumer while hiding unnecessary implementation details.

In C#, abstraction is mainly achieved using interfaces and abstract classes.

Simple real-world example

When you use an ATM:

You know:
→ Withdraw money
→ Deposit money
→ Check balance

You don't need to know:
→ How the bank verifies the transaction
→ How the database is updated
→ How the transaction is processed internally

That's abstraction.

2. Why do we need Abstraction?

Interview-Ready Answer

Abstraction reduces complexity by hiding implementation details and exposing only the functionality that consumers need. It also helps create loosely coupled and maintainable applications.

For example, instead of exposing:

Validate card
Connect to bank
Check balance
Debit account
Update transaction
Generate receipt

we expose:

Withdraw(amount);

The caller doesn't need to know the internal process.

3. How do we achieve Abstraction in C#?

The two primary mechanisms are:

Abstraction
   │
   ├── Abstract Classes
   │
   └── Interfaces

Abstract class

public abstract class Payment
{
    public abstract void Pay(decimal amount);
}

Interface

public interface IPaymentService
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

Both define what should be done without requiring the consumer to know the implementation details.

4. What is an Abstract Class?

Interview-Ready Answer

An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated directly. It is designed to act as a base class and can contain both abstract members without implementation and concrete members with implementation. Microsoft Learn

Example:

public abstract class Payment
{
    public abstract void Pay(decimal amount);

    public void LogPayment()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Payment logged");
    }
}

A derived class provides the implementation:

public class CreditCardPayment : Payment
{
    public override void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Paid {amount} using Credit Card");
    }
}

You cannot do:

Payment payment = new Payment(); // ❌

But you can do:

Payment payment = new CreditCardPayment(); // ✅

5. What is an Interface?

Interview-Ready Answer

An interface defines a contract that implementing classes or structs must fulfill. A type can implement multiple interfaces, even though it can have only one direct base class. Modern C# interfaces can also contain default implementations and other members. Microsoft Learn

Example:

public interface IPayment
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

Implementation:

public class CreditCardPayment : IPayment
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Credit card payment");
    }
}

Usage:

IPayment payment = new CreditCardPayment();

payment.Pay(1000);

The caller only depends on:

IPayment

rather than the concrete implementation.

6. Abstract Class vs Interface

This is extremely important because it connects abstraction with your upcoming topics.

Abstract ClassInterface
Cannot be instantiatedCannot be instantiated directly
Can contain implemented membersCan define contracts and, in modern C#, default implementations
Can contain fields/stateCan contain certain fields/members under modern C# rules, but is primarily used as a contract
Can have constructorsCannot have instance constructors
Supports single class inheritanceA class can implement multiple interfaces
Represents shared base behavior/stateUsually represents a capability/contract
Can use protected membersContract members without implementation are public by default

C# allows a class to inherit from only one direct base class, while it can implement multiple interfaces. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

I use an abstract class when related classes need to share common state or implementation along with some required behavior. I use an interface when I mainly want to define a contract or capability that can be implemented by otherwise unrelated types.

7. Real-World Example: Payment System

Suppose your application supports:

Credit Card
UPI
PayPal
Net Banking

Instead of making the caller understand every implementation:

public interface IPaymentService
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

Then:

public class UpiPayment : IPaymentService
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Processing UPI payment");
    }
}
public class CreditCardPayment : IPaymentService
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Processing credit card payment");
    }
}

The consumer only knows:

IPaymentService payment;

payment.Pay(5000);

It doesn't need to know how UPI or credit-card processing works internally.

That's abstraction.

8. Is Abstraction the same as Encapsulation?

No.

This is a very common interview question.

Encapsulation

Protects and controls the object's internal state.

Example:

private decimal balance;

Abstraction

Hides unnecessary implementation complexity and exposes essential functionality.

Example:

public interface IPaymentService
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

Easy comparison

EncapsulationAbstraction
Protects data/stateHides implementation complexity
Focuses on how data is accessedFocuses on what functionality is exposed
Uses access modifiers, properties, methodsUses interfaces, abstract classes
Data hiding is part of itComplexity hiding is the main idea

Easy memory trick

Encapsulation → Protect the data.

Abstraction → Hide the complexity.

9. Can an Abstract Class contain non-abstract methods?

Yes.

This is important.

public abstract class Employee
{
    public abstract void CalculateSalary();

    public void DisplayCompanyName()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("ABC Technologies");
    }
}

Here:

CalculateSalary()
→ abstract → derived class must implement

DisplayCompanyName()
→ concrete → already implemented

An abstract class does not have to contain an abstract member; it can be abstract simply to prevent direct instantiation and serve as a base type. Microsoft Learn

10. Can an Abstract Class have a Constructor?

Yes.

Very common interview question.

public abstract class Vehicle
{
    protected string brand;

    protected Vehicle(string brand)
    {
        this.brand = brand;
    }

    public abstract void Start();
}

Derived class:

public class Car : Vehicle
{
    public Car(string brand) : base(brand)
    {
    }

    public override void Start()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{brand} started");
    }
}

Interview answer

Yes, an abstract class can have constructors. The constructor is executed when an instance of a concrete derived class is created.

11. Can we create an object of an Abstract Class?

No.

abstract class Animal
{
}

This is invalid:

Animal animal = new Animal(); // ❌

But this is valid:

Animal animal = new Dog(); // ✅

assuming Dog : Animal.

Why?

Because the abstract class represents an incomplete/base abstraction intended to be specialized by derived classes. Microsoft Learn

12. Can an Abstract Class have zero abstract methods?

Yes.

public abstract class Logger
{
    public void Log(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(message);
    }
}

This is valid.

Why make it abstract?

To prevent direct instantiation and force consumers to work with derived types.

Interview answer

Yes. An abstract class doesn't need to contain an abstract member. It can be abstract simply to prevent direct instantiation or to establish a common base type.

13. Can an Abstract Class be sealed?

No.

These concepts conflict:

abstract class A
{
}

means:

This class must be inherited to create a concrete implementation.

Whereas:

sealed class A
{
}

means:

This class cannot be inherited.

So:

abstract sealed class A // ❌

is not valid for a normal class declaration.

14. Can an Abstract Class implement an Interface?

Yes.

public interface IPayment
{
    void Pay();
}

public abstract class Payment : IPayment
{
    public abstract void Pay();
}

The abstract class can leave the interface member abstract and let concrete derived classes implement it.

This is supported by C#'s interface mapping rules. Microsoft Learn

15. Can an Interface inherit from another Interface?

Yes.

public interface IAnimal
{
    void Eat();
}

public interface IDog : IAnimal
{
    void Bark();
}

A class implementing IDog must provide the required members from the interface hierarchy.

public class Labrador : IDog
{
    public void Eat()
    {
    }

    public void Bark()
    {
    }
}

Interfaces can also inherit from multiple interfaces. Microsoft Learn

16. Can a class implement multiple interfaces?

Yes.

This is one of the biggest advantages of interfaces.

public interface IPrintable
{
    void Print();
}

public interface IScannable
{
    void Scan();
}

public class Printer : IPrintable, IScannable
{
    public void Print()
    {
    }

    public void Scan()
    {
    }
}

A class can have only one direct base class, but can implement multiple interfaces. Microsoft Learn

17. Can an Interface contain implementation?

Modern C#: Yes.

This is an important modern C# interview point.

Interfaces can provide default implementations:

public interface ILogger
{
    void Log(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(message);
    }
}

A class implementing the interface can use the default implementation unless it provides its own implementation.

Modern interfaces can also contain various members, including static members and default implementations. Microsoft Learn

Interview tip

If an interviewer asks:

"Can interfaces have implementation?"

Don't simply say "No."

Say:

"Traditionally interfaces represented contracts without implementation, but modern C# supports default interface implementations, so interfaces can contain implementation as well."

That's the more current answer.

18. What is the purpose of Abstraction in a Web API?

This is particularly relevant to your .NET experience.

Suppose your controller needs a payment service.

Instead of:

public class PaymentController
{
    private CreditCardPayment payment;
}

we can depend on:

public class PaymentController
{
    private readonly IPaymentService paymentService;

    public PaymentController(IPaymentService paymentService)
    {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}

Now the controller doesn't care whether the implementation is:

CreditCardPayment
UPIPayment
PayPalPayment
MockPaymentService

It only knows:

IPaymentService

This is abstraction and also sets up loose coupling + Dependency Injection, which you'll study later.

19. What is "programming to an abstraction"?

Interview-Ready Answer

Programming to an abstraction means depending on an interface or abstract type rather than a concrete implementation.

Instead of:

private SqlPaymentService paymentService;

prefer:

private IPaymentService paymentService;

Then:

IPaymentService
       ↑
       │
 ┌─────┴──────────┐
 │                │
UPIPayment   CardPayment

The higher-level code depends on the contract rather than a specific implementation.

This becomes especially important when we reach Dependency Inversion Principle and Dependency Injection.

20. Abstraction vs Concrete Implementation

Suppose:

public interface INotificationService
{
    void Send(string message);
}

Implementations:

public class EmailNotification : INotificationService
{
    public void Send(string message)
    {
        // Email logic
    }
}
public class SmsNotification : INotificationService
{
    public void Send(string message)
    {
        // SMS logic
    }
}

Consumer:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly INotificationService notificationService;

    public OrderService(INotificationService notificationService)
    {
        this.notificationService = notificationService;
    }

    public void PlaceOrder()
    {
        // Order logic

        notificationService.Send("Order placed");
    }
}

OrderService doesn't know whether notification is sent using:

Email
SMS
Push notification
WhatsApp

That's a practical example of abstraction.

21. Most Important Interview Question

"Explain abstraction with a real-world example."

Strong 30-second answer

Abstraction means exposing only the essential functionality and hiding unnecessary implementation details. For example, in a payment system, I can define an IPaymentService with a Pay() method. Different implementations such as UPI and credit card can implement that interface. The caller only depends on IPaymentService and doesn't need to know how each payment method works internally.

22. Common Tricky Questions

Q: Can an abstract class be instantiated?

No.

Q: Can an abstract class have constructors?

Yes.

Q: Can an abstract class have concrete methods?

Yes.

Q: Can an abstract class have no abstract methods?

Yes.

Q: Can an abstract class implement an interface?

Yes.

Q: Can an interface have implementation?

Yes, modern C# supports default interface implementations. Microsoft Learn

Q: Can a class implement multiple interfaces?

Yes.

Q: Can a class inherit multiple classes?

No.

Q: Can an interface inherit multiple interfaces?

Yes. Microsoft Learn

Q: Can an abstract class be sealed?

No.

⭐ Priority for Your Interviews

🔴 Must Know

  1. Definition of abstraction
  1. Why abstraction is needed
  1. Abstract class
  1. Interface
  1. Abstract class vs interface
  1. Encapsulation vs abstraction
  1. Real-world payment/service example
  1. Abstract class constructor
  1. Abstract class concrete methods
  1. Multiple interface implementation

🟡 Strong 3+ YOE Level

  1. Programming to abstraction
  1. Abstraction in ASP.NET Core
  1. Interface + Dependency Injection
  1. Default interface implementation
  1. Abstract class implementing interface

🧠 Easy Memory Trick

Abstraction = Hide complexity, expose essential behavior.

And remember:

Abstract Class
     ↓
Shared base + shared state/implementation
     +
Abstract members that derived classes must implement


Interface
     ↓
Contract/capability
     +
Multiple interfaces can be implemented
     +
Modern C# supports default implementations

7. Inheritance in C#

Inheritance is a core OOP concept and very important for .NET interviews. It allows a derived class to reuse, extend, or modify behavior from a base class. C# supports single class inheritance, while a class can implement multiple interfaces. Microsoft Learn

1. What is Inheritance?

Interview-Ready Answer

Inheritance is an OOP mechanism where a derived class inherits accessible members and behavior from a base class and can extend or modify that behavior.

It is mainly used when there is a genuine "is-a" relationship between the types.

Example

public class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee is working");
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public void WriteCode()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer is writing code");
    }
}

Now:

Developer developer = new Developer();

developer.Name = "Saurabh";
developer.Work();       // Inherited
developer.WriteCode();  // Own method

Developer is an Employee, so inheritance makes sense.

2. Why do we use Inheritance?

Interview-Ready Answer

We use inheritance to reuse common functionality, create specialized versions of a base type, and avoid duplicating common code.

Example:

Employee
   │
   ├── Developer
   ├── Tester
   └── Manager

Common properties:

Name
EmployeeId
Department

can exist in Employee, while specialized behavior belongs in the derived classes.

Microsoft describes inheritance as allowing classes to reuse, extend, and modify behavior from another class. Microsoft Learn

3. What is a Base Class and Derived Class?

Base Class

The class being inherited from.

public class Employee
{
}

Derived Class

The class that inherits from it.

public class Developer : Employee
{
}

So:

Employee  → Base class
Developer → Derived class

Interview answer

The base class contains common functionality, while the derived class inherits that functionality and can add or specialize behavior.

4. How do you implement inheritance in C#?

Use :.

public class Employee
{
    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Working");
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public void Code()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Coding");
    }
}

The syntax is:

class DerivedClass : BaseClass
{
}

5. What is an "is-a" relationship?

This is an important design question.

Inheritance should generally represent an is-a relationship.

Developer is an Employee
Car is a Vehicle
Dog is an Animal
Manager is an Employee

So:

public class Developer : Employee
{
}

makes sense.

But:

Car is an Engine ❌
Employee is a Database ❌

These aren't appropriate inheritance relationships.

Interview-ready answer

Inheritance should normally represent an "is-a" relationship where the derived type is a specialized form of the base type.

Microsoft specifically describes inheritance as expressing an "is-a" relationship. Microsoft Learn

6. What members are inherited?

A derived class inherits members from its base class, subject to accessibility.

For example:

public class Employee
{
    public string Name;
    protected int Age;
    private decimal salary;
}

A derived class can directly access:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public void Test()
    {
        Name = "Saurabh"; // ✅
        Age = 25;         // ✅

        // salary = 50000; // ❌
    }
}
