The private member exists as part of the base-class portion of the object, but it isn't directly accessible from the derived class. Microsoft Learn

7. Are constructors inherited?

No.

This is a very common interview question.

public class Employee
{
    public Employee(string name)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(name);
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
}

Developer does not inherit the constructor of Employee.

The derived class must define its own constructor and call the base constructor when needed:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public Developer(string name) : base(name)
    {
    }
}

Interview answer

Constructors are not inherited. Each class defines its own constructors, but a derived constructor can invoke a base-class constructor using base(...). Microsoft Learn

8. Does a derived class inherit private members?

This question requires a precise answer.

Interview-ready answer

The base object's state includes its private members, but derived-class code cannot directly access those private members.

Example:

public class Parent
{
    private int value = 10;
}

public class Child : Parent
{
    public void Test()
    {
        // Console.WriteLine(value); // ❌
    }
}

If derived classes need direct access, use protected:

public class Parent
{
    protected int value = 10;
}

Then:

public class Child : Parent
{
    public void Test()
    {
        Console.WriteLine(value); // ✅
    }
}

9. Can C# support multiple class inheritance?

No.

This is extremely important.

You cannot do:

public class C : A, B  // ❌
{
}

where both A and B are classes.

C# supports single inheritance for classes. Microsoft Learn

But multiple interfaces are allowed

public class Developer : Employee, IDeveloper, ITeamMember
{
}

Here:

Employee     → Base class
IDeveloper   → Interface
ITeamMember  → Interface

Interview answer

C# doesn't support multiple inheritance of classes, but a class can inherit from one base class and implement multiple interfaces.

10. Can a derived class inherit from another derived class?

Yes.

Inheritance can form a hierarchy.

public class Employee
{
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
}

public class SeniorDeveloper : Developer
{
}

Relationship:

Employee
   ↑
Developer
   ↑
SeniorDeveloper

This is called multilevel inheritance.

Inheritance is transitive, so SeniorDeveloper also has the inherited members available through Developer and Employee, subject to accessibility. Microsoft Learn

11. What is hierarchical inheritance?

Multiple classes inherit from the same base class.

          Employee
         /        \
   Developer     Tester

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public void Work()
    {
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
}

public class Tester : Employee
{
}

Both Developer and Tester reuse Employee functionality.

12. What is multilevel inheritance?

A derived class becomes the base class for another class.

Employee
   ↓
Developer
   ↓
SeniorDeveloper

Example:

public class Employee
{
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
}

public class SeniorDeveloper : Developer
{
}

13. What is the difference between inheritance and interface implementation?

Inheritance

Represents an is-a relationship.

Developer : Employee

Interface implementation

Usually represents a can-do/capability relationship.

Developer : ICodeReviewer

A developer is an Employee.

A developer can review code.

Microsoft specifically distinguishes the inheritance "is-a" relationship from interfaces, which are intended to express capabilities. Microsoft Learn

14. Can a class inherit from an abstract class?

Yes.

public abstract class Employee
{
    public abstract void Work();
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer is coding");
    }
}

The derived class must implement inherited abstract members unless the derived class is itself abstract. Microsoft Learn

15. Can a class inherit from a sealed class?

No.

public sealed class Employee
{
}

This is invalid:

public class Developer : Employee // ❌
{
}

Interview answer

A sealed class cannot be used as a base class. We use sealed when we want to prevent further inheritance. Microsoft Learn

16. What is base keyword?

The base keyword allows a derived class to access members of its base class.

Example

public class Employee
{
    public virtual void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee working");
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        base.Work();

        Console.WriteLine("Developer coding");
    }
}

Output:

Employee working
Developer coding

It can also be used to call a base constructor:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public Developer(string name) : base(name)
    {
    }
}

17. What is constructor execution order in inheritance?

This is a very common practical question.

Consider:

public class Employee
{
    public Employee()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee constructor");
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public Developer()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer constructor");
    }
}

Then:

Developer developer = new Developer();

Output:

Employee constructor
Developer constructor

Interview answer

When a derived object is created, the base-class constructor executes before the derived-class constructor.

Conceptually:

Create Developer
       ↓
Employee constructor
       ↓
Developer constructor

18. What happens if the base class has a parameterized constructor?

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public Employee(string name)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(name);
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public Developer(string name) : base(name)
    {
    }
}

The derived constructor explicitly calls:

base(name)

Interview answer

If the base class doesn't have an accessible parameterless constructor, the derived constructor must explicitly call an appropriate base constructor.

19. Can a derived class override every base method?

No.

A method must be overridable.

For example:

public class Employee
{
    public void Work()
    {
    }
}

You cannot:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work() // ❌
    {
    }
}

The base method must generally be:

virtual
abstract
override

to participate in overriding. Microsoft Learn

We'll go deeply into this in your next topic: Polymorphism.

20. What is the difference between virtual, override, and new?

This is technically part of your next topic, but inheritance questions often lead here.

virtual

Base class allows overriding:

public virtual void Work()
{
}

override

Derived class replaces the virtual/abstract implementation:

public override void Work()
{
}

new

Derived class hides the base member:

public new void Work()
{
}

Important distinction:

override → polymorphic overriding
new      → member hiding

Microsoft documents new as a way to explicitly indicate that a derived member hides a base member rather than overrides it. Microsoft Learn

We'll cover the behavior and interview traps in detail under Polymorphism.

21. Does inheritance always improve code reuse?

No.

This is a good Senior-level design question.

Inheritance can create strong coupling between the base and derived classes.

For example:

BaseClass
    ↓
DerivedClass
    ↓
AnotherDerivedClass
    ↓
AnotherDerivedClass2

A change in the base class can potentially affect many derived classes.

That's why inheritance should be used when there is a meaningful is-a relationship, not merely because code can be reused.

Strong interview answer

Inheritance provides code reuse, but I wouldn't use it only for code reuse. If the relationship is not genuinely "is-a", composition is often a better design.

This leads directly into your later topic:

Composition vs Inheritance.

22. Inheritance vs Composition

Inheritance

Developer IS-A Employee
class Developer : Employee
{
}

Composition

Developer HAS-A Logger
class Developer
{
    private readonly Logger logger;

    public Developer(Logger logger)
    {
        this.logger = logger;
    }
}

Interview answer

Inheritance represents an is-a relationship and reuses behavior through a class hierarchy. Composition represents a has-a relationship by building a class using other objects. Composition generally gives more flexibility when behavior needs to vary independently.

You'll study this formally later in your sequence.

23. Real-World .NET Example

Imagine an application with different employees:

public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee logged in");
    }
}

Developer:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public void WriteCode()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Writing code");
    }
}

Manager:

public class Manager : Employee
{
    public void ConductMeeting()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Conducting meeting");
    }
}

Hierarchy:

              Employee
              /      \
             /        \
      Developer       Manager
         |               |
     WriteCode()    ConductMeeting()

Common functionality stays in Employee.

Specialized functionality stays in the derived classes.

24. What is implicit inheritance from System.Object?

All C# classes ultimately derive from System.Object, directly or indirectly. Microsoft Learn

For example:

public class Employee
{
}

is conceptually:

Employee
   ↓
System.Object

That's why every normal C# class has methods such as:

ToString()
Equals()
GetHashCode()
GetType()

available from Object.

25. Do structs support class inheritance?

No.

Structs don't participate in class inheritance hierarchies, although they can implement interfaces. Microsoft Learn

For example:

struct Employee : SomeClass // ❌
{
}

is not allowed.

But:

struct Employee : IEmployee // ✅
{
}

is allowed.

This becomes important later when we cover:

Struct vs Class.

🧠 30-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer simply asks "What is inheritance in C#?", you can say:

Inheritance allows a derived class to reuse and extend the functionality of a base class. In C#, a class can inherit from only one base class, but it can implement multiple interfaces. I use inheritance when there is a genuine "is-a" relationship, such as Developer being an Employee. The derived class can add its own functionality and can override virtual or abstract members when customization is required. Microsoft Learn

8. Polymorphism in C#

Polymorphism is one of the most important OOP interview topics for a .NET developer. The word means "many forms."

In C#, polymorphism allows the same interface/base-class reference to work with different concrete implementations. With virtual members, the implementation that runs is selected based on the object's runtime type. Microsoft Learn

For your interviews, the most important part is:

Polymorphism
│
├── Compile-time polymorphism
│   └── Method overloading
│
└── Runtime polymorphism
    ├── virtual
    ├── override
    ├── abstract
    └── new / method hiding

1. What is Polymorphism?

Interview-Ready Answer

Polymorphism means one interface or base-type reference can represent different implementations.

In C#, it allows us to write code against a common base class or interface while the appropriate implementation is selected depending on the object.

Simple example

public class Animal
{
    public virtual void Speak()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Animal speaks");
    }
}

public class Dog : Animal
{
    public override void Speak()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Dog barks");
    }
}

public class Cat : Animal
{
    public override void Speak()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Cat meows");
    }
}

Now:

Animal animal1 = new Dog();
Animal animal2 = new Cat();

animal1.Speak(); // Dog barks
animal2.Speak(); // Cat meows

Both variables are declared as Animal, but different implementations execute.

That's runtime polymorphism. Microsoft Learn

2. What are the types of Polymorphism?

For interview purposes, know these two:

1. Compile-time polymorphism

Usually achieved through method overloading.

public void Add(int a, int b)
{
}

public void Add(int a, int b, int c)
{
}

public void Add(double a, double b)
{
}

The compiler determines which method to call based on the arguments.

2. Runtime polymorphism

Achieved through mechanisms such as:

virtual + override
abstract + override
interface implementations

The actual implementation can be selected at runtime.

Microsoft describes runtime polymorphism through derived objects being treated as base objects and virtual methods dispatching to the appropriate override. Microsoft Learn

3. What is Compile-Time Polymorphism?

Interview-Ready Answer

Compile-time polymorphism occurs when the compiler determines which method should be called during compilation. In C#, method overloading is the common example.

Example:

public class Calculator
{
    public int Add(int a, int b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }

    public int Add(int a, int b, int c)
    {
        return a + b + c;
    }

    public double Add(double a, double b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }
}

Usage:

var calculator = new Calculator();

calculator.Add(10, 20);
calculator.Add(10, 20, 30);
calculator.Add(10.5, 20.5);

The compiler selects the appropriate overload based on the method arguments.

4. What is Runtime Polymorphism?

Interview-Ready Answer

Runtime polymorphism occurs when a base-class or interface reference refers to a derived implementation, and the appropriate implementation is selected at runtime.

Example:

public class Payment
{
    public virtual void Pay()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Generic payment");
    }
}

public class UpiPayment : Payment
{
    public override void Pay()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("UPI payment");
    }
}

public class CardPayment : Payment
{
    public override void Pay()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Card payment");
    }
}

Then:

Payment payment;

payment = new UpiPayment();
payment.Pay();       // UPI payment

payment = new CardPayment();
payment.Pay();       // Card payment

The same Payment reference can represent different implementations.

5. What is the virtual keyword?

Interview-Ready Answer

virtual allows a base-class method, property, indexer, or event to be overridden by a derived class. Lab Algebra

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public virtual void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee working");
    }
}

Now a derived class can override it:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer coding");
    }
}

Without virtual, the base method cannot be overridden.

6. What is the override keyword?

Interview-Ready Answer

override provides a new implementation for an inherited virtual, abstract, or override member. The base member must be overridable. Lab Algebra

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public virtual void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee working");
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer coding");
    }
}

Now:

Employee employee = new Developer();

employee.Work();

Output:

Developer coding

This is runtime polymorphism.

7. Why do we need both virtual and override?

Think of it as:

Base class
    ↓
virtual
"Derived classes are allowed to change this behavior."

Derived class
    ↓
override
"I am providing that changed behavior."

Example:

class Employee
{
    public virtual void Work()
    {
    }
}

class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
    }
}

Interview answer

virtual enables overriding in the base class, while override provides the derived implementation.

8. What happens if the base method isn't virtual?

You cannot use override.

public class Employee
{
    public void Work()
    {
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work() // ❌
    {
    }
}

Compilation error.

Instead, you would be hiding the method:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public new void Work()
    {
    }
}

9. What is new in method hiding?

This is one of your highest-priority interview topics.

Interview-Ready Answer

The new keyword hides a member inherited from the base class. It does not override the base member. When using method hiding, the method selected depends on the compile-time type of the reference. Microsoft Learn

Example:

public class Employee
{
    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee working");
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public new void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer coding");
    }
}

Now:

Developer developer = new Developer();

developer.Work();

Output:

Developer coding

But:

Employee employee = new Developer();

employee.Work();

Output:

Employee working

Why?

Because new is hiding, not overriding.

10. override vs new

This is a must-know interview comparison.

override

class Employee
{
    public virtual void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee");
    }
}

class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer");
    }
}
Employee e = new Developer();

e.Work();

Output:

Developer

new

class Employee
{
    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee");
    }
}

class Developer : Employee
{
    public new void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer");
    }
}
Employee e = new Developer();

e.Work();

Output:

Employee

The key difference

overridenew
Overrides base virtual/abstract memberHides base member
Runtime polymorphismMember hiding
Runtime type matters for virtual dispatchCompile-time/reference type determines member lookup
Base method must be virtual/abstract/overrideBase member doesn't need to be virtual
Designed for polymorphic behaviorCreates a separate member with same name

Microsoft explicitly notes that with hiding, the called method depends on the variable's compile-time type, unlike virtual overriding. Microsoft Learn

11. What is Method Hiding?

Interview-Ready Answer

Method hiding occurs when a derived class declares a method with the same name and signature as a base-class method, typically using the new keyword.

Example:

public class Base
{
    public void Display()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Base");
    }
}

public class Derived : Base
{
    public new void Display()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Derived");
    }
}
Derived d = new Derived();
d.Display();

Output:

Derived

But:

Base b = new Derived();
b.Display();

Output:

Base

12. What if we don't write new?

Interesting interview question.

class Base
{
    public void Display()
    {
    }
}

class Derived : Base
{
    public void Display()
    {
    }
}

The compiler warns that Derived.Display() hides the inherited member.

If hiding is intentional, use:

public new void Display()
{
}

The new keyword explicitly tells the compiler that the hiding is intentional. Lab Algebra

13. What is the difference between Method Overloading and Method Overriding?

Very common interview question.

OverloadingOverriding
Same method nameSame method signature
Different parametersSame parameters
Usually same classBase + derived class
Compile-time polymorphismRuntime polymorphism
No virtual requiredRequires virtual/abstract/override chain
Compiler selects overloadRuntime dispatch selects override

Example — Overloading

void Print(int value)
{
}

void Print(string value)
{
}

Example — Overriding

class Animal
{
    public virtual void Speak()
    {
    }
}

class Dog : Animal
{
    public override void Speak()
    {
    }
}

14. What is the difference between Overriding and Method Hiding?

Overriding

class Base
{
    public virtual void Display()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Base");
    }
}

class Derived : Base
{
    public override void Display()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Derived");
    }
}
Base obj = new Derived();

obj.Display();

Output:

Derived

Hiding

class Base
{
    public void Display()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Base");
    }
}

class Derived : Base
{
    public new void Display()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Derived");
    }
}
Base obj = new Derived();

obj.Display();

Output:

Base

Interview one-liner

Override is polymorphic; new is hiding.

15. What is runtime type vs compile-time type?

This is extremely important for understanding polymorphism.

Consider:

Employee employee = new Developer();

There are two types involved:

Compile-time type → Employee
Runtime type      → Developer

The compiler sees:

Employee

The actual object is:

Developer

With an overridden virtual method:

employee.Work();

the runtime dispatches to:

Developer.Work()

because the method participates in virtual dispatch. Microsoft Learn

16. What is Runtime Dispatch?

Interview-Ready Answer

Runtime dispatch is the mechanism where, for a virtual method call, the runtime determines which overridden implementation should execute based on the object's runtime type.

Example:

Employee employee = new Developer();

employee.Work();

Conceptually:

Reference type
     ↓
 Employee
     ↓
Virtual method call
     ↓
Runtime checks actual object
     ↓
 Developer
     ↓
Developer.Work()

This is the core mechanism behind runtime polymorphism.

17. Can a private method be overridden?

No.

Example:

class Base
{
    private void Display()
    {
    }
}

A derived class cannot override it because it isn't accessible to the derived class and isn't a virtual member available for overriding.

You can define another method with the same name, but that is a separate method, not an override.

18. Can a static method be overridden?

No.

Static members belong to the type rather than participating in instance virtual dispatch.

You can hide a static member using new, but you don't override it.

class Base
{
    public static void Display()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Base");
    }
}

class Derived : Base
{
    public new static void Display()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Derived");
    }
}

This is hiding, not runtime overriding.

19. Can properties be overridden?

Yes.

virtual and override can be used with properties.

public class Employee
{
    public virtual string Role
    {
        get { return "Employee"; }
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override string Role
    {
        get { return "Developer"; }
    }
}

Microsoft notes that virtual, override, and new can also apply to properties, indexers, and events. Microsoft Learn

20. Can events be overridden?

Yes.

Virtual members can include:

  • Methods
  • Properties
  • Indexers
  • Events

Fields cannot be declared virtual. Microsoft Learn

21. Can an override method be further overridden?

Yes.

Consider:

class A
{
    public virtual void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("A");
    }
}

class B : A
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("B");
    }
}

class C : B
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("C");
    }
}

Then:

A obj = new C();

obj.Work();

Output:

C

Virtual behavior continues through the inheritance chain unless explicitly stopped. Microsoft Learn

22. How do you stop further overriding?

Use:

sealed override

Example:

class B : A
{
    public sealed override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("B");
    }
}

Now:

class C : B
{
    public override void Work() // ❌
    {
    }
}

The override is sealed, so further derived classes cannot override that virtual member. Microsoft Learn

23. What is base used for with overriding?

A derived override can call the base implementation using base.

public class Employee
{
    public virtual void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Common employee work");
    }
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        base.Work();

        Console.WriteLine("Developer-specific work");
    }
}

Output:

Common employee work
Developer-specific work

Interview answer

base allows the derived class to explicitly invoke the base-class implementation.

Microsoft also recommends considering the base implementation when overriding behavior so the derived class can preserve the base class's expected behavior where appropriate. Microsoft Learn

24. Real-World Example: Payment Processing

This is a very good example for a .NET interview.

public abstract class Payment
{
    public abstract void ProcessPayment();
}

Different implementations:

public class UpiPayment : Payment
{
    public override void ProcessPayment()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Processing UPI payment");
    }
}
public class CardPayment : Payment
{
    public override void ProcessPayment()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Processing card payment");
    }
}

Now your service can work with the base type:

public void Process(Payment payment)
{
    payment.ProcessPayment();
}

Usage:

Process(new UpiPayment());
Process(new CardPayment());

The calling code doesn't need separate logic like:

if (paymentType == "UPI")
{
}
else if (paymentType == "CARD")
{
}

Each implementation provides its own behavior.

25. Real-World ASP.NET Core Example

Suppose your application has:

INotificationService
       ↑
       │
 ┌─────┼─────────┐
 │     │         │
Email  SMS      Push

Interface:

public interface INotificationService
{
    void Send(string message);
}

Implementations:

public class EmailNotification : INotificationService
{
    public void Send(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Sending Email");
    }
}
public class SmsNotification : INotificationService
{
    public void Send(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Sending SMS");
    }
}

Your service depends on:

private readonly INotificationService notificationService;

rather than:

private readonly EmailNotification notificationService;

This combines:

Abstraction
+
Polymorphism
+
Loose coupling
+
Dependency Injection

You'll see these concepts repeatedly in ASP.NET Core.

🔥 26. Most Important Output-Based Interview Question

Consider:

class A
{
    public virtual void Show()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("A");
    }
}

class B : A
{
    public override void Show()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("B");
    }
}

A obj = new B();

obj.Show();

Output

B

Why?

Because Show() is virtual and overridden.

Compile-time type → A
Runtime type      → B
                     ↓
               B.Show()

This is runtime polymorphism. Microsoft Learn

🔥 27. Another Important Output Question

class A
{
    public void Show()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("A");
    }
}

class B : A
{
    public new void Show()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("B");
    }
}

A obj = new B();

obj.Show();

Output

A

Why?

Because this is method hiding, not overriding.

The compile-time/reference type is:

A

Therefore:

A.Show()

is selected.

🔥 28. The Most Important virtual vs new Example

Remember this code:

class A
{
    public virtual void Show()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("A");
    }
}

class B : A
{
    public override void Show()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("B");
    }
}

class C : A
{
    public new void Show()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("C");
    }
}

Now:

A x = new B();
A y = new C();

x.Show();
y.Show();

Output

B
A

Why?

B → override → runtime dispatch
C → new      → hiding

This is one of the best examples to memorize for interviews.

29. Can new be used with override together?

No.

You cannot write:

public new override void Show() // ❌

They have different meanings:

override → participate in overriding
new      → hide inherited member

The two modifiers are mutually exclusive for the same member. Lab Algebra

30. What is the benefit of Runtime Polymorphism?

Interview-Ready Answer

Runtime polymorphism allows us to write code against a common abstraction instead of hard-coding concrete implementations. This makes the code easier to extend and maintain.

For example:

public void SendNotification(INotificationService service)
{
    service.Send("Order placed");
}

The method can work with:

EmailNotification
SmsNotification
PushNotification

without changing its implementation.

31. Why is Polymorphism important in SOLID design?

Polymorphism is heavily used with the Open/Closed Principle.

Suppose:

public void ProcessPayment(Payment payment)
{
    payment.Process();
}

You can add:

UPIPayment
CardPayment
PayPalPayment
CryptoPayment

without changing the core processing code, provided each follows the abstraction.

This allows the system to be extended through new implementations.

QuestionPriority
What is polymorphism?🔴 Must Know

What is method overloading?🔴 Must Know

What is virtual?🔴 Must Know
What is override?🔴 Must Know
What is new?🔴 Must Know
Override vs new🔴 Must Know
Method hiding🔴 Must Know

What is runtime dispatch?🔴 Must Know

Can private methods be overridden?🟡

base with override🟡

🧠 The 5 Things You Must Remember

1. virtual

"Derived classes CAN override me."

2. override

"I am replacing the virtual/abstract behavior."

3. new

"I am hiding the base member."

4. override → runtime type

Base x = new Derived();
x.Method(); → Derived.Method()

5. new → compile-time/reference type

Base x = new Derived();
x.Method(); → Base.Method()

🎯 Best 30-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer asks "Explain polymorphism in C#.", say:

Polymorphism means one interface or base-type reference can represent multiple implementations. In C#, we commonly have compile-time polymorphism through method overloading and runtime polymorphism through virtual and abstract members, overrides, and interface implementations. For example, if Payment is a base class and UPIPayment and CardPayment derive from it, I can use a Payment reference and call Process(). The runtime invokes the appropriate overridden implementation based on the actual object type. Microsoft Learn

9. Abstract Class

An abstract class is an incomplete base class that cannot be instantiated directly. It can contain both implemented members and abstract members that derived non-abstract classes must implement. Microsoft Learn

1. What is an Abstract Class?

Interview-Ready Answer

An abstract class is a class declared with the abstract keyword that is designed to be used as a base class. We cannot create an object of an abstract class directly. It can contain both concrete members with implementation and abstract members without implementation.

Example

public abstract class Payment
{
    public void ValidatePayment()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Validating payment...");
    }

    public abstract void ProcessPayment();
}

Derived class:

public class CreditCardPayment : Payment
{
    public override void ProcessPayment()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Processing credit card payment...");
    }
}

Usage:

Payment payment = new CreditCardPayment();

payment.ValidatePayment();
payment.ProcessPayment();

Real-World Scenario

Suppose your application supports:

  • Credit Card
  • UPI
  • PayPal

All payments need common validation, but the actual payment processing differs.

So:

Payment
   |
   +-- CreditCardPayment
   +-- UpiPayment
   +-- PayPalPayment

The common behavior belongs in the abstract class, while payment-specific behavior is abstract.

2. Can we create an object of an Abstract Class?

Answer

No.

Payment payment = new Payment(); // ❌ Compile-time error

But we can create a reference whose type is abstract:

Payment payment = new CreditCardPayment(); // ✅

This is because the actual object is of the concrete derived class.

Microsoft's C# specification explicitly states that using new directly on an abstract class is a compile-time error. Microsoft Learn

Interview Follow-up

Q: Then why can we have a reference of an abstract class?

Because the reference can point to an object of any concrete class derived from that abstract class. This is commonly used for polymorphism.

3. Can an Abstract Class have normal/concrete methods?

Answer

Yes.

This is one of the most important points.

public abstract class Employee
{
    public void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee logged in");
    }

    public abstract void CalculateSalary();
}

Here:

Login()             → Concrete method
CalculateSalary()   → Abstract method

Real-World Example

Every employee can log in:

public void Login()

But salary calculation may differ:

public abstract void CalculateSalary();

For example:

Employee
   |
   +-- FullTimeEmployee
   +-- ContractEmployee

Each can implement salary calculation differently.

4. Can an Abstract Class exist without an Abstract Method?

Answer

Yes.

This is a common interview trick.

public abstract class Employee
{
    public void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Login");
    }
}

This is completely valid.

An abstract class does not have to contain an abstract method. Its purpose can simply be to prevent direct instantiation and provide a common base implementation. Microsoft Learn

Interview Answer

An abstract class can contain zero or more abstract members. We can make a class abstract simply when we don't want it to be instantiated directly.

5. What is an Abstract Method?

Interview-Ready Answer

An abstract method is a method declared with the abstract keyword that does not contain an implementation. A non-abstract derived class must provide its implementation using override.

Example:

public abstract class Animal
{
    public abstract void MakeSound();
}

Derived class:

public class Dog : Animal
{
    public override void MakeSound()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Bark");
    }
}

Notice:

public abstract void MakeSound();

There is no method body.

Microsoft specifies that abstract methods have no implementation and must be implemented by non-abstract derived classes. Microsoft Learn

6. What happens if a derived class doesn't implement an abstract method?

Suppose:

public abstract class Animal
{
    public abstract void MakeSound();
}

And:

public class Dog : Animal
{
}

This produces a compile-time error because Dog is concrete but hasn't implemented MakeSound().

Solution 1 — Implement it

public class Dog : Animal
{
    public override void MakeSound()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Bark");
    }
}

Solution 2 — Make Dog abstract

public abstract class Dog : Animal
{
}

An abstract derived class can inherit the abstract member without implementing it. Microsoft Learn

Interview Answer

A concrete derived class must implement all inherited abstract members. However, if the derived class is also abstract, it can defer the implementation to a further derived class.

7. Can an Abstract Class have a Constructor?

Answer

Yes.

This is very commonly asked.

public abstract class Employee
{
    protected Employee()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee constructor");
    }

    public abstract void Work();
}

Derived class:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public Developer()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer constructor");
    }

    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Writing code");
    }
}
Developer developer = new Developer();

Output:

Employee constructor
Developer constructor

Why?

Even though we cannot instantiate Employee directly, its constructor is executed when a derived class object is created.

Interview Answer

Yes, an abstract class can have constructors. The constructor is useful for initializing common state, and it executes as part of constructing a derived-class object.

8. Why would an Abstract Class need a Constructor?

Suppose:

public abstract class Employee
{
    protected string Name;

    protected Employee(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }

    public abstract void Work();
}

Then:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public Developer(string name) : base(name)
    {
    }

    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} is coding");
    }
}

Usage:

var developer = new Developer("Saurabh");

The abstract class initializes the common state.

Real-World Scenario

If every employee needs:

  • Employee ID
  • Name
  • Department

you can initialize common information in the abstract base class.

9. Can an Abstract Class have Fields and Properties?

Answer

Yes.

It can contain:

  • Fields
  • Properties
  • Methods
  • Constructors
  • Events
  • Static members
  • Abstract members
  • Virtual members

Example:

public abstract class Employee
{
    protected int EmployeeId;

    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Login successful");
    }

    public abstract void Work();
}

This is one of the major differences from how beginners often think about abstraction: an abstract class isn't simply a collection of method signatures.

10. Can an Abstract Class have static members?

Answer

Yes.

public abstract class Employee
{
    public static int EmployeeCount { get; set; }

    public abstract void Work();
}

You can access:

Employee.EmployeeCount++;

You don't need an instance.

11. Can an Abstract Class have Virtual Methods?

Answer

Yes.

An abstract class can contain:

public virtual void Login()
{
    Console.WriteLine("Default login");
}

and:

public abstract void Work();

So the same abstract class can contain:

Concrete method
Virtual method
Abstract method
Fields
Properties
Constructor

Example:

public abstract class Employee
{
    public void CommonMethod()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Common");
    }

    public virtual void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Default Login");
    }

    public abstract void Work();
}

12. Difference between Abstract Method and Virtual Method

This is a very important interview question.

AbstractVirtual
No implementationHas implementation
Must be overridden by concrete derived classOverride is optional
Declared with abstractDeclared with virtual
Derived class must implementDerived class can use base implementation
Used when implementation is mandatoryUsed when default implementation exists

Example:

public abstract class Employee
{
    public abstract void Work();

    public virtual void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Default login");
    }
}

Derived class:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Writing code");
    }

    // Login() does not need to be overridden
}

Easy Memory Trick

Abstract = MUST implement

Virtual = CAN override

13. Can an Abstract Class inherit another Abstract Class?

Answer

Yes.

public abstract class Employee
{
    public abstract void Work();
}

public abstract class Developer : Employee
{
    public abstract void WriteCode();
}

Then:

public class BackendDeveloper : Developer
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Working");
    }

    public override void WriteCode()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Writing C# code");
    }
}

This creates:

Employee
   ↓
Developer
   ↓
BackendDeveloper

The intermediate abstract class can continue to define abstract behavior.

14. Can an Abstract Class implement an Interface?

Answer

Yes.

public interface ILogger
{
    void Log();
}

public abstract class Service : ILogger
{
    public abstract void Log();

    public void Validate()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Validation");
    }
}

Then:

public class OrderService : Service
{
    public override void Log()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Order logged");
    }
}

This is useful when you want:

  • interface-based abstraction
  • plus shared implementation/state in the abstract class.

15. Can an Abstract Class be Sealed?

Answer

No.

These two concepts conflict:

abstract class A
{
}

means:

This class must be inherited.

Whereas:

sealed class B
{
}

means:

This class cannot be inherited.

Therefore:

public abstract sealed class Test
{
}

is invalid.

The C# specification explicitly prohibits an abstract class from also being sealed. Microsoft Learn

Memory Trick

abstract → MUST inherit
sealed   → CANNOT inherit

16. Can an Abstract Class have Private Members?

Answer

Yes.

public abstract class Employee
{
    private decimal salary;

    protected Employee(decimal salary)
    {
        this.salary = salary;
    }
}

The derived class cannot directly access:

salary

because it is private.

But the abstract class itself can use it through methods/properties.

This is useful for encapsulating common internal state.

17. Can an Abstract Class have Protected Members?

Answer

Yes, and this is very common.

public abstract class Employee
{
    protected string Department;

    protected Employee(string department)
    {
        Department = department;
    }
}

Derived classes can access:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public Developer() : base("IT")
    {
        Console.WriteLine(Department);
    }
}

18. What is the Real-World Use of an Abstract Class?

Consider a notification system in your .NET application.

You have:

Notification
    |
    +-- EmailNotification
    +-- SmsNotification
    +-- PushNotification

Common functionality:

public abstract class Notification
{
    public void Validate()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Validating notification");
    }

    public abstract void Send(string message);
}

Email:

public class EmailNotification : Notification
{
    public override void Send(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Sending Email: {message}");
    }
}

SMS:

public class SmsNotification : Notification
{
    public override void Send(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Sending SMS: {message}");
    }
}

Now:

Notification notification = new EmailNotification();

notification.Validate();
notification.Send("Hello");

This combines:

Abstraction + Inheritance + Polymorphism

That's exactly why abstract classes are frequently used in OOP designs.

19. Abstract Class vs Normal Class

Abstract ClassNormal Class
Cannot be instantiated directlyCan be instantiated
Can contain abstract membersCannot contain abstract members
Can contain concrete membersCan contain concrete members
Can have constructorsCan have constructors
Can have fields/propertiesCan have fields/properties
Can have virtual membersCan have virtual members
Designed as a base typeCan be used independently

20. Abstract Class vs Interface

You already studied abstraction, and Interface is the next topic, so for now remember the basic distinction.

Abstract Class

Use when related classes share:

  • common state
  • common implementation
  • common constructor logic
  • common behavior
public abstract class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Login()
    {
    }

    public abstract void Work();
}

Interface

Use primarily to define a contract/capability.

public interface IReportGenerator
{
    void GenerateReport();
}

A class can derive from only one direct base class but can implement multiple interfaces. Microsoft Learn

Don't worry about memorizing the complete comparison yet—we'll cover Interface vs Abstract Class as topic #11 in your sequence.

21. Can an Abstract Class contain an Abstract Property?

Answer

Yes.

public abstract class Employee
{
    public abstract decimal Salary { get; }
}

Derived class:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override decimal Salary => 100000;
}

Abstract members aren't limited to methods. C# also supports abstract properties and events. Microsoft Learn

22. Can an Abstract Class contain an Abstract Event?

Answer

Yes.

public abstract class NotificationService
{
    public abstract event EventHandler NotificationSent;
}

A concrete derived class must implement it.

This is less frequently asked, but worth knowing for senior-level interviews.

23. Can an Abstract Method be Private?

Answer

No.

This doesn't make sense:

public abstract class Test
{
    private abstract void Execute(); // ❌
}

An abstract member must be implemented by a derived class, but a private member isn't accessible to derived classes.

The C# language rules don't allow a private member to be abstract. Microsoft Learn

24. Can an Abstract Method be Static?

Answer

No.

public abstract static void Execute(); // ❌

An abstract member requires derived-class implementation through overriding, while static members don't participate in instance virtual dispatch.

The C# specification prohibits combining abstract with static. Microsoft Learn

25. Can an Abstract Method also be Virtual?

You may see:

public abstract virtual void Execute();

This is invalid.

An abstract method is already virtual in behavior.

Correct:

public abstract void Execute();

The C# specification describes an abstract method as implicitly virtual, so you don't write virtual separately. Microsoft Learn

Easy Interview Answer

An abstract method is implicitly virtual, so we use abstract rather than abstract virtual.

26. What happens when an Abstract Class has a Virtual Method?

Example:

public abstract class Employee
{
    public virtual void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee Login");
    }

    public abstract void Work();
}

Derived:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer Work");
    }

    public override void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer Login");
    }
}

Here:

Login()
→ virtual
→ overriding is optional

Work()
→ abstract
→ overriding is mandatory for Developer

27. What is abstract override?

This is a more advanced interview question.

Consider:

public class Base
{
    public virtual void Execute()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Base");
    }
}

Now:

public abstract class Middle : Base
{
    public abstract override void Execute();
}

This means:

Middle is forcing its derived classes to provide a new implementation of a method that originally had an implementation in Base.

Then:

public class Child : Middle
{
    public override void Execute()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Child");
    }
}

This is valid C#. The language specification explicitly allows an abstract class to override a virtual member with an abstract member. Microsoft Learn

Interview Priority

Medium/Low for most 3+ YOE interviews, but good to know if the interviewer goes deep.

28. Can an Abstract Class be used as a Method Parameter?

Yes.

public void ProcessPayment(Payment payment)
{
    payment.ProcessPayment();
}

You can pass:

var payment = new CreditCardPayment();

ProcessPayment(payment);

This is a common use of polymorphism.

The method doesn't need to know the exact concrete payment type.

29. Why Use Abstract Class Instead of Just a Normal Base Class?

Suppose:

public class Animal
{
    public virtual void MakeSound()
    {
    }
}

Now someone can do:

Animal animal = new Animal();

But maybe a generic Animal should never exist in your domain.

You want:

Animal
   ↓
Dog
Cat
Bird

but never:

Animal object itself

Then:

public abstract class Animal
{
    public abstract void MakeSound();
}

forces consumers to use a concrete derived type.

Interview Answer

I use an abstract class when the base type represents a general concept that should not be instantiated directly, while still providing shared state or implementation to derived classes.

30. Abstract Class — Most Important Interview Questions

For your 3+ YOE interview, prioritize these:

🔴 Must Know

  1. What is an abstract class?
  1. Can we instantiate an abstract class?
  1. Can an abstract class have concrete methods?
  1. Can an abstract class have no abstract methods?
  1. What is an abstract method?
  1. What happens if a derived class doesn't implement an abstract method?
  1. Can an abstract class have a constructor?
  1. Why does an abstract class need a constructor?
  1. Abstract method vs virtual method.
  1. Abstract class vs normal class.
  1. Can an abstract class have fields/properties?
  1. Can an abstract class implement an interface?

🟡 Strong Interview Level

  1. Can an abstract class inherit another abstract class?
  1. Can an abstract class contain static members?
  1. Can an abstract class have private/protected members?
  1. Can an abstract class have virtual methods?
  1. Can an abstract class have abstract properties?
  1. Can an abstract class have abstract events?
  1. Can an abstract class be sealed?
  1. Can an abstract method be private?
  1. Can an abstract method be static?
  1. Can an abstract method be virtual?
  1. What is abstract override?

🎯 30-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer asks:

"What is an abstract class in C#?"

Say:

An abstract class is a base class that cannot be instantiated directly. It is used when we want to provide common state or implementation to derived classes while also forcing derived classes to implement certain behavior. An abstract class can contain fields, properties, constructors, concrete methods, virtual methods, and abstract members. A concrete derived class must implement all inherited abstract members. I would typically use an abstract class when related classes share common behavior or state but have some behavior that needs to vary between implementations.

That's a strong answer for your experience level.

Yes — that question should definitely be included, and it is an important follow-up.

Can an abstract method be overridden?

Yes. In fact, a concrete derived class must override an inherited abstract method.

public abstract class Animal
{
    public abstract void MakeSound();
}

public class Dog : Animal
{
    public override void MakeSound()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Bark");
    }
}

Here:

Animal.MakeSound()
       ↓
    abstract
       ↓
Dog.MakeSound()
       ↓
    override

Interview-ready answer

Yes, an abstract method can and must be overridden by a non-abstract derived class. An abstract method has no implementation in the base class, so the derived class provides the implementation using the override keyword.

Important follow-up

Q: Can an abstract method be overridden by another abstract method?

Yes. An abstract class can override an inherited virtual/abstract member and keep it abstract:

public abstract class Animal
{
    public abstract void MakeSound();
}

public abstract class Mammal : Animal
{
    public abstract override void MakeSound();
}

public class Dog : Mammal
{
    public override void MakeSound()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Bark");
    }
}

So for your interview notes, add:

Abstract method → must be overridden by a concrete derived class; an abstract derived class can defer the implementation further.

10. Interface — C# Interview Preparation

The simplest definition is:

An interface defines a contract that a class or struct agrees to implement. A type can implement multiple interfaces, and an interface can inherit from multiple interfaces. Microsoft Learn

1. What is an Interface?

Interview-Ready Answer

An interface is a contract that defines what a class should provide, without requiring the class to inherit a particular implementation hierarchy. A class or struct that implements an interface must provide implementations for its required members.

Example:

public interface IPayment
{
    void ProcessPayment();
}

Implementation:

public class CreditCardPayment : IPayment
{
    public void ProcessPayment()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Processing credit card payment");
    }
}

Usage:

IPayment payment = new CreditCardPayment();

payment.ProcessPayment();

Real-World Scenario

Imagine your application supports:

IPayment
   |
   +── CreditCardPayment
   +── UpiPayment
   +── PayPalPayment

All payment types must provide:

ProcessPayment()

But each implementation can work differently.

2. Why do we use Interfaces?

Interview-Ready Answer

We use interfaces to define contracts, achieve loose coupling, support polymorphism, and allow a class to implement multiple capabilities.

For example:

public interface IEmailSender
{
    void SendEmail(string message);
}

Then:

public class SmtpEmailSender : IEmailSender
{
    public void SendEmail(string message)
    {
        // SMTP implementation
    }
}

Later we can have:

public class SendGridEmailSender : IEmailSender
{
    public void SendEmail(string message)
    {
        // SendGrid implementation
    }
}

The consuming code can depend on:

IEmailSender

instead of:

SmtpEmailSender

This is especially important in Dependency Injection, which we'll cover later.

3. Can a Class Implement an Interface?

Yes.

Syntax:

public class Developer : IEmployee
{
}

Example:

public interface IEmployee
{
    void Work();
}

public class Developer : IEmployee
{
    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Developer is working");
    }
}

The : is used for both:

  • class inheritance
  • interface implementation

But conceptually:

class Developer : Employee
        ↓
      inherits

class Developer : IEmployee
        ↓
      implements

4. Does a Class have to Implement Every Interface Member?

For interface members that don't already have an implementation, a concrete implementing type must provide an implementation.

public interface IEmployee
{
    void Work();
    void Login();
}

This is incomplete:

public class Developer : IEmployee
{
    public void Work()
    {
    }
}

Login() is missing.

You need:

public class Developer : IEmployee
{
    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Working");
    }

    public void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Logging in");
    }
}

Or make the class abstract:

public abstract class Developer : IEmployee
{
}

A concrete implementing type must provide or inherit implementations for the required interface members. Microsoft Learn

5. Can a Class Implement Multiple Interfaces?

Yes — very important.

This is one of the major advantages of interfaces.

public interface IReadable
{
    void Read();
}

public interface IWritable
{
    void Write();
}

public class FileManager : IReadable, IWritable
{
    public void Read()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Reading");
    }

    public void Write()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Writing");
    }
}

A class can implement multiple interfaces. Microsoft Learn

Memory Trick

Class
  ↓
One base class

Class
  ↓
Multiple interfaces

For example:

public class Developer : Employee, IDeveloper, ITeamMember
{
}

6. Can an Interface Inherit Another Interface?

Yes.

public interface IEmployee
{
    void Work();
}

public interface IDeveloper : IEmployee
{
    void WriteCode();
}

Now:

public class BackendDeveloper : IDeveloper
{
    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Working");
    }

    public void WriteCode()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Writing C#");
    }
}

IDeveloper inherits IEmployee, so BackendDeveloper needs to implement both contracts.

7. Can an Interface Inherit Multiple Interfaces?

Yes.

public interface IDeveloper
{
    void WriteCode();
}

public interface IEmployee
{
    void Login();
}

public interface ISeniorDeveloper : IDeveloper, IEmployee
{
    void ReviewCode();
}

Now:

ISeniorDeveloper
      |
      +── IDeveloper
      |
      +── IEmployee
      |
      +── ReviewCode()

Interfaces can inherit from multiple base interfaces. Microsoft Learn

This is different from class inheritance.

8. Can an Interface Contain Methods?

Yes.

Traditional interface:

public interface IPayment
{
    void ProcessPayment();
}

The method has no implementation.

Modern C# also supports interface methods with default implementations, which we'll discuss shortly. Microsoft Learn

9. Can an Interface Contain Properties?

Yes.

public interface IEmployee
{
    int EmployeeId { get; set; }

    string Name { get; }
}

Implementation:

public class Employee : IEmployee
{
    public int EmployeeId { get; set; }

    public string Name { get; set; }
}

10. Can an Interface Contain Fields?

This is a tricky modern-C# question.

An interface cannot have ordinary instance fields like a class:

public interface IEmployee
{
    // ❌ No instance field
    // private int employeeId;
}

But interfaces can contain certain static fields/constants in modern C#.

For normal application-level interface design, think:

Interface
→ Contract
→ Methods
→ Properties
→ Events
→ Indexers

rather than storing instance state.

11. Can an Interface Have Constructors?

Normally, no instance constructors.

You don't create an interface object:

IPayment payment = new IPayment(); // ❌

Interfaces don't have instance constructors because they don't represent an instantiable object.

Modern C# does have static constructors for interfaces, but this is an advanced feature and rarely relevant to normal .NET interviews. Microsoft Learn

12. Can We Create an Object of an Interface?

No.

IPayment payment = new IPayment(); // ❌

But we can create a concrete object and store it in an interface reference:

IPayment payment = new CreditCardPayment(); // ✅

This is extremely important for understanding polymorphism.

Interface reference
       ↓
Concrete object
       ↓
CreditCardPayment

13. Why Use an Interface Reference?

Consider:

IPayment payment = new CreditCardPayment();

payment.ProcessPayment();

The calling code only knows:

IPayment

It doesn't need to know:

CreditCardPayment

Later:

IPayment payment = new UpiPayment();

The calling code can remain the same.

Real-World Example

In an ASP.NET Core application:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IPaymentService _paymentService;

    public OrderService(IPaymentService paymentService)
    {
        _paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}

OrderService depends on the interface, not a specific implementation.

This leads directly into:

Dependency Injection + Dependency Inversion

which you'll study later.

14. Can an Interface Contain Events?

Yes.

public interface INotificationService
{
    event EventHandler NotificationSent;
}

A class can implement it:

public class NotificationService : INotificationService
{
    public event EventHandler NotificationSent;
}

15. Can an Interface Contain Indexers?

Yes.

public interface IRepository
{
    string this[int id] { get; }
}

Implementation:

public class Repository : IRepository
{
    public string this[int id]
    {
        get
        {
            return $"Item {id}";
        }
    }
}

16. What Access Modifier Do Interface Members Have?

This is a common interview question.

For interface members without implementation, they are implicitly public.

Example:

public interface IEmployee
{
    void Work();
}

is effectively:

public interface IEmployee
{
    public void Work();
}

For interface members with default implementations, modern C# has more nuanced accessibility rules. Microsoft Learn

For your normal interview answer:

Traditional abstract interface members are public by default.

17. Can We Write private Methods in an Interface?

Yes — in modern C#.

This is an advanced feature.

public interface ILogger
{
    void Log()
    {
        Validate();
        Console.WriteLine("Logging");
    }

    private void Validate()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Validating");
    }
}

Private interface members are useful for supporting implementation details of default interface methods.

For your interview preparation:

Know it, but don't prioritize it over core interface concepts.

18. What is Default Interface Implementation?

This is an important modern C# topic.

Interfaces can provide a default implementation for some members.

public interface ILogger
{
    void Log()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Default logging");
    }
}

Then:

public class FileLogger : ILogger
{
}

The class doesn't have to provide its own Log() because the interface already provides an implementation.

However:

var logger = new FileLogger();

// logger.Log(); ❌

The default interface member is accessed through an interface reference:

ILogger logger = new FileLogger();

logger.Log(); // ✅

Microsoft documents default interface implementations as a way for interfaces to provide implementation while allowing implementing types to override it. Microsoft Learn

Interview Answer

Modern C# allows interfaces to contain default implementations. This helps evolve interfaces by adding behavior without necessarily requiring every existing implementation to immediately provide that member.

19. Why Were Default Interface Implementations Introduced?

Imagine:

public interface ILogger
{
    void Log();
}

You have 100 classes implementing it.

Later you want:

void LogError();

Traditionally, every implementation would need to implement the new method.

Default implementation allows the interface itself to provide behavior.

public interface ILogger
{
    void Log();

    void LogError()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Error");
    }
}

This can help evolve interfaces while preserving existing implementations. Microsoft Learn

20. Can an Interface Have Static Members?

Yes.

Modern C# interfaces can contain static members.

For example:

public interface IUtility
{
    static void Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Hello");
    }
}

There are also static abstract and static virtual interface members in modern C#, mainly useful for generic abstractions and operator-like contracts. Microsoft Learn

For your 3+ YOE interview:

Know that they exist, but don't prioritize them over normal interface implementation.

21. Can an Interface be abstract?

You don't normally write:

public abstract interface IPayment

An interface is already a contract/abstraction, so abstract isn't used like it is with classes.

Think:

public interface IPayment
{
}

22. Can an Interface be sealed?

No.

An interface is designed to be implemented/inherited by other types/interfaces, so sealed interface isn't valid.

23. Can a Struct Implement an Interface?

Yes.

This is an important point.

public interface IPrintable
{
    void Print();
}

public struct Report : IPrintable
{
    public void Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Printing report");
    }
}

Interfaces can be implemented by both classes and structs. Microsoft Learn

24. Can a Record Implement an Interface?

Yes.

public interface IAuditable
{
    void Audit();
}

public record Employee(string Name) : IAuditable
{
    public void Audit()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Auditing");
    }
}

Interfaces can be implemented by classes, structs, and records.

25. What happens if Two Interfaces Have the Same Method?

Example:

public interface IPrinter
{
    void Print();
}

public interface IScanner
{
    void Print();
}

A class can provide one implementation:

public class Machine : IPrinter, IScanner
{
    public void Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Printing");
    }
}

Both interfaces will use the same implementation.

IPrinter printer = new Machine();
IScanner scanner = new Machine();

printer.Print();
scanner.Print();

Both call:

Machine.Print()

Microsoft documents this as normal interface mapping when the signatures match. Microsoft Learn

26. What if I Need Different Implementations for the Two Interfaces?

This is where Explicit Interface Implementation comes in.

public interface IPrinter
{
    void Print();
}

public interface IScanner
{
    void Print();
}

public class Machine : IPrinter, IScanner
{
    void IPrinter.Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Printer implementation");
    }

    void IScanner.Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Scanner implementation");
    }
}

Usage:

IPrinter printer = new Machine();
IScanner scanner = new Machine();

printer.Print();
scanner.Print();

Output:

Printer implementation
Scanner implementation

But:

Machine machine = new Machine();

machine.Print(); // ❌

The explicit implementations are accessed through their respective interface references. Microsoft Learn

Don't go too deep into this yet—we have it as topic #12: Explicit Interface Implementation.

27. Interface vs Inheritance

Suppose:

public class Dog : Animal

This represents:

Dog is an Animal.

Whereas:

public class Dog : IWalkable

represents:

Dog can walk / supports this capability.

A useful mental model:

Inheritance
    ↓
IS-A relationship

Interface
    ↓
CAN-DO / CONTRACT

Example:

public class Developer : Employee, ICodeReviewer, IMentor

Here:

Developer IS AN Employee

Developer CAN review code

Developer CAN mentor

28. Interface vs Abstract Class — Basic Difference

We'll cover this in depth as Topic #11, but you should already know the core distinction.

Interface

Primarily defines a contract/capability:

public interface IPayment
{
    void Process();
}

Abstract Class

Can define a common base with state + implementation + abstract behavior:

public abstract class Payment
{
    protected decimal Amount;

    public void Validate()
    {
    }

    public abstract void Process();
}

Memory Trick

Interface → Contract

Abstract Class → Contract + Shared Base Implementation/State

29. Interface and Polymorphism

This is extremely important.

public interface IPayment
{
    void Process();
}

public class CreditCardPayment : IPayment
{
    public void Process()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Credit Card");
    }
}

public class UpiPayment : IPayment
{
    public void Process()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("UPI");
    }
}

Now:

IPayment payment;

payment = new CreditCardPayment();
payment.Process();

payment = new UpiPayment();
payment.Process();

Output:

Credit Card
UPI

This is runtime polymorphism through an interface.

30. Interface in ASP.NET Core — Real-World Example

This is particularly important for your .NET interviews.

Suppose you have:

public interface IOrderService
{
    Task CreateOrderAsync();
}

Implementation:

public class OrderService : IOrderService
{
    public async Task CreateOrderAsync()
    {
        // Business logic
    }
}

Register it:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

Controller:

public class OrdersController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IOrderService _orderService;

    public OrdersController(IOrderService orderService)
    {
        _orderService = orderService;
    }
}

The controller depends on:

IOrderService

rather than:

OrderService

This gives you:

  • Loose coupling
  • Easier testing
  • Replaceable implementations
  • Dependency Injection
  • Better maintainability

This is one of the most useful ways to explain interfaces in a real .NET project interview.

31. Why are Interfaces useful for Unit Testing?

Suppose:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IPaymentService _paymentService;

    public OrderService(IPaymentService paymentService)
    {
        _paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}

During testing, you can provide a mock implementation of:

IPaymentService

instead of calling the actual payment provider.

For example, with Moq:

var mockPayment = new Mock<IPaymentService>();

mockPayment
    .Setup(x => x.ProcessPayment())
    .Returns(true);

This is a very practical interview connection:

Interface
   ↓
Loose Coupling
   ↓
Dependency Injection
   ↓
Mocking
   ↓
Unit Testing

For your 3+ YOE target, I'd prioritize them like this:

🔴 Must Know

  1. What is an interface?
  1. Why do we use interfaces?
  1. How do you implement an interface?
  1. Can a class implement multiple interfaces?
  1. Can an interface inherit another interface?
  1. Can an interface inherit multiple interfaces?
  1. Can we instantiate an interface?
  1. Why can we use an interface reference?
  1. Does a class have to implement all interface members?
  1. Can an interface contain methods/properties/events?
  1. Interface vs abstract class — basic understanding.
  1. How are interfaces used in ASP.NET Core?
  1. How does an interface support polymorphism?
  1. Interface and Dependency Injection relationship.

🟡 Strong Interview Level

  1. What happens if two interfaces have the same method?
  1. How do you provide different implementations for them?
  1. What is explicit interface implementation?
  1. Can a struct implement an interface?
  1. Can an abstract class implement an interface?
  1. Can an interface inherit multiple interfaces?
  1. Can an interface have default implementations?
  1. Why were default interface implementations introduced?

  1. What access modifiers can interface members have?
  1. Can interfaces have private methods?

  1. Static virtual interface members
  1. Interface mapping
