  1. Default interface implementation behavior
  1. Interface variance — later under Generics

🎯 30-Second Interview Answer

If they ask:

"What is an interface in C#?"

Say:

An interface is a contract that defines a set of members that an implementing type should provide. It helps achieve loose coupling, abstraction, and polymorphism. Unlike class inheritance, a class can implement multiple interfaces. In ASP.NET Core, interfaces are commonly used with Dependency Injection, where a service depends on an abstraction rather than a concrete implementation. For example, an IOrderService can be implemented by OrderService, and the controller can depend on IOrderService, making the code easier to test and maintain.

🧠 Remember

INTERFACE
   │
   ├── Contract
   │
   ├── Multiple interfaces
   │
   ├── Polymorphism
   │
   ├── Loose coupling
   │
   ├── Dependency Injection
   │
   ├── Unit testing / Mocking
   │
   └── Modern C#
        └── Default implementations

11. Interface vs Abstract Class — C# Interview Preparation

The key idea is:

Abstract class = common base + shared state/implementation + abstraction

Interface = contract/capability + loose coupling

A class can have only one direct base class, but it can implement multiple interfaces. Microsoft Learn

1. What is the main difference between an Interface and Abstract Class?

Interview-Ready Answer

An abstract class is used when related classes share common state or implementation, while an interface is mainly used to define a contract or capability that different types can implement. A class can inherit from only one direct base class but can implement multiple interfaces.

Example

Abstract class:

public abstract class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee Login");
    }

    public abstract void Work();
}

Interface:

public interface IReportGenerator
{
    void GenerateReport();
}

Here:

Employee
   ↓
Developer
   ↓
shares common employee behavior/state

IReportGenerator
   ↓
defines a capability/contract

2. Can an Abstract Class have implemented methods while an Interface cannot?

Old/Traditional Answer

Historically, this was a major difference.

Abstract class:

public abstract class Payment
{
    public void Validate()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Validation");
    }

    public abstract void Process();
}

Traditional interface:

public interface IPayment
{
    void Process();
}

However, modern C# interfaces can also provide default implementations. Microsoft Learn

So don't say in an interview:

"Interfaces cannot have implementations."

That is outdated.

Better answer

An abstract class can naturally contain shared implementation and state. Modern C# interfaces can also contain default implementations, but an abstract class is generally the better choice when shared state, constructors, or substantial common implementation is required.

3. Can an Abstract Class have fields while an Interface cannot have instance fields?

Yes.

Abstract class:

public abstract class Employee
{
    protected int employeeId;
    protected string name;
}

An interface cannot contain ordinary instance fields. Its properties don't automatically create per-instance storage. Microsoft Learn

For example:

public interface IEmployee
{
    int EmployeeId { get; set; }
}

The implementing class owns the actual storage:

public class Developer : IEmployee
{
    public int EmployeeId { get; set; }
}

Interview Answer

An abstract class can maintain instance state through fields, whereas an interface doesn't provide instance state. Interface properties define a contract; the implementing type provides the storage and implementation.

4. Can an Abstract Class have a Constructor?

Yes.

public abstract class Employee
{
    protected Employee(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }

    public string Name { get; }
}

Derived class:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public Developer(string name) : base(name)
    {
    }
}

The base constructor runs when the derived object is created.

Interface?

Interfaces don't have instance constructors. Microsoft Learn

Interview Answer

Abstract classes can have constructors because they can own and initialize common state. Interfaces don't have instance constructors because they don't represent an instantiable object with instance state.

5. Can a Class inherit an Abstract Class and implement an Interface at the same time?

Yes — extremely important.

public abstract class Employee
{
    public abstract void Work();
}

public interface IReportGenerator
{
    void GenerateReport();
}

public class Developer : Employee, IReportGenerator
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Writing code");
    }

    public void GenerateReport()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Generating report");
    }
}

This is very common in real applications.

              Employee
                  ↓
              Developer
              ↙       ↘
       Work()       IReportGenerator
                       ↓
                GenerateReport()

Remember the syntax

The base class comes first:

class Developer : Employee, IReportGenerator

not:

class Developer : IReportGenerator, Employee // ❌

Microsoft's current C# reference specifies that when a base type list contains both a base class and interfaces, the base class must come first. Microsoft Learn

6. Why can a class implement multiple interfaces but inherit only one class?

C# supports single class inheritance:

public class Developer : Employee
{
}

But multiple interfaces:

public class Developer : Employee, IDeveloper, IMentor, IReviewer
{
}

Why?

Multiple class inheritance can create ambiguity around:

  • inherited implementation
  • state
  • constructors
  • member conflicts

Interfaces primarily define contracts/capabilities, making multiple implementation practical.

Microsoft confirms that a class can implement multiple interfaces even though it can have only one direct base class. Microsoft Learn

Interview Answer

C# allows only one direct base class to avoid the complexity of multiple class inheritance, but allows multiple interfaces because they represent contracts or capabilities rather than multiple class-state hierarchies.

7. When should I use an Abstract Class?

Use an abstract class when the derived classes are closely related and share common implementation or state.

Example

public abstract class Employee
{
    protected string Name;

    protected Employee(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }

    public void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} logged in");
    }

    public abstract void Work();
}

Then:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public Developer(string name) : base(name)
    {
    }

    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Writing code");
    }
}

Good use case

Employee
   ├── Developer
   ├── Tester
   └── Manager

All employees share:

  • Name
  • Employee ID
  • Login
  • Logout
  • common validation

but their work differs.

8. When should I use an Interface?

Use an interface when you want to define a capability or contract, especially when unrelated classes may implement that capability.

Example:

public interface INotificationSender
{
    void Send(string message);
}

Implementations:

public class EmailSender : INotificationSender
{
    public void Send(string message)
    {
        // Email
    }
}
public class SmsSender : INotificationSender
{
    public void Send(string message)
    {
        // SMS
    }
}

These classes don't necessarily need to share a common base class.

Memory trick

Abstract class → IS-A relationship

Interface → CAN-DO capability

For example:

Developer IS AN Employee

Developer CAN:
    → GenerateReport
    → ReviewCode
    → Mentor

9. Can an Abstract Class implement an Interface?

Yes.

public interface IEmployee
{
    void Work();
}

public abstract class Employee : IEmployee
{
    public abstract void Work();
}

The abstract class is effectively saying:

"I accept this contract, but I'll leave the actual implementation to my concrete derived classes."

Then:

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Coding");
    }
}

This is explicitly supported by C#. Microsoft Learn

10. Can an Interface inherit from another Interface?

Yes.

public interface IEmployee
{
    void Work();
}

public interface IDeveloper : IEmployee
{
    void WriteCode();
}

And multiple:

public interface ISeniorDeveloper : IDeveloper, IReviewer
{
    void Mentor();
}

Interfaces can inherit multiple base interfaces. Microsoft Learn

An abstract class cannot inherit multiple classes.

11. Abstract Class vs Interface — Interview Table

This is the table you should memorize.

FeatureAbstract ClassInterface
Instantiation❌ Cannot instantiate❌ Cannot instantiate
Instance fields✅ Yes❌ No
Properties✅ Yes✅ Yes
Constructors✅ Yes❌ No instance constructors
Concrete methods✅ Yes✅ Modern C# supports default implementations
Abstract members✅ Yes✅ Members without bodies are abstract by default
Virtual members✅ Yes✅ Modern C# supports virtual/default members
Multiple inheritance❌ Multiple classes not allowed✅ Multiple interfaces
Class can implement multiple?N/A✅ Yes
Shared state✅ Yes❌ No instance state
Access modifiersFull flexibilityInterface member rules differ; traditional abstract members are public
Static members✅ Yes✅ Modern C# supports static members
Main purposeCommon base + shared implementation/stateContract/capability
RelationshipUsually IS-AUsually CAN-DO
DI usagePossibleVery common
Mocking/testingPossibleVery common

Modern C# has made interfaces more capable than they were historically, including default implementations and static abstract/virtual members. Microsoft Learn

12. Which is Better for Dependency Injection: Interface or Abstract Class?

Don't answer simply "interface is better."

Interview-Ready Answer

Both can be used with Dependency Injection, but interfaces are very commonly used because they represent contracts and allow multiple implementations without forcing a class hierarchy. They also make dependencies easy to replace during testing.

Example:

public interface IEmailService
{
    Task SendAsync(string message);
}

Implementation:

public class EmailService : IEmailService
{
    public Task SendAsync(string message)
    {
        // Send email
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

Registration:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IEmailService, EmailService>();

Consumer:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IEmailService _emailService;

    public OrderService(IEmailService emailService)
    {
        _emailService = emailService;
    }
}

This is a very strong real-world .NET interview example.

13. Which is Better for Unit Testing?

Again, don't say one is universally better.

But interfaces are frequently convenient:

public interface IPaymentService
{
    bool ProcessPayment();
}

Production:

public class PaymentService : IPaymentService
{
    public bool ProcessPayment()
    {
        // Real payment logic
        return true;
    }
}

Test:

var mock = new Mock<IPaymentService>();

mock.Setup(x => x.ProcessPayment())
    .Returns(true);

Then your service can depend on:

IPaymentService

instead of the concrete implementation.

Interview Answer

Interfaces make it easy to substitute implementations, which is particularly useful for mocking external dependencies such as payment gateways, repositories, email services, or HTTP clients.

14. Real-World .NET Example — Abstract Class + Interfaces

This is a great senior-level example.

Suppose you're building an order system.

public interface IAuditable
{
    void Audit();
}
public abstract class Order
{
    public int OrderId { get; set; }

    public void Validate()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Order validated");
    }

    public abstract void Process();
}

Then:

public class OnlineOrder : Order, IAuditable
{
    public override void Process()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Processing online order");
    }

    public void Audit()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Auditing online order");
    }
}

Here:

Order
 ├── Common state
 │     └── OrderId
 │
 ├── Common behavior
 │     └── Validate()
 │
 └── Variable behavior
       └── Process()

IAuditable
 └── Audit()

This demonstrates why the two concepts aren't necessarily competitors.

You can use both together.

15. What if I Need State?

Prefer an abstract class when the abstraction needs shared instance state.

Example:

public abstract class Payment
{
    protected decimal Amount;

    protected Payment(decimal amount)
    {
        Amount = amount;
    }

    public abstract void Process();
}

An interface wouldn't be appropriate for storing Amount as instance state.

16. What if I Need Multiple Capabilities?

Prefer interfaces.

public class Developer :
    Employee,
    ICodeReviewer,
    IMentor,
    IReportGenerator
{
}

This is a strong reason interfaces are common in larger applications.

17. What if Two Unrelated Classes Need the Same Capability?

Interface is a good fit.

public interface ILoggable
{
    void Log();
}

Then:

public class Order : ILoggable
{
    public void Log()
    {
    }
}

and:

public class Payment : ILoggable
{
    public void Log()
    {
    }
}

Order and Payment don't need to belong to the same inheritance hierarchy.

18. Tricky Interview Question: Can an Interface Have Implementation?

Correct answer

Yes, in modern C#.

public interface ILogger
{
    void Log()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Default logging");
    }
}

Don't say:

"Interfaces cannot have implementation."

Instead:

Traditionally interface members were contracts without implementations, but modern C# supports default interface implementations.

Microsoft's current documentation explicitly lists default implementations as an interface feature. Microsoft Learn

19. Tricky Question: Can an Interface Have a Constructor?

Answer

An interface cannot have an instance constructor.
IPayment payment = new IPayment(); // ❌

The interface itself isn't instantiated.

C#'s language specification explicitly disallows instance constructors in interfaces. Microsoft Learn

20. Tricky Question: Can an Interface Have Fields?

Answer

It cannot have ordinary instance fields. Modern C# does support static fields in interfaces, but an interface cannot use instance fields to store per-object state.

This distinction is useful for a senior interview because simply saying "interfaces can't have fields" is now incomplete. Microsoft Learn

21. Tricky Question: Can an Abstract Class implement Multiple Interfaces?

Yes.

public abstract class Employee :
    IAuditable,
    ITrackable
{
}

And a concrete class can inherit that abstract class and implement additional interfaces:

public class Developer :
    Employee,
    ICodeReviewer
{
}

22. The Best Way to Explain the Difference in an Interview

If the interviewer asks:

"When would you choose an interface versus an abstract class?"

Give this answer:

I would use an abstract class when the types have a strong common relationship and need shared state, constructors, or common implementation. I would use an interface when I want to define a contract or capability that can be implemented by different and potentially unrelated types. Interfaces are also useful for loose coupling and Dependency Injection.

Then give an example:

For example, I might have an abstract Employee class containing common employee state and behavior, while interfaces such as IReportGenerator or IAuditable represent capabilities that different classes can implement.

That's a very strong 3+ YOE answer.

Tier 1 — Must Know

  1. What is the difference between an interface and abstract class?
  1. When would you choose an interface?
  1. When would you choose an abstract class?
  1. Can an abstract class implement an interface?
  1. Can a class inherit an abstract class and implement interfaces?
  1. Why can a class implement multiple interfaces?
  1. Can an interface contain implementation?
  1. Can an abstract class have constructors?
  1. Can an interface have constructors?
  1. Can an interface have fields?
  1. Can an abstract class have fields?
  1. Can an interface inherit multiple interfaces?

Tier 2 — Strong 3+ YOE

  1. Interface vs abstract class for Dependency Injection.
  1. Interface vs abstract class for unit testing.
  1. Interface reference vs abstract class reference.
  1. How does interface polymorphism work?
  1. What happens if two interfaces contain the same method?
  1. When would you use explicit interface implementation?
  1. Can a struct implement an interface?
  1. Can an abstract class partially implement an interface?
  1. Can an interface have default implementations?
  1. Why were default interface implementations introduced?

Tier 3 — Advanced

  1. Static abstract interface members.
  1. Static virtual interface members.
  1. Interface mapping.
  1. Reabstraction.
  1. Default interface implementation resolution.
  1. Interface inheritance conflicts.

🎯 One-Line Memory Trick

ABSTRACT CLASS
= "These classes belong to the same family."

INTERFACE
= "These types support the same capability."

Example:

Employee                         IAuditable
   │                                 │
   ├── Developer                     ├── Developer
   ├── Tester                        ├── Order
   └── Manager                       └── Payment

Abstract class → shared identity/state/implementation

Interface → shared contract/capability

30-Second Final Answer

An abstract class is useful when related classes need a common base with shared state, constructors, and implementation, while an interface is mainly used to define a contract or capability. A class can inherit only one direct base class but can implement multiple interfaces. In a .NET application, I would commonly use an abstract class for a domain hierarchy such as Employee, and interfaces such as IEmailService or IRepository for loose coupling and Dependency Injection. Modern C# also supports default interface implementations, so interfaces are more capable than the traditional contract-only model. Microsoft Learn

12. Explicit Interface Implementation

The core idea:

Explicit interface implementation allows a class to provide a specific implementation for an interface member that is accessible only through that interface reference. Microsoft Learn

1. What is Explicit Interface Implementation?

Interview-Ready Answer

Explicit interface implementation is a way of implementing an interface member by prefixing the member with the interface name. The member is then accessible only through a reference of that interface type, not directly through the class object.

Example:

public interface IPrinter
{
    void Print();
}

public class Document : IPrinter
{
    void IPrinter.Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Printing document");
    }
}

Usage:

Document document = new Document();

// document.Print(); // ❌ Compile-time error

IPrinter printer = document;

printer.Print(); // ✅

Microsoft documents that an explicitly implemented member isn't accessible directly through the class instance; it is accessed through the interface reference. Microsoft Learn

2. Why do we need Explicit Interface Implementation?

The most common reason is when a class implements two interfaces having the same member name/signature, but you want different behavior.

Example:

public interface IPrinter
{
    void Print();
}

public interface IScanner
{
    void Print();
}

If you use normal implementation:

public class Machine : IPrinter, IScanner
{
    public void Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Printing...");
    }
}

Both interfaces use the same implementation.

IPrinter printer = new Machine();
IScanner scanner = new Machine();

printer.Print();
scanner.Print();

Both call:

Machine.Print()

That's perfectly valid. Microsoft Learn

But what if you want different implementations?

That's where explicit implementation comes in.

3. How do you implement two interfaces with the same method differently?

public interface IPrinter
{
    void Print();
}

public interface IScanner
{
    void Print();
}

public class Machine : IPrinter, IScanner
{
    void IPrinter.Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Printing document");
    }

    void IScanner.Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Scanning document");
    }
}

Now:

IPrinter printer = new Machine();
IScanner scanner = new Machine();

printer.Print();
scanner.Print();

Output:

Printing document
Scanning document

The important syntax

void IPrinter.Print()

and:

void IScanner.Print()

The interface name is explicitly included.

4. Can we call an explicitly implemented method directly through the class?

No.

Machine machine = new Machine();

machine.Print(); // ❌

There is no directly accessible Print() member on Machine.

Instead:

IPrinter printer = machine;

printer.Print(); // ✅

or:

IScanner scanner = machine;

scanner.Print(); // ✅

This restricted accessibility is one of the defining characteristics of explicit implementation. Microsoft Learn

5. Why is it not accessible through the class?

Because explicit interface implementation is specifically designed to keep that implementation associated with the interface contract rather than exposing it as a normal public class member.

Think:

Machine
   │
   ├── IPrinter.Print()
   │       ↓
   │   only IPrinter reference
   │
   └── IScanner.Print()
           ↓
       only IScanner reference

6. Does Explicit Interface Implementation use public?

No.

This is a common interview trick.

Correct:

void IPrinter.Print()
{
}

Incorrect:

public void IPrinter.Print()
{
}

You cannot specify a normal access modifier such as public or private on an explicit interface member implementation. Microsoft Learn

Interview Answer

An explicit interface implementation doesn't use an access modifier because it isn't accessed as a normal member of the implementing class. It is accessed through the interface.

7. Can we use override with Explicit Interface Implementation?

No.

Don't write:

public override void IPrinter.Print()
{
}

or:

override void IPrinter.Print()
{
}

Explicit interface implementation is not class inheritance overriding.

Correct:

void IPrinter.Print()
{
}

8. Explicit vs Implicit Interface Implementation

This is a very important comparison.

Implicit implementation

public interface IPrinter
{
    void Print();
}

public class Printer : IPrinter
{
    public void Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Print");
    }
}

You can call:

Printer printer = new Printer();

printer.Print(); // ✅

You can also call:

IPrinter printer = new Printer();

printer.Print(); // ✅

Explicit implementation

public class Printer : IPrinter
{
    void IPrinter.Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Print");
    }
}

Now:

Printer printer = new Printer();

printer.Print(); // ❌

But:

IPrinter printer = new Printer();

printer.Print(); // ✅

Easy memory trick

Implicit
→ public method
→ accessible through class
→ accessible through interface

Explicit
→ interface-qualified method
→ NOT accessible through class
→ accessible through interface

9. Why would you choose Explicit Implementation?

There are several important reasons.

Reason 1 — Two interfaces have the same method

IPrinter.Print()
IScanner.Print()

but you want different behavior.

Reason 2 — Hide an interface-specific member from the public class API

Suppose:

public interface IInternalProcessor
{
    void InternalProcess();
}

You don't want:

Processor processor = new Processor();

processor.InternalProcess();

to be part of the normal public API.

You can explicitly implement it:

public class Processor : IInternalProcessor
{
    void IInternalProcessor.InternalProcess()
    {
        // internal implementation
    }
}

Now consumers using the class don't see it as a normal public member.

Microsoft specifically notes that explicit implementations can keep interface implementations out of the public surface of the implementing type. Microsoft Learn

10. Real-World Example

Imagine a multifunction device:

Machine
   ├── IPrinter
   │      └── Print()
   │
   └── IScanner
          └── Print()

The word Print() means different things depending on the interface.

public interface IPrinter
{
    void Print();
}

public interface IScanner
{
    void Print();
}

public class MultiFunctionMachine : IPrinter, IScanner
{
    void IPrinter.Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Printing physical document");
    }

    void IScanner.Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Scanning document");
    }
}

Usage:

IPrinter printer = new MultiFunctionMachine();
printer.Print();

IScanner scanner = new MultiFunctionMachine();
scanner.Print();

Output:

Printing physical document
Scanning document

This is a classic interview example.

11. Can Explicit Implementation be used for Properties?

Yes.

It's not limited to methods.

public interface IUser
{
    string Name { get; }
}

public interface IEmployee
{
    string Name { get; }
}

Explicit implementation:

public class Person : IUser, IEmployee
{
    string IUser.Name => "User Name";

    string IEmployee.Name => "Employee Name";
}

Usage:

IUser user = new Person();
IEmployee employee = new Person();

Console.WriteLine(user.Name);
Console.WriteLine(employee.Name);

Output:

User Name
Employee Name

Explicit interface implementation supports methods, properties, events, and indexers. Microsoft Learn

12. Can Explicit Implementation be used for Events?

Yes.

public interface INotifier
{
    event EventHandler NotificationSent;
}

public class NotificationService : INotifier
{
    event EventHandler INotifier.NotificationSent;
}

The event is accessed through the interface.

13. Can Explicit Implementation be used for Indexers?

Yes.

For example:

public interface IData
{
    string this[int index] { get; }
}

Explicit implementation:

public class Data : IData
{
    string IData.this[int index]
    {
        get { return $"Item {index}"; }
    }
}

14. What happens if two interfaces have the same method and we use normal implementation?

Example:

public interface IA
{
    void Execute();
}

public interface IB
{
    void Execute();
}

Class:

public class Service : IA, IB
{
    public void Execute()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Execute");
    }
}

Then:

IA a = new Service();
IB b = new Service();

a.Execute();
b.Execute();

Both call:

Service.Execute()

This is called one implementation satisfying both interface members. Microsoft Learn

15. What if I want different implementations?

Use explicit implementation:

public class Service : IA, IB
{
    void IA.Execute()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("IA implementation");
    }

    void IB.Execute()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("IB implementation");
    }
}

Then:

IA a = new Service();
IB b = new Service();

a.Execute();
b.Execute();

Output:

IA implementation
IB implementation

16. Does Explicit Interface Implementation support polymorphism?

Yes.

This is important.

IA service = new Service();

service.Execute();

The runtime uses the implementation corresponding to IA.

And:

IB service = new Service();

service.Execute();

uses the implementation corresponding to IB.

So the interface reference determines which explicit implementation is accessed.

17. Can an Explicit Interface Method be called inside the class?

Not directly using the class member syntax.

For example:

public class Service : IA
{
    void IA.Execute()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Execute");
    }

    public void Run()
    {
        // Execute(); // ❌
    }
}

You can cast this to the interface:

public void Run()
{
    ((IA)this).Execute();
}

Now it can be invoked.

18. Is Explicit Interface Implementation private?

This is a tricky interview question.

The best answer is:

It behaves like a private member when accessed through the class, because it isn't accessible through the class type. But it is accessible through the interface reference.

Microsoft describes explicit implementations as having unusual accessibility: they are not accessible through the class, but are accessible through the interface. Microsoft Learn

So don't simply say:

"It's private."

Better:

It is interface-only accessible.

19. Can we explicitly implement an interface member without listing the interface?

No.

Suppose:

public interface IPrinter
{
    void Print();
}

This is invalid:

public class Printer
{
    void IPrinter.Print()
    {
    }
}

The class needs to implement the interface:

public class Printer : IPrinter
{
    void IPrinter.Print()
    {
    }
}

The interface must be part of the class's implemented interfaces/base interface list. Microsoft Learn

20. Can a derived class explicitly implement an interface already implemented by the base class?

This is a more advanced question.

Suppose:

public interface IPrinter
{
    void Print();
}

public class BasePrinter : IPrinter
{
    public void Print()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Base");
    }
}

A derived class doesn't simply re-explicitly implement IPrinter.Print() unless the interface is part of the derived type's relevant interface list.

For normal interviews, remember:

Explicit implementation is tied to an interface that the implementing type is declaring/implementing in its interface list, subject to the language's interface mapping rules. Microsoft Learn

This is advanced, so don't spend much study time here yet.

21. Explicit Interface Implementation with IDisposable

This is a very useful real-world .NET example.

You may see:

public class Resource : IDisposable
{
    void IDisposable.Dispose()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Cleaning resources");
    }
}

Now:

Resource resource = new Resource();

// resource.Dispose(); // ❌

But:

IDisposable disposable = resource;

disposable.Dispose(); // ✅

This pattern can be useful when you want an interface-specific operation without exposing it as a normal member of the class.

Microsoft's specification itself uses IDisposable.Dispose() as an example of explicit implementation. Microsoft Learn

22. Explicit Interface Implementation vs Method Overloading

Don't confuse these.

Overloading

public void Print()
{
}

public void Print(string text)
{
}

Same method name, different parameters.

Explicit interface implementation

void IPrinter.Print()
{
}

void IScanner.Print()
{
}

Same method name/signature, but different interface contracts.

23. Common Interview Trap

Question:

public interface IA
{
    void Test();
}

public interface IB
{
    void Test();
}

public class C : IA, IB
{
    public void Test()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("C");
    }
}

What happens?

Answer:

Both:

IA a = new C();
IB b = new C();

call:

C.Test()

There is no ambiguity because one public method can satisfy both interfaces. Microsoft Learn

24. Another Interview Trap

Question:

What happens here?

public class C : IA, IB
{
    void IA.Test()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("A");
    }

    void IB.Test()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("B");
    }
}

Then:

C obj = new C();

obj.Test();

Answer:

Compile-time error.

Because Test() isn't exposed as a normal member of C.

You need:

IA a = obj;
a.Test();

or:

IB b = obj;
b.Test();

25. Implicit vs Explicit — Quick Table

FeatureImplicitExplicit
Syntaxpublic void Print()void IPrinter.Print()
Access through class✅❌
Access through interface✅✅
Access modifierUsually public❌ Not specified
Different implementation per interface❌✅
Hides interface member from class API❌✅
Common useNormal interface implementationConflicting members / interface-specific behavior

  1. What happens when two interfaces have the same method?
  1. How do you provide different implementations?

  1. Can properties be explicitly implemented?

🎯 30-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer asks:

"What is explicit interface implementation and when would you use it?"

Say:

Explicit interface implementation allows a class to implement an interface member using the interface-qualified name, such as void IPrinter.Print(). The member is then accessible only through an IPrinter reference and not directly through the class object. I would mainly use it when a class implements multiple interfaces with conflicting members and needs different implementations, or when I want an interface-specific member to stay out of the class's normal public API. Microsoft Learn

🧠 Remember this pattern

Interface
   ↓
IPrinter.Print()
   ↓
void IPrinter.Print()
   ↓
Only through IPrinter reference

And the most important interview scenario:

IPrinter.Print()  → Printing
IScanner.Print()  → Scanning
       ↓
Explicit Interface Implementation

13. Composition

What you should remember first

Composition means building a class by combining it with objects of other classes, instead of inheriting from them.

The relationship is usually described as "has-a", whereas inheritance represents "is-a". Microsoft similarly distinguishes inheritance as an is-a relationship and interface capabilities as a can-do relationship. Microsoft Learn

Common Interview Questions

1. What is Composition in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer

Composition is an OOP technique where a class contains objects of other classes and uses their functionality instead of inheriting from them.

It represents a has-a relationship.

Example

public class Engine
{
    public void Start()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Engine started");
    }
}

public class Car
{
    private Engine _engine;

    public Car()
    {
        _engine = new Engine();
    }

    public void StartCar()
    {
        _engine.Start();
        Console.WriteLine("Car started");
    }
}

Here:

Car HAS-A Engine

Car doesn't inherit from Engine.

It contains an Engine object and delegates the work to it.

Real-World Scenario

A car has an engine.

You wouldn't normally model:

Car : Engine

because a car is not an engine.

Instead:

Car
 └── Engine

That's composition.

2. What is the difference between Composition and Inheritance?

You will study the detailed comparison in Topic 14, but you should already know the basic distinction.

CompositionInheritance
Has-a relationshipIs-a relationship
Combines objectsExtends a base class
More flexibleMore tightly coupled
Behavior can often be changed by replacing dependencyBehavior is defined through class hierarchy
Car has EngineDog is Animal

Example

Inheritance:

public class Dog : Animal
{
}
Dog IS-A Animal

Composition:

public class Car
{
    private Engine _engine;
}
Car HAS-A Engine

Microsoft's C# documentation describes inheritance as creating specialized types from a base type, while classes can also combine functionality through contained objects. Microsoft Learn

3. Why would you use Composition?

Interview-Ready Answer

I use composition when a class needs functionality from another class but doesn't have an is-a relationship with it. It helps reduce coupling and allows behavior to be changed or replaced more easily.

Example

Suppose you have:

public class EmailSender
{
    public void SendEmail(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Email sent");
    }
}

Instead of making:

public class OrderService : EmailSender
{
}

you can use:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly EmailSender _emailSender;

    public OrderService(EmailSender emailSender)
    {
        _emailSender = emailSender;
    }

    public void PlaceOrder()
    {
        // Place order

        _emailSender.SendEmail("Order placed");
    }
}

Now:

OrderService HAS-A EmailSender

This is a much more natural relationship.

4. Can Composition be used with interfaces?

Yes. This is extremely important for .NET interviews.

Instead of depending directly on a concrete class:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly EmailSender _emailSender;
}

you can depend on an abstraction:

public interface INotificationService
{
    void Send(string message);
}

Implementation:

public class EmailNotificationService : INotificationService
{
    public void Send(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Email sent");
    }
}

Then:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly INotificationService _notificationService;

    public OrderService(INotificationService notificationService)
    {
        _notificationService = notificationService;
    }

    public void PlaceOrder()
    {
        _notificationService.Send("Order placed");
    }
}

Now:

OrderService
      |
      | HAS-A
      ↓
INotificationService
      ↑
      |
EmailNotificationService

This is a very common design in ASP.NET Core applications.

.NET's built-in DI system supports registering abstractions with implementations and injecting the dependency into the consuming class. Microsoft Learn

5. Is Composition the same as Dependency Injection?

No.

This is a very common interview trap.

Composition

Composition means:

A class uses/contains another object.

Dependency Injection

DI means:

The dependency is supplied from outside the class rather than the class creating it itself.

Compare:

Composition without DI

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly EmailSender _emailSender;

    public OrderService()
    {
        _emailSender = new EmailSender();
    }
}

OrderService contains/uses EmailSender.

That's composition.

But it is tightly coupled because OrderService creates the dependency itself.

Composition + DI

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly INotificationService _notificationService;

    public OrderService(INotificationService notificationService)
    {
        _notificationService = notificationService;
    }
}

Now the dependency is supplied externally.

That's:

Composition
     +
Dependency Injection
     +
Abstraction

Microsoft's DI guidance specifically notes that directly instantiating dependent classes couples the consuming code to a particular implementation. Microsoft Learn

6. What are the advantages of Composition?

Interview-Ready Answer

The main advantages are loose coupling, flexibility, better testability, and easier maintenance. We can change or replace one component without changing the class that uses it.

Example

Suppose:

public interface IPaymentService
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

You have:

public class CreditCardPayment : IPaymentService
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Credit Card Payment");
    }
}

and:

public class UpiPayment : IPaymentService
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("UPI Payment");
    }
}

Your service depends on:

IPaymentService

rather than:

CreditCardPayment

So the implementation can be changed.

OrderService
     |
     ↓
IPaymentService
   /       \
UPI      CreditCard

7. How does Composition improve testability?

Interview-Ready Answer

Because dependencies can be supplied from outside, we can replace real dependencies with mock or fake implementations during unit testing.

Production

OrderService
    ↓
RealPaymentService

Unit Test

OrderService
    ↓
MockPaymentService

Example:

public interface IPaymentService
{
    bool Pay(decimal amount);
}

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IPaymentService _paymentService;

    public OrderService(IPaymentService paymentService)
    {
        _paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public bool PlaceOrder(decimal amount)
    {
        return _paymentService.Pay(amount);
    }
}

For testing, you can provide a fake:

public class FakePaymentService : IPaymentService
{
    public bool Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        return true;
    }
}

Then:

var service = new OrderService(
    new FakePaymentService()
);

bool result = service.PlaceOrder(1000);

This is one reason composition + interfaces + DI are so common in ASP.NET Core applications.

8. Does Composition mean the contained object's lifetime is always tied to the containing object?

No.

This is an important nuance.

Composition can mean one object owns another object, but C# itself doesn't enforce a universal ownership/lifetime rule merely because one class has a field referencing another object.

For example:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly ILogger<OrderService> _logger;

    public OrderService(ILogger<OrderService> logger)
    {
        _logger = logger;
    }
}

OrderService has a reference to a logger, but its lifetime is managed by the application's dependency-injection system.

So don't say:

"Composition always means the child object dies when the parent dies."

That's too strong for C#/.NET.

9. What is the difference between Composition and Aggregation?

This can appear in senior interviews.

Both represent has-a relationships, but the ownership semantics differ conceptually.

Composition

The containing object strongly owns the contained object.

House
 └── Room

Conceptually, the room is part of the house.

Aggregation

The containing object uses another object, but that object can exist independently.

Department
 └── Employee

An employee can exist even if the department object is removed.

Interview Answer

Composition generally represents stronger ownership, while aggregation represents a weaker association where the contained object can exist independently. In C#, these are design concepts rather than separate language keywords.

That's a good senior-level answer.

10. Give a real-world example of Composition in ASP.NET Core.

This is particularly relevant to your .NET experience.

Imagine an OrderService.

It needs:

  • repository
  • payment service
  • notification service
  • logger

Instead of inheriting from these classes:

public class OrderService : Repository
{
}

you compose the service from dependencies:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;
    private readonly IPaymentService _paymentService;
    private readonly INotificationService _notificationService;

    public OrderService(
        IOrderRepository repository,
        IPaymentService paymentService,
        INotificationService notificationService)
    {
        _repository = repository;
        _paymentService = paymentService;
        _notificationService = notificationService;
    }

    public void PlaceOrder()
    {
        // Save order
        _repository.Save();

        // Process payment
        _paymentService.Pay();

        // Notify customer
        _notificationService.Send();
    }
}

Conceptually:

                 OrderService
                      |
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        ↓             ↓             ↓
 IOrderRepository IPaymentService INotificationService

This is composition, and when those dependencies are provided through the constructor by the ASP.NET Core DI container, it also demonstrates Dependency Injection. Microsoft Learn

11. What is "Composition over Inheritance"?

Interview-Ready Answer

Composition over inheritance means preferring object composition when we want to reuse behavior, instead of creating deep inheritance hierarchies.

I would use inheritance when there is a genuine is-a relationship, and composition when the relationship is has-a or when behavior needs to be easily replaceable.

Example

Avoid:

PaymentService
     ↓
CreditCardPayment
     ↓
PremiumCreditCardPayment
     ↓
InternationalPremiumCreditCardPayment

if the hierarchy is only being created for code reuse.

Instead:

PaymentService
      |
      ↓
IPaymentStrategy
   /        \
CreditCard   UPI

The behavior can be composed.

This idea is closely related to the Strategy pattern, where behavior is delegated rather than inherited. Microsoft describes Strategy as using delegation while Template Method uses inheritance. Microsoft Learn

12. What is the biggest disadvantage of Composition?

Interview-Ready Answer

Composition can introduce more objects, interfaces, and dependencies, which can make a simple design unnecessarily complex if used without a clear reason.

For example, don't create:

Customer
 ↓
ICustomerNameService
 ↓
CustomerNameService

just to return:

customer.Name

For a simple operation, that would be unnecessary abstraction.

Microsoft's DI guidance similarly notes that dependency injection can introduce additional complexity and isn't always appropriate for small or dependency-free classes. Microsoft Learn

13. Can Composition and Inheritance be used together?

Absolutely.

Real applications commonly use both.

public class BaseController
{
    protected readonly ILogger _logger;

    public BaseController(ILogger logger)
    {
        _logger = logger;
    }
}

Then:

public class OrderController : BaseController
{
    private readonly IOrderService _orderService;

    public OrderController(
        ILogger logger,
        IOrderService orderService)
        : base(logger)
    {
        _orderService = orderService;
    }
}

Here:

OrderController IS-A BaseController

through inheritance.

And:

OrderController HAS-A IOrderService

through composition.

Excellent interview statement

Inheritance and composition aren't mutually exclusive. A class can inherit common behavior from a base class while composing other behaviors through dependencies.

3+ YOE Priority

For your target interviews, prioritize these:

PriorityQuestion
🔴 Very HighWhat is Composition?
🔴 Very HighComposition vs Inheritance
🔴 Very HighWhy prefer Composition?
🔴 Very HighComposition + Interface
🔴 Very HighComposition + Dependency Injection
🟠 HighHow does Composition improve testability?
🟠 HighComposition vs Aggregation
🟠 HighComposition over Inheritance
🟡 MediumObject lifetime in Composition
🟡 MediumCan Composition and Inheritance coexist?

Likely Follow-Up Questions

If you answer:

"Composition helps with loose coupling."

The interviewer may immediately ask:

"How?"

Answer:

By depending on abstractions such as interfaces and injecting implementations, the consuming class doesn't need to know the concrete implementation.

Then they may ask:

"How does that help testing?"

We can provide a mock or fake implementation instead of the real dependency.

Then:

"What does ASP.NET Core use for this?"

ASP.NET Core has a built-in dependency injection container where services can be registered and injected, commonly through constructors. Microsoft Learn

That's a very common interview chain:

Composition
    ↓
Loose Coupling
    ↓
Interface
    ↓
Dependency Injection
    ↓
Testability
    ↓
SOLID / DIP

⭐ 30-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer simply asks "What is Composition?", say:

Composition is an OOP technique where a class uses or contains objects of other classes instead of inheriting from them. It represents a has-a relationship. For example, a Car has an Engine. In real-world .NET applications, we commonly use composition with interfaces and dependency injection, such as an OrderService having an IOrderRepository and IPaymentService. This helps reduce coupling, improve flexibility, and make the code easier to test. Microsoft Learn

🧠 Memory Trick

Inheritance  → IS-A
Composition  → HAS-A
Interface    → CAN-DO
DI           → DEPENDENCY IS PROVIDED FROM OUTSIDE

14. Composition vs Inheritance

The key idea is:

Inheritance = IS-A relationship

Composition = HAS-A relationship

Microsoft describes inheritance as creating specialized types from a base type, while a derived class can reuse, extend, or modify the base behavior. A C# class can have only one direct base class. Microsoft Learn

1. What is the difference between Composition and Inheritance?

Interview-Ready Answer

Inheritance represents an "is-a" relationship, where a derived class specializes a base class. Composition represents a "has-a" relationship, where a class uses another object as one of its dependencies.

I use inheritance when there is a strong and natural hierarchy between the types. I prefer composition when I mainly need to reuse or delegate behavior.

Inheritance

public class Animal
{
    public void Eat()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Eating");
    }
}

public class Dog : Animal
{
}
Dog IS-A Animal

Composition

public class Engine
{
    public void Start()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Engine started");
    }
}

public class Car
{
    private readonly Engine _engine;

    public Car(Engine engine)
    {
        _engine = engine;
    }

    public void Start()
    {
        _engine.Start();
    }
}
Car HAS-A Engine

2. What is the main advantage of Inheritance?

Interview-Ready Answer

Inheritance allows a derived class to reuse and specialize functionality from a base class. It is useful when multiple types share a genuine common abstraction and behavior.

For example:

public abstract class Employee
{
    public string Name { get; set; }

    public void Login()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Employee logged in");
    }

    public abstract decimal CalculateSalary();
}

public class Developer : Employee
{
    public override decimal CalculateSalary()
    {
        return 80000;
    }
}

Here:

Developer IS-A Employee

Developer inherits common functionality and provides specialized behavior.

C# supports this kind of specialization through inheritance, and derived classes can override virtual or abstract members. Microsoft Learn

3. What is the main advantage of Composition?

Interview-Ready Answer

Composition allows us to assemble behavior from separate components without creating a rigid inheritance hierarchy. This generally makes the design more flexible because dependencies can be replaced independently.

Example:

public interface IPaymentService
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

public class UpiPayment : IPaymentService
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("UPI payment");
    }
}

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IPaymentService _paymentService;

    public OrderService(IPaymentService paymentService)
    {
        _paymentService = paymentService;
    }

    public void PlaceOrder(decimal amount)
    {
        _paymentService.Pay(amount);
    }
}

Now OrderService doesn't care whether payment is:

UPI
Credit Card
Debit Card
Wallet
Net Banking

It depends on the abstraction:

OrderService
      ↓
IPaymentService
   ↙       ↘
UPI      CreditCard

4. Why is Composition often preferred over Inheritance?

Interview-Ready Answer

Composition can reduce coupling between classes and allows behavior to be changed by replacing dependencies rather than modifying an inheritance hierarchy. It is especially useful when the relationship isn't naturally an "is-a" relationship.

Consider this:

public class EmailService
{
    public void SendEmail()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Email sent");
    }
}

public class OrderService : EmailService
{
}

This technically works, but ask:

Is an OrderService an EmailService?

No.

It merely uses an email service.

So composition is more appropriate:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly EmailService _emailService;

    public OrderService(EmailService emailService)
    {
        _emailService = emailService;
    }
}
OrderService HAS-A EmailService

5. Does Composition completely replace Inheritance?

No.

This is an important interview point.

Good answer:

No. Composition is not a replacement for inheritance in every situation. If there is a genuine "is-a" relationship and the derived type is a meaningful specialization of the base type, inheritance can be appropriate. Composition is preferable when we are primarily combining or delegating behavior.

For example:

Dog IS-A Animal

is a natural inheritance relationship.

But:

OrderService HAS-A PaymentService

is naturally composition.

Microsoft's inheritance guidance specifically describes inheritance as appropriate for specialization where the derived type is a type of the base type. Microsoft Learn

6. How does inheritance create tight coupling?

Consider:

public class Report
{
    public virtual void Generate()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Generating report");
    }
}

public class PdfReport : Report
{
    public override void Generate()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Generating PDF");
    }
}

PdfReport is tightly connected to the structure and behavior of Report.

Changes to the base class can potentially affect derived classes.

For example, if Report introduces:

protected string FilePath;

or changes the behavior of:

Generate()

the derived classes may need to adapt.

Interview phrasing

Inheritance creates a stronger coupling because the derived class depends on the base class's contract and implementation details.

A derived class inherits members from its base class, although constructors and finalizers are not inherited. Microsoft Learn

7. How does Composition reduce coupling?

Instead of:

public class OrderService : PaymentService
{
}

use:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IPaymentService _paymentService;

    public OrderService(IPaymentService paymentService)
    {
        _paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}

Now:

OrderService
      ↓
IPaymentService
      ↑
      |
 ┌────┴─────┐
UPI      CreditCard

OrderService doesn't depend on a particular implementation.

Interview Answer

Composition combined with interfaces and dependency injection allows the consuming class to depend on an abstraction rather than a concrete implementation, which makes the system easier to modify and test.

8. Which is better for code reuse: Composition or Inheritance?

Don't say:

"Composition is always better."

Instead say:

Both support reuse, but they do it differently. Inheritance reuses behavior through a class hierarchy, while composition reuses behavior by delegating work to other objects. The appropriate choice depends on the relationship and design requirements.

Inheritance

BaseClass
    ↑
    |
DerivedClass

Composition

Class A
   |
   ↓
Class B

9. Can Composition provide polymorphism?

Yes.

This is an important connection.

public interface INotificationService
{
    void Send(string message);
}

Implementations:

public class EmailNotification : INotificationService
{
    public void Send(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Email");
    }
}

public class SmsNotification : INotificationService
{
    public void Send(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("SMS");
    }
}

Consumer:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly INotificationService _notification;

    public OrderService(INotificationService notification)
    {
        _notification = notification;
    }

    public void PlaceOrder()
    {
        _notification.Send("Order placed");
    }
}

Now:

new OrderService(new EmailNotification());

or:

new OrderService(new SmsNotification());

The consuming class remains unchanged.

This gives you polymorphic behavior through composition.

10. What is "Composition over Inheritance"?

Interview-Ready Answer

Composition over inheritance is a design principle that suggests using object composition to reuse and combine behavior when inheritance would create an unnecessary or rigid hierarchy.

It doesn't mean:

Never use inheritance.

It means:

Don't use inheritance merely for code reuse when composition is more appropriate.

Bad reason for inheritance

I need this method
       ↓
I'll inherit the entire class

Better approach

I need this behavior
       ↓
Compose the required component

11. Give a real-world .NET example.

Suppose you're building an e-commerce application.

You have:

OrderService

It needs:

  • Order Repository
  • Payment Service
  • Notification Service
  • Logger

You wouldn't normally do:

public class OrderService
    : OrderRepository,
      PaymentService,
      NotificationService
{
}

Apart from the fact that C# doesn't allow multiple base classes, the design itself is wrong because OrderService isn't a repository, payment service, or notification service.

Instead:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;
    private readonly IPaymentService _payment;
    private readonly INotificationService _notification;

    public OrderService(
        IOrderRepository repository,
        IPaymentService payment,
        INotificationService notification)
    {
        _repository = repository;
        _payment = payment;
        _notification = notification;
    }
}

Conceptually:

                    OrderService
                         |
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          ↓              ↓              ↓
   IOrderRepository  IPaymentService  INotificationService

This is a very realistic ASP.NET Core design.

12. Can inheritance and composition exist in the same class?

Yes.

This is actually common in real applications.

public class BaseController
{
    protected readonly ILogger _logger;

    public BaseController(ILogger logger)
    {
        _logger = logger;
    }
}

public class OrderController : BaseController
{
    private readonly IOrderService _orderService;

    public OrderController(
        ILogger logger,
        IOrderService orderService)
        : base(logger)
    {
        _orderService = orderService;
    }
}

Here:

OrderController IS-A BaseController

because of inheritance.

And:

OrderController HAS-A IOrderService

because of composition.

Strong interview statement

Inheritance and composition are complementary. I can use inheritance for a genuine type hierarchy and composition for external behavior or services that the class needs.

13. What happens when an inheritance hierarchy becomes too deep?

This is a common senior-level follow-up.

Imagine:

Entity
  ↓
AuditableEntity
  ↓
UserEntity
  ↓
EmployeeEntity
  ↓
DeveloperEntity
  ↓
SeniorDeveloperEntity

As the hierarchy grows, understanding where behavior comes from becomes harder.

You can end up with:

  • tight coupling
  • difficult maintenance
  • fragile base-class behavior
  • complicated overrides
  • difficult testing
  • unexpected behavior from inherited members

C# inheritance allows derived classes to extend base classes, but the language permits only one direct base class, so inheritance hierarchies can become an important architectural decision. Microsoft Learn

Composition can instead allow smaller independent components:

Developer
 ├── SalaryCalculator
 ├── NotificationService
 ├── SkillManager
 └── ProjectAssignment

14. What is the "fragile base class" problem?

Interview-Ready Answer

The fragile base class problem occurs when changes to a base class unexpectedly affect derived classes because derived classes depend on the base class's behavior or implementation.

Example:

public class BaseService
{
    public virtual void Process()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Base processing");
    }
}

Derived:

public class OrderService : BaseService
{
    public override void Process()
    {
        // Depends on assumptions about BaseService
        base.Process();

        Console.WriteLine("Order processing");
    }
}

If the base implementation changes significantly, the derived behavior may change as well.

This is one reason composition can be preferable when you don't actually need inheritance.

15. Interview Scenario: Which would you choose?

Interviewer:

"You have a PaymentService and OrderService. Should OrderService inherit PaymentService?"

Good Answer:

No, I would normally use composition. OrderService is not a PaymentService; it uses payment functionality. I would define an IPaymentService abstraction and inject it into OrderService. This gives us a has-a relationship, reduces coupling, and makes it easier to replace or mock the payment implementation.

This is exactly the kind of reasoning interviewers look for.

🔥 Quick Comparison Table

AspectCompositionInheritance
RelationshipHas-aIs-a
ReuseDelegationInherited behavior
CouplingGenerally lowerGenerally higher
FlexibilityHighLower
Runtime replacementEasy with interfaces/DIMore restricted
Multiple behaviorsEasy to composeC# allows only one base class
TestingOften easierCan be more difficult in deep hierarchies
Best forCombining behaviorSpecializing a type
ExampleOrderService HAS-A PaymentServiceDog IS-A Animal

C# classes can inherit from one base class while implementing multiple interfaces. Microsoft Learn

⭐ Most Important Interview Rule

Remember this decision process:

             Do I need reuse?
                    |
                   YES
                    ↓
           Is there an IS-A
             relationship?
              /        \
            YES         NO
             ↓           ↓
        Inheritance   Composition

But add one more question:

Is the relationship genuinely
a specialization of the base type?
              |
          YES → Inheritance
              |
           NO → Composition

Don't choose inheritance simply because it allows you to reuse code.

🎯 3+ YOE Priority

🔴 Must Know

  1. Composition vs Inheritance
  1. IS-A vs HAS-A
  1. Why composition reduces coupling
  1. Composition over inheritance
  1. Real-world .NET example
  1. Composition + Interface + DI

🟠 Strong Interview Level

  1. Deep inheritance hierarchy problems
  1. Fragile base class problem
  1. Composition and polymorphism
  1. Composition and inheritance together

🟡 Advanced

  1. Aggregation vs composition
  1. Ownership/lifetime semantics
  1. Design implications of inheritance hierarchies

🎤 30-Second Interview Answer

If they ask:

"Composition vs Inheritance?"

Say:

Inheritance represents an "is-a" relationship, while composition represents a "has-a" relationship. Inheritance is useful when a class is a genuine specialization of another class, such as Dog inheriting from Animal. Composition is useful when a class needs another object's functionality, such as OrderService having an IPaymentService. I generally prefer composition for combining behavior because it can reduce coupling and allows dependencies to be replaced more easily, especially when combined with interfaces and dependency injection.

🧠 One-line memory trick

Inheritance  → IS-A → specialization
Composition  → HAS-A → collaboration

15. SOLID Principles

SOLID is a group of five object-oriented design principles:

LetterPrincipleSimple Meaning
SSingle Responsibility PrincipleOne class → one responsibility
OOpen/Closed PrincipleOpen for extension, closed for modification
LLiskov Substitution PrincipleChild should safely replace parent
IInterface Segregation PrinciplePrefer small, focused interfaces
DDependency Inversion PrincipleDepend on abstractions, not concrete implementations

Microsoft's .NET architecture guidance identifies these same five principles and emphasizes their role in decoupling application layers. Microsoft Learn

For interviews, don't just memorize the definitions. You should be able to explain the problem → violation → improved design → real-world example.

1. What is SOLID?

Interview-Ready Answer

SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles that help us build software that is easier to maintain, extend, test, and understand.

The five principles are SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, and DIP.

Real-World Scenario

Imagine an e-commerce application.

Without SOLID, one OrderService might:

OrderService
 ├── Validate Order
 ├── Save to Database
 ├── Process Payment
 ├── Send Email
 ├── Generate Invoice
 ├── Generate PDF
 └── Log Everything

As the application grows, changing one feature can affect unrelated functionality.

SOLID encourages us to separate responsibilities and dependencies.

S — Single Responsibility Principle

2. What is SRP?

Interview-Ready Answer

Single Responsibility Principle says that a class should have one responsibility and one reason to change.

A very useful interview phrase is:

One responsibility → one reason to change.

Microsoft's architecture guidance uses essentially this definition: an object should have only one responsibility and should change only when that responsibility changes. Microsoft Learn

3. Give an example of violating SRP.

Consider:

public class OrderService
{
    public void CreateOrder()
    {
        // Create order
    }

    public void SaveToDatabase()
    {
        // Save order
    }

    public void SendEmail()
    {
        // Send email
    }

    public void GenerateInvoice()
    {
        // Generate invoice
    }
}

This class has multiple responsibilities:

OrderService
 ├── Order creation
 ├── Database persistence
 ├── Email
 └── Invoice generation

Different reasons can cause the class to change.

That's an SRP violation.

4. How would you apply SRP here?

Split the responsibilities:

public class OrderService
{
    public void CreateOrder()
    {
        // Order business logic
    }
}
public class OrderRepository
{
    public void Save()
    {
        // Database logic
    }
}
public class EmailService
{
    public void Send()
    {
        // Email logic
    }
}
public class InvoiceService
{
    public void Generate()
    {
        // Invoice logic
    }
}

Now each class has a clearer responsibility.

Real-world example

In your .NET Web API experience, you might have:

Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Repository
   ↓
Database

Instead of putting controller logic, business logic, and SQL/database logic into one class.

5. Does SRP mean a class can have only one method?

No.

Interview-Ready Answer

No. SRP doesn't mean a class must contain only one method. It means the methods should belong to the same responsibility and the class should have a coherent reason to change.

For example:

public class OrderValidator
{
    public bool ValidateOrder(Order order)
    {
        // validation
    }

    public bool ValidateItems(Order order)
    {
        // validation
    }

    public bool ValidateCustomer(Order order)
    {
        // validation
    }
}

Multiple methods are perfectly fine because they belong to the same responsibility:

OrderValidator → Order validation

O — Open/Closed Principle

6. What is OCP?

Interview-Ready Answer

The Open/Closed Principle says that software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.

In simple terms, we should be able to add new behavior without repeatedly modifying stable existing code.

Microsoft's C# SOLID guidance describes OCP as open for extension and closed for modification. Microsoft Learn

7. Give an example of violating OCP.

Imagine:

public class PaymentService
{
    public void Pay(string paymentType)
    {
        if (paymentType == "UPI")
        {
            // UPI payment
        }
        else if (paymentType == "Card")
        {
            // Card payment
        }
        else if (paymentType == "PayPal")
        {
            // PayPal payment
        }
    }
}

Now suppose tomorrow you add:

Wallet
Net Banking
Crypto

You have to keep modifying:

PaymentService

That's a sign the design isn't easily extensible.

8. How would you apply OCP?

Use an abstraction:

public interface IPayment
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

Implementations:

public class UpiPayment : IPayment
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("UPI Payment");
    }
}
public class CardPayment : IPayment
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Card Payment");
    }
}

Now:

public class PaymentService
{
    private readonly IPayment _payment;

    public PaymentService(IPayment payment)
    {
        _payment = payment;
    }

    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        _payment.Pay(amount);
    }
}

Adding:

public class WalletPayment : IPayment
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Wallet Payment");
    }
}

doesn't require modifying PaymentService.

That's OCP.

PaymentService
      ↓
   IPayment
   /  |   \
 UPI Card Wallet

9. Is OCP saying we should never modify existing code?

No.

This is a good follow-up.

Interview Answer

No. OCP doesn't mean existing code can never be modified. It means we should design frequently extended areas so that new behavior can often be added through new implementations or extensions rather than repeatedly changing stable core logic.

That's a much more accurate answer than:

"Never modify existing code."

L — Liskov Substitution Principle

10. What is LSP?

Interview-Ready Answer

The Liskov Substitution Principle says that objects of a derived type should be usable wherever the base type is expected without breaking the correctness or expected behavior of the program.

Microsoft's C# guidance similarly describes LSP around safely substituting inheritors for their base types. Microsoft Learn

The simple interview version:

Child should be safely replaceable by parent.

11. Give a simple LSP example.

Suppose:

public class Bird
{
    public virtual void Fly()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Flying");
    }
}

Then:

public class Sparrow : Bird
{
}

This works naturally:

Bird bird = new Sparrow();

bird.Fly();

Sparrow behaves as expected when used as a Bird.

12. Give an example of violating LSP.

A classic example:

public class Bird
{
    public virtual void Fly()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Flying");
    }
}

Now:

public class Penguin : Bird
{
    public override void Fly()
    {
        throw new NotSupportedException();
    }
}

Now:

Bird bird = new Penguin();

bird.Fly();

throws an exception.

The base abstraction promised:

Bird → Fly()

but the derived type cannot fulfill that expected behavior.

That's an LSP problem.

13. How would you fix the Penguin example?

Don't force all birds into the same abstraction.

Use a more appropriate abstraction:

public abstract class Bird
{
    public abstract void Move();
}

Flying birds:

public interface IFlyingBird
{
    void Fly();
}

Then:

public class Sparrow : Bird, IFlyingBird
{
    public override void Move()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Flying");
    }

    public void Fly()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Flying");
    }
}

Penguin:

public class Penguin : Bird
{
    public override void Move()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Walking");
    }
}

Now the abstraction matches the actual capabilities.

14. Is LSP only about inheritance?

Mostly, but the principle is broader.

Interview Answer

LSP is most commonly discussed with inheritance and polymorphism, but the underlying idea is that an implementation must honor the behavioral contract expected by the abstraction.

For example, if:

IStorage storage

promises:

Save()
Load()

an implementation shouldn't unexpectedly make Save() unusable when the contract implies it should work.

I — Interface Segregation Principle

15. What is ISP?

Interview-Ready Answer

The Interface Segregation Principle says that clients should not be forced to depend on methods they don't need.

In practice, we prefer smaller, focused interfaces instead of one large interface containing unrelated responsibilities.

Microsoft's SOLID guidance similarly recommends focused interfaces and warns against forcing implementations to support functionality they don't need. Microsoft Learn

16. Give an example of violating ISP.

Suppose:

public interface IWorker
{
    void Work();
    void Eat();
    void Sleep();
}

Now:

public class Robot : IWorker
{
    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Robot working");
    }

    public void Eat()
    {
        throw new NotSupportedException();
    }

    public void Sleep()
    {
        throw new NotSupportedException();
    }
}

This is a design problem.

The robot doesn't need:

Eat()
Sleep()

17. How would you apply ISP?

Split the interface:

public interface IWorkable
{
    void Work();
}
public interface IEatable
{
    void Eat();
}
public interface ISleepable
{
    void Sleep();
}

Human:

public class Human : IWorkable, IEatable, ISleepable
{
    public void Work() { }
    public void Eat() { }
    public void Sleep() { }
}

Robot:

public class Robot : IWorkable
{
    public void Work()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Robot working");
    }
}

Now each class implements only the capabilities it actually needs.

18. Is a smaller interface always better?

Not necessarily.

Interview Answer

ISP doesn't mean every interface should contain only one method. The goal is to keep interfaces cohesive and focused around a meaningful client or capability.

For example:

public interface IOrderRepository
{
    Order GetById(int id);
    void Add(Order order);
    void Update(Order order);
}

This can be perfectly reasonable because the methods are related to one responsibility.

D — Dependency Inversion Principle

19. What is DIP?

Interview-Ready Answer

The Dependency Inversion Principle says that high-level modules should not depend directly on low-level implementation details. Both should depend on abstractions.

A shorter interview version:

Depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.

Microsoft's architecture guidance describes dependency inversion as directing dependencies toward abstractions rather than implementation details, which helps produce loosely coupled, testable, and maintainable systems. Microsoft Learn

20. Give an example of violating DIP.

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly SqlOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService()
    {
        _repository = new SqlOrderRepository();
    }
}

Problem:

OrderService
     ↓
SqlOrderRepository

OrderService directly depends on the concrete implementation.

If tomorrow you want:

SqlOrderRepository
      ↓
MongoOrderRepository

you need to modify OrderService.

It also makes testing harder because the class creates its own database dependency.

ASP.NET Core's documentation explicitly notes that directly creating dependencies couples a class to a particular implementation and makes substitution for testing more difficult. Microsoft Learn

21. How would you apply DIP?

Create an abstraction:

public interface IOrderRepository
{
    void Save(Order order);
}

Implementation:

public class SqlOrderRepository : IOrderRepository
{
    public void Save(Order order)
    {
        // SQL Server logic
    }
}

Service:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }

    public void CreateOrder(Order order)
    {
        _repository.Save(order);
    }
}

Now:

             IOrderRepository
              ↑           ↑
              |           |
      SqlRepository   MockRepository
              ↑
              |
        OrderService

OrderService doesn't care which implementation is used.

22. Is DIP the same as Dependency Injection?

No.

This is a very important interview question.

DIP

A design principle: depend on abstractions rather than concrete implementations.

DI

A technique/pattern for supplying dependencies from outside the class.

Example:

public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
{
    _repository = repository;
}

That's constructor injection.

ASP.NET Core has a built-in DI container that registers services and injects them into consuming classes. Microsoft Learn

Easy memory trick

DIP = WHAT we should depend on

DI  = HOW the dependency is provided

23. How are all five SOLID principles connected?

This is a very strong Senior-level question.

Think about this design:

                    OrderService
                         |
                         ↓
                 IOrderRepository
                         |
                         ↓
                SqlOrderRepository

SRP

Each class has a focused responsibility.

OrderService → business logic
Repository   → persistence

OCP

New repository implementations can be added:

SqlRepository
MongoRepository
InMemoryRepository

without changing OrderService.

LSP

Any valid IOrderRepository implementation should honor the expected repository contract.

ISP

Keep interfaces focused:

IOrderRepository
IPaymentService
INotificationService

instead of one giant:

IApplicationService

DIP

OrderService depends on:

IOrderRepository

rather than:

SqlOrderRepository

Overall

SRP → responsibilities
OCP → extensibility
LSP → substitutability
ISP → focused contracts
DIP → loose dependencies

24. Give a real-world ASP.NET Core SOLID example.

A typical design:

Controller
    ↓
IOrderService
    ↓
OrderService
    ↓
IOrderRepository
    ↓
OrderRepository
    ↓
SQL Server

And perhaps:

OrderService
    ├── IPaymentService
    ├── INotificationService
    └── IOrderRepository

ASP.NET Core's built-in DI system allows these abstractions and implementations to be registered and injected. Microsoft Learn

Example:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IPaymentService, PaymentService>();

Then:

public class OrderService : IOrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;
    private readonly IPaymentService _paymentService;

    public OrderService(
        IOrderRepository repository,
        IPaymentService paymentService)
    {
        _repository = repository;
        _paymentService = paymentService;
    }
}

This is where Composition + Interfaces + DIP + DI come together.

25. What happens if a class has too many dependencies?

This is a nice Senior-level follow-up.

Suppose:

public OrderService(
    IRepository repository,
    IPayment payment,
    IEmail email,
    ISms sms,
    ILogger logger,
    IInvoice invoice,
    IAnalytics analytics,
    IAudit audit)
{
}

Don't automatically conclude:

"DI is bad."

Instead:

A large number of dependencies can be a design signal that the class has too many responsibilities. I would examine whether the class should be split into smaller cohesive services.

Microsoft's DI guidance explicitly identifies many injected dependencies as a possible sign that a class has too many responsibilities and may violate SRP. Microsoft Learn

🔥 SOLID Interview Scenario

Interviewer:

"You have a PaymentService with a large switch statement for UPI, Card, Wallet and Net Banking. Which SOLID principle is violated?"

Answer:

Primarily:

OCP, because adding a new payment type requires modifying the existing service.

Then propose:

public interface IPaymentMethod
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

Implement:

UPIPayment
CardPayment
WalletPayment
NetBankingPayment

and inject/use the abstraction.

Interviewer:

"But now you have many classes. Isn't that overengineering?"

Answer:

It depends on the expected change and complexity. If payment methods are expected to grow or vary independently, separate implementations provide useful extensibility. For a very small, stable requirement, a simple implementation may be sufficient. SOLID principles are design guidelines, not rules that require maximum abstraction everywhere.

This is a very mature answer.

🔥 Another Interview Scenario

Interviewer:

"Which SOLID principle does Dependency Injection help achieve?"

Answer:

DI is a technique that commonly helps implement the Dependency Inversion Principle. By injecting an abstraction such as an interface rather than directly creating a concrete implementation, we reduce coupling and improve testability. Microsoft Learn

Don't say:

"DI and DIP are the same."

They aren't.

SOLID vs OOP Concepts

You should understand how these topics connect to what we've already studied:

OOP
│
├── Encapsulation
│
├── Abstraction
│
├── Inheritance
│
├── Polymorphism
│
└── Composition
       │
       ↓
     SOLID
       │
       ├── SRP
       ├── OCP
       ├── LSP
       ├── ISP
       └── DIP
              │
              ↓
        Dependency Injection

This is why we studied Composition before SOLID.

🎯 3+ YOE Priority

🔴 Must Know

  1. What is SOLID?
  1. SRP definition + example
  1. OCP definition + example
  1. LSP definition + example
  1. ISP definition + example
  1. DIP definition + example
  1. DIP vs DI
  1. SOLID in ASP.NET Core
  1. Composition + DIP + DI
  1. Identify SOLID violations from code

🟠 Strong Senior-Level

  1. SRP vs separation of methods
  1. OCP with Strategy pattern
