26. 30-Second Interview Answer ⭐

If they ask:

"Explain value types and reference types in C#."

Say:

"C# types are broadly divided into value types and reference types. A value-type variable contains the value itself, so assigning or passing it by value creates a copy. Examples are int, bool, structs and enums. A reference-type variable contains a reference to an object, so assigning it copies the reference and both variables can point to the same object. Classes, arrays and strings are reference types. One important point is that reference types are still passed by value by default—the reference itself is copied. Also, I wouldn't simply equate value types with stack and reference types with heap because storage depends on context." Microsoft Learn

🧠 Final Memory Model

C# TYPES
   │
   ├── VALUE TYPES
   │     │
   │     ├── int
   │     ├── bool
   │     ├── enum
   │     └── struct
   │
   │     Assignment → COPY VALUE
   │
   └── REFERENCE TYPES
         │
         ├── class
         ├── array
         ├── string
         ├── interface
         └── delegate

         Assignment → COPY REFERENCE

20. Records & Immutability in C#

Class / Struct
      ↓
Value vs Reference Semantics
      ↓
Equality
      ↓
Immutability
      ↓
Records
      ↓
with expressions

Microsoft describes records as types optimized for storing data, with compiler-generated value equality, readable ToString(), and nondestructive with expressions. A record can be either a record class or record struct. Microsoft Learn

1. What is a Record in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer

A record is a C# type designed primarily for data-centric objects. It provides built-in value-based equality, readable ToString(), and support for creating modified copies using with expressions.

Example:

public record Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    string Department
);

Usage:

var e1 = new Employee(1, "Saurabh", "IT");
var e2 = new Employee(1, "Saurabh", "IT");

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2);

Output:

True

Even though e1 and e2 are separate objects, their data is equal.

That's one of the biggest differences between a record and a normal class. Microsoft Learn

2. Why were Records introduced?

Interview-Ready Answer

Records were introduced to make it easier to create data-focused types where equality is based on the data rather than object identity, without manually implementing Equals(), GetHashCode(), ==, ToString(), and copying logic.

Without a record, you might write:

public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

Then you'd potentially need to implement equality yourself.

With a record:

public record Employee(int Id, string Name);

The compiler generates important members for you. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

DTOs are a common example:

public record EmployeeDto(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    string Department
);

This is useful when the primary purpose of the type is carrying data between layers or APIs.

3. What is the difference between Class and Record?

⭐ Very Common Interview Question

FeatureClassRecord Class
Default equalityReference-basedValue-based
==Usually reference equalityValue-based
Equals()Usually reference equality unless overriddenCompiler-generated value equality
GetHashCode()Usually object-based unless overriddenCompiler-generated
ToString()Type name by defaultData-oriented representation
with expressionNoYes
Primary constructor syntaxModern C# supports itYes
Best suited forBehavior/entitiesData-centric models

Example:

class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
}
var e1 = new Employee { Id = 1, Name = "Saurabh" };
var e2 = new Employee { Id = 1, Name = "Saurabh" };

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2);

Usually:

False

Because they're different objects.

Now:

record Employee(int Id, string Name);

var e1 = new Employee(1, "Saurabh");
var e2 = new Employee(1, "Saurabh");

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2);

Output:

True

Records use value-based equality by default. Microsoft Learn

4. What is record class?

A record class is a reference type with record behavior.

public record class Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name
);

You can also simply write:

public record Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name
);

When record is used without struct, it means record class. Microsoft Learn

Important

record class
      ↓
Reference Type
      ↓
Reference copied during assignment
      ↓
Value-based equality

So records do not mean "value type."

That's an important interview trap.

5. What is record struct?

A record struct is a value type with record features.

public record struct Point(
    int X,
    int Y
);

Example:

var p1 = new Point(10, 20);
var p2 = p1;

p2.X = 100;

Console.WriteLine(p1.X); // 10
Console.WriteLine(p2.X); // 100

Because record struct has value semantics.

Microsoft explicitly distinguishes record class and record struct: the former copies references on assignment, while the latter copies data. Microsoft Learn

Memory Trick

record class
    ↓
reference type
    ↓
value equality

record struct
    ↓
value type
    ↓
value equality

6. What is the difference between record, record class, and record struct?

Interview-Ready Answer

record Employee(...);

is essentially:

record class Employee(...);

Both are reference types.

But:

record struct Point(...);

is a value type.

Table

recordrecord classrecord struct
Underlying typeClassClassStruct
Reference typeYesYesNo
Value typeNoNoYes
Value equalityYesYesYes
withYesYesYes
InheritanceYesYesNo

Record classes support inheritance; record structs don't. Microsoft Learn

7. What is Immutability?

⭐ Must Know

Interview-Ready Answer

Immutability means that after an object has been created, its state cannot be changed. Instead of modifying the existing object, we create a new object with the required changes.

For example:

public record Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name
);

You generally initialize it:

var employee = new Employee(1, "Saurabh");

Instead of directly modifying its generated positional properties, you can create a modified copy:

var updatedEmployee =
    employee with { Name = "Rahul" };

Now:

employee
Name = Saurabh

updatedEmployee
Name = Rahul

The original remains unchanged. Microsoft Learn

8. What is an initonly Property?

This is extremely important because it is one of the main mechanisms for creating immutable-style objects.

public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; init; }
    public string Name { get; init; }
}

You can initialize:

var employee = new Employee
{
    Id = 1,
    Name = "Saurabh"
};

But after initialization:

employee.Name = "Rahul"; // ❌

The init accessor allows assignment during object initialization, but not normal mutation afterward. Microsoft Learn

9. init vs set

Very Common Interview Question

set

public string Name { get; set; }

Can be changed after construction:

employee.Name = "Rahul";

init

public string Name { get; init; }

Can only be assigned during initialization:

var employee = new Employee
{
    Name = "Saurabh"
};

After initialization:

employee.Name = "Rahul"; // ❌

Interview Answer

"set allows modification after initialization, whereas init allows the property to be assigned only during object initialization. init is useful for creating immutable-style objects." Microsoft Learn

10. Is a Record Automatically Immutable?

⭐ Important Trap

Not necessarily.

A common statement is:

"Records are immutable."

That's too broad.

Records provide features that make immutable designs easy, but records themselves can contain mutable properties.

For example:

public record Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

These properties are mutable.

You can also have:

public record Employee
{
    public int Id { get; init; }
    public string Name { get; init; }
}

This is much more immutable-style.

Microsoft explicitly notes that immutability is common with records but isn't an absolute requirement. Microsoft Learn

Strong Interview Answer

"Records support immutable design, but a record is not automatically deeply immutable. We can still define mutable properties or contain mutable reference-type objects."

11. What is a with Expression?

⭐ Must Know

A with expression creates a modified copy of an existing record.

public record Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    string Department
);

Original:

var e1 = new Employee(
    1,
    "Saurabh",
    "IT"
);

Create modified copy:

var e2 = e1 with
{
    Name = "Rahul"
};

Now:

e1
Id = 1
Name = Saurabh
Department = IT

e2
Id = 1
Name = Rahul
Department = IT

The original isn't modified. Microsoft Learn

12. Why is with useful?

Interview-Ready Answer

with is useful when I want to preserve the original object and create a modified version. It's especially useful with immutable data models.

Real-World Example

Imagine an API request:

public record EmployeeRequest(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    string Department
);

You receive:

var request = new EmployeeRequest(
    101,
    "Saurabh",
    "Engineering"
);

You want another version:

var updatedRequest = request with
{
    Department = "Architecture"
};

You haven't mutated the original request.

This makes data transformations easier to reason about.

13. Is with a Deep Copy?

⭐ Senior-Level Trap

No.

with generally performs a shallow copy.

Consider:

public record Employee(
    string Name,
    List<string> Skills
);
var e1 = new Employee(
    "Saurabh",
    new List<string> { "C#", "React" }
);

var e2 = e1 with
{
    Name = "Rahul"
};

The Name value changes in the new record.

But the Skills list reference can still be shared:

e1
 ├── Name
 └── Skills ─────┐
                 ↓
              List object
                 ↑
                 └──── e2

So:

e2.Skills.Add("Azure");

can also be observed through e1.Skills.

Microsoft explicitly describes with copying reference-type properties as references, making the operation shallow for those members. Microsoft Learn

Interview Answer

"with creates a nondestructive copy, but it is not a general-purpose deep-copy mechanism. Reference-type members can still be shared."

14. What members does the compiler generate for a Record?

⭐ Important 3+ YOE Question

For records, the compiler generates several members.

Important ones include:

Equals()
GetHashCode()
==
!=
ToString()

Records also implement IEquatable<T>.

Positional records additionally get properties and a Deconstruct() method. Microsoft Learn

Example:

public record Employee(int Id, string Name);

You can do:

var e1 = new Employee(1, "Saurabh");
var e2 = new Employee(1, "Saurabh");

Console.WriteLine(e1.Equals(e2)); // True
Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2);      // True

Console.WriteLine(e1);

The compiler provides the record-oriented behavior.

15. What is Value-Based Equality in Records?

⭐ Extremely Important

For a normal class:

class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
}

Two objects:

var e1 = new Employee { Id = 1 };
var e2 = new Employee { Id = 1 };

are different objects.

Default:

e1 == e2

is:

False

For:

record Employee(int Id);
var e1 = new Employee(1);
var e2 = new Employee(1);

Then:

e1 == e2

is:

True

because records use value-based equality. Microsoft Learn

16. Record Class: Reference Semantics + Value Equality

This is one of the most important concepts.

Don't think:

"Records are value types."

That's incorrect.

A record class is still a reference type:

record Employee(int Id);
var e1 = new Employee(1);
var e2 = e1;

Both point to the same object:

e1 ─────┐
        ↓
     Employee
      Id = 1
        ↑
        └──── e2

But equality is value-based:

var e3 = new Employee(1);

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e3);

Output:

True

So remember:

record class
    ↓
Reference semantics
    +
Value-based equality
``` :chatgpt-content-reference{index="15"}


---

# 17. Record Struct: Value Semantics + Value Equality

```csharp
public record struct Point(int X, int Y);
var p1 = new Point(10, 20);
var p2 = p1;

Assignment copies the value.

And:

var p3 = new Point(10, 20);

Console.WriteLine(p1 == p3);

returns:

True

So:

record struct
      ↓
Value semantics
      +
Value-based equality
``` :chatgpt-content-reference{index="16"}


---

# 18. What is a Positional Record?

A positional record uses constructor-like syntax:

```csharp
public record Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    string Department
);

The compiler generates properties and other record members for you.

Usage:

var employee = new Employee(
    101,
    "Saurabh",
    "Engineering"
);

You can also deconstruct it:

var (id, name, department) = employee;

Positional records provide a concise way to define data-centric types. Microsoft Learn

19. Can Records Have Methods?

Yes.

This is a common misconception.

public record Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name
)
{
    public string GetDisplayName()
    {
        return $"{Id} - {Name}";
    }
}

Then:

var employee = new Employee(1, "Saurabh");

Console.WriteLine(employee.GetDisplayName());

Records can contain behavior.

Interview Answer

"Records are optimized for data-centric types, but they can still contain methods, properties, constructors and other members."

20. Can Records Inherit?

Record Classes: Yes

public record Employee(int Id);

public record Manager(int Id, int TeamSize)
    : Employee(Id);

Record classes can participate in record inheritance hierarchies. Microsoft Learn

Record Structs: No

record struct Point;

A record struct cannot inherit from another record struct.

Memory Trick

record class  → inheritance ✅
record struct → inheritance ❌

21. Should we use Records for Entity Framework Core Entities?

⭐ Very Important .NET Interview Question

Generally, be careful.

Microsoft's current records guidance says to avoid records for Entity Framework Core entity types because EF Core relies on reference identity for tracking entities. Microsoft Learn

For example:

public record Customer
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

This may look attractive because it's concise, but an EF Core entity generally has entity identity and lifecycle, which fits a class-oriented model better.

Interview Answer

"I would generally use normal classes for EF Core entities because entities have identity and EF Core's change tracking relies on identity/reference behavior. I'd use records more naturally for DTOs, requests, responses, or immutable data models."

22. Record vs DTO

Records are often useful for DTOs.

For example:

public record EmployeeResponse(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    string Department
);

Controller:

[HttpGet]
public EmployeeResponse GetEmployee()
{
    return new EmployeeResponse(
        101,
        "Saurabh",
        "Engineering"
    );
}

Why?

DTOs are primarily about carrying data.

Records give you:

  • concise syntax
  • value equality
  • readable ToString()
  • convenient immutable-style properties
  • with expressions

This aligns well with the data-centric purpose of records. Microsoft Learn

23. What is Shallow Immutability?

⭐ Senior-Level Question

Suppose:

public record Employee
{
    public string Name { get; init; }
    public List<string> Skills { get; init; }
}

After initialization:

employee.Name = "Rahul"; // ❌
employee.Skills = new List<string>(); // ❌

But:

employee.Skills.Add("Azure"); // ✅

may still be allowed.

Why?

Because init prevents changing the reference stored in Skills, but it doesn't make the referenced List<string> itself immutable.

So:

Property reference → immutable
Object referenced   → potentially mutable

Microsoft explicitly calls this shallow immutability. Microsoft Learn

24. How do you create a More Truly Immutable Model?

Instead of:

public List<string> Skills { get; init; }

you could expose:

public IReadOnlyList<string> Skills { get; init; }

and ensure the underlying collection isn't exposed for mutation.

Or use immutable collections where appropriate.

For example:

public record Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name,
    IReadOnlyList<string> Skills
);

Interview Answer

"init provides shallow immutability. For stronger immutability, I also need to ensure the objects referenced by properties are themselves immutable or aren't exposed through mutable APIs."

25. Why is Immutability useful?

Interview-Ready Answer

Immutability makes objects easier to reason about because their state doesn't unexpectedly change after creation. It can also simplify concurrent code and makes objects safer to use when their hash code must remain stable while they're stored in hash-based collections.

Microsoft identifies thread safety and stable hash codes as examples where immutability can be useful. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

Imagine multiple services working with:

EmployeeRequest

If the object is immutable:

Service A ──┐
Service B ──┼── EmployeeRequest
Service C ──┘

Nobody unexpectedly changes its state.

Instead:

Original
   ↓
with
   ↓
New Version

26. Record vs Struct vs Class — Important Comparison

FeatureClassRecord ClassStructRecord Struct
Reference type✅✅❌❌
Value type❌❌✅✅
Value equality by default❌✅Equals value-based✅
with❌✅❌✅
Inheritance✅✅❌❌
Good for entities✅Usually not idealUsually notUsually not
Good for DTO/data✅✅Sometimes✅
Immutable-style designManualEasyPossibleEasy
Copy semanticsReferenceReferenceValueValue

Records add data-oriented behavior while preserving whether the underlying type is a class or struct. Microsoft Learn

27. Common Interview Traps

❌ "Record is a value type."

Incorrect.

record class → reference type
record struct → value type

❌ "Records are always immutable."

Incorrect.

Records can contain mutable properties.

Better:

Records make immutable-style design easier, but immutability isn't automatic or necessarily deep.

❌ "with modifies the original object."

Incorrect.

with creates a modified copy.

var e2 = e1 with { Name = "Rahul" };

e1 remains unchanged. Microsoft Learn

❌ "with performs deep cloning."

Incorrect.

It's generally a shallow copy with respect to reference-type members. Microsoft Learn

❌ "Record class uses reference equality."

Incorrect.

It has reference semantics but value-based equality.

That's a very important distinction.

21. Equality in C# — ==, Equals(), ReferenceEquals(), GetHashCode()

This is a very important 3+ YOE / Senior interview topic because interviewers often give you two objects and ask:

"What will ==, Equals(), and ReferenceEquals() return?"

The most important thing to remember is:

==              → Equality operator; behavior depends on the type
Equals()        → Logical/value equality as defined by the type
ReferenceEquals → Same exact object?
GetHashCode()   → Hash representation used by hash-based collections

C# supports both value equality and reference equality, and different types can define different equality semantics. Microsoft Learn

1. What is Equality in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer

Equality determines whether two values or objects should be considered equal. In C#, equality can mean either same object/reference or same logical value, depending on the type and how equality is implemented.

For example:

int a = 10;
int b = 10;

Console.WriteLine(a == b); // True

For a normal class:

class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
}
var e1 = new Employee { Id = 1 };
var e2 = new Employee { Id = 1 };

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2); // False

The two class objects contain the same data, but they are different objects.

2. What is == in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer

== is the equality operator. Its behavior depends on the type. For normal reference types, it usually checks whether both references refer to the same object. But types can overload == to provide value-based comparison.

Example:

class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
}

var e1 = new Employee { Id = 1 };
var e2 = new Employee { Id = 1 };
var e3 = e1;

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2); // False
Console.WriteLine(e1 == e3); // True

Why?

e1 ─────┐
        ↓
      Object A

e3 ─────┘

e2 ─────→ Object B

e1 and e3 point to the same object.

Microsoft documents that normal reference types use reference equality for == unless the type overloads the operator. Microsoft Learn

3. What is Equals()?

Interview-Ready Answer

Equals() is a method used to determine whether two values or objects are logically equal according to the type's equality implementation.

Example:

var e1 = new Employee { Id = 1 };
var e2 = new Employee { Id = 1 };

Console.WriteLine(e1.Equals(e2));

For a normal class that hasn't overridden Equals(), this will normally be:

False

because the default Object.Equals() behavior for reference types is based on identity.

But a class can override it:

public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public override bool Equals(object? obj)
    {
        return obj is Employee other &&
               Id == other.Id;
    }

    public override int GetHashCode()
    {
        return Id.GetHashCode();
    }
}

Now:

var e1 = new Employee { Id = 1 };
var e2 = new Employee { Id = 1 };

Console.WriteLine(e1.Equals(e2)); // True

4. What is ReferenceEquals()?

⭐ Very Important

Interview-Ready Answer

ReferenceEquals() checks whether two references point to the exact same object. It checks identity and cannot be customized by overriding Equals() or ==.

Example:

var e1 = new Employee { Id = 1 };
var e2 = new Employee { Id = 1 };
var e3 = e1;

Console.WriteLine(
    ReferenceEquals(e1, e2)
); // False

Console.WriteLine(
    ReferenceEquals(e1, e3)
); // True

Even if Employee.Equals() is overridden to compare Id, ReferenceEquals() still checks object identity.

Microsoft specifically describes ReferenceEquals() as the direct identity check. Microsoft Learn

5. == vs Equals() vs ReferenceEquals()

⭐ Memorize This Table

==Equals()ReferenceEquals()
TypeOperatorMethodStatic method
ChecksDepends on typeLogical equality defined by typeObject identity
Can be overloaded/overridden== can be overloadedEquals() can be overriddenNo
Normal class defaultReference equalityReference equalityReference equality
RecordValue equalityValue equalityIdentity
StringContent equalityContent equalityIdentity
Main purposeEquality syntaxLogical equalitySame object?

6. What happens with Strings?

⭐ Common Interview Trap

string is a reference type, but it provides value/content equality.

string s1 = "Hello";
string s2 = "Hello";

Console.WriteLine(s1 == s2);
Console.WriteLine(s1.Equals(s2));

Both return:

True

Because string defines equality based on its content.

Microsoft explicitly notes that although strings are classes, == and Equals() compare string content rather than object identity. Microsoft Learn

But:

Console.WriteLine(
    ReferenceEquals(s1, s2)
);

should not be used to determine string content equality.

Interview Answer

"string is a reference type, but it overloads equality so that == and Equals() compare the string contents."

7. What happens with Records?

This connects directly to the previous topic.

public record Employee(
    int Id,
    string Name
);
var e1 = new Employee(1, "Saurabh");
var e2 = new Employee(1, "Saurabh");

Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2);
Console.WriteLine(e1.Equals(e2));
Console.WriteLine(ReferenceEquals(e1, e2));

Output:

True
True
False

Why?

e1 == e2
    ↓
Value equality
    ↓
same data → True

e1.Equals(e2)
    ↓
Value equality
    ↓
same data → True

ReferenceEquals
    ↓
same object?
    ↓
No → False

Records generate value-based equality members automatically. Microsoft Learn

8. What is the difference between Reference Equality and Value Equality?

⭐ Very Important

Reference Equality

Two objects are equal if they are the same object.

Object A
   ↑
   ├── e1
   └── e2

Therefore:

ReferenceEquals(e1, e2) // True

Value Equality

Two objects are equal if their relevant data is equal.

Object A
Id = 1

Object B
Id = 1

Different objects, same logical value.

Therefore:

e1.Equals(e2) // True

if the type defines equality that way.

Interview Answer

"Reference equality compares identity, while value equality compares the logical data represented by the objects."

9. What is GetHashCode()?

⭐ Must Know

Interview-Ready Answer

GetHashCode() returns an integer hash value representing the object. It's primarily used by hash-based collections such as Dictionary<TKey,TValue> and HashSet<T>.

Example:

var employee = new Employee
{
    Id = 101
};

int hash = employee.GetHashCode();

Hash-based collections use the hash code to efficiently locate potential matches.

10. Why must Equals() and GetHashCode() be consistent?

⭐ Extremely Important Interview Question

The rule is:

If two objects are equal according to Equals(), they must return the same hash code.

For example:

public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public override bool Equals(object? obj)
    {
        return obj is Employee other &&
               Id == other.Id;
    }

    public override int GetHashCode()
    {
        return Id.GetHashCode();
    }
}

Now:

var e1 = new Employee { Id = 10 };
var e2 = new Employee { Id = 10 };
e1.Equals(e2)       // True
e1.GetHashCode()    // same
e2.GetHashCode()    // same

Important:

The reverse is not guaranteed:

Same hash code
     ≠
Objects are equal

Two different objects can have the same hash code. This is called a hash collision.

Microsoft explicitly states that equal objects must have equal hash codes, but unequal objects can still have identical hash codes. Microsoft Learn

11. Why is GetHashCode() important for Dictionary and HashSet?

Consider:

var employees = new HashSet<Employee>();

When you do:

employees.Add(e1);

and later:

employees.Contains(e2);

the collection uses equality and hashing to determine whether an equivalent item already exists.

That's why if you override Equals(), you should also override GetHashCode() consistently. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

Suppose:

Employee Id = 101

is your logical identity.

Then two separate objects:

Employee A → Id 101
Employee B → Id 101

should potentially represent the same logical employee.

Your equality and hash code should therefore both be based on the same identity definition.

12. What happens if I override Equals() but not GetHashCode()?

⭐ Interview Trap

Bad implementation:

public override bool Equals(object? obj)
{
    return obj is Employee other &&
           Id == other.Id;
}

but:

// GetHashCode not overridden

This violates the equality/hash-code contract.

You can get incorrect behavior in:

HashSet<Employee>
Dictionary<Employee, ...>

Interview Answer

"If I override Equals() to define value equality, I should also override GetHashCode() using the same equality-defining fields."

Microsoft explicitly recommends overriding both consistently. Microsoft Learn

13. What is IEquatable<T>?

⭐ Strong 3+ YOE Question

IEquatable<T> provides a strongly typed equality method:

public interface IEquatable<T>
{
    bool Equals(T? other);
}

Example:

public class Employee : IEquatable<Employee>
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public bool Equals(Employee? other)
    {
        return other is not null &&
               Id == other.Id;
    }
}

You should normally also override:

Equals(object?)
GetHashCode()

to keep all equality mechanisms consistent. Microsoft recommends this consistency when implementing IEquatable<T>. Microsoft Learn

14. Why use IEquatable<T>?

Interview-Ready Answer

IEquatable<T> provides a strongly typed equality comparison and can avoid unnecessary boxing for value types compared through their concrete type. It is also used by generic collections for equality operations.

For example:

public struct EmployeeId : IEquatable<EmployeeId>
{
    public int Value { get; }

    public bool Equals(EmployeeId other)
    {
        return Value == other.Value;
    }
}

Generic collections can use the strongly typed equality implementation.

Microsoft notes that IEquatable<T> is used by generic collections such as Dictionary<TKey,TValue> and List<T> for equality operations. Microsoft Learn

15. Should IEquatable<T>.Equals() and Equals(object) agree?

Absolutely.

You want:

Equals(T)
      ↓
same equality rules
      ↓
Equals(object)
      ↓
same equality rules
      ↓
GetHashCode()

Example:

public class Employee : IEquatable<Employee>
{
    public int Id { get; }

    public bool Equals(Employee? other)
    {
        return other is not null &&
               Id == other.Id;
    }

    public override bool Equals(object? obj)
    {
        return Equals(obj as Employee);
    }

    public override int GetHashCode()
    {
        return Id.GetHashCode();
    }
}

This gives consistent equality behavior.

16. How do you correctly implement equality in a class?

⭐ Senior Interview Question

A common pattern is:

public sealed class Employee : IEquatable<Employee>
{
    public int Id { get; }
    public string Name { get; }

    public Employee(int id, string name)
    {
        Id = id;
        Name = name;
    }

    public bool Equals(Employee? other)
    {
        return other is not null &&
               Id == other.Id &&
               Name == other.Name;
    }

    public override bool Equals(object? obj)
    {
        return Equals(obj as Employee);
    }

    public override int GetHashCode()
    {
        return HashCode.Combine(Id, Name);
    }

    public static bool operator ==(
        Employee? left,
        Employee? right)
    {
        return Equals(left, right);
    }

    public static bool operator !=(
        Employee? left,
        Employee? right)
    {
        return !Equals(left, right);
    }
}

What is important here?

All equality mechanisms use the same fields:

Id
Name

So:

Equals()
GetHashCode()
==
!=

remain consistent.

Microsoft's equality guidance recommends keeping these members consistent when implementing custom value equality. Microsoft Learn

17. Why use HashCode.Combine()?

Instead of manually calculating a hash:

return Id.GetHashCode() ^ Name.GetHashCode();

prefer:

return HashCode.Combine(Id, Name);

Example:

public override int GetHashCode()
{
    return HashCode.Combine(Id, Name);
}

It provides a convenient way to combine multiple values into a hash code.

The important rule is:

Fields used by Equals()
        ↓
same fields
        ↓
GetHashCode()

18. What are the equality rules?

Interviewers may ask about the equality contract.

For a well-defined equality relation, it should be:

Reflexive

x.Equals(x) == true

Symmetric

x.Equals(y) == y.Equals(x)

Transitive

If:

x == y
y == z

then:

x == z

Consistent

Repeated equality checks should give consistent results as long as the relevant state doesn't change.

Null

For a reference type:

x.Equals(null) → false

when x is a non-null instance.

These properties are important when implementing custom equality.

19. Can == and Equals() return different results?

Yes.

This is a very good interview question.

For a normal class:

class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public override bool Equals(object? obj)
    {
        return obj is Employee other &&
               Id == other.Id;
    }

    public override int GetHashCode()
    {
        return Id.GetHashCode();
    }
}

If you don't overload ==:

var e1 = new Employee { Id = 1 };
var e2 = new Employee { Id = 1 };

Console.WriteLine(e1.Equals(e2)); // True
Console.WriteLine(e1 == e2);      // False

Why?

Equals()
   ↓
Your override
   ↓
Compare Id

==
   ↓
Class didn't overload it
   ↓
Reference equality

This is why custom equality implementations should keep equality operations consistent. Microsoft recommends defining ==/!= when appropriate so the operator and Equals() semantics align. Microsoft Learn

20. What does ReferenceEquals() do with Value Types?

⭐ Tricky Question

Consider:

int a = 10;
int b = 10;

Console.WriteLine(
    ReferenceEquals(a, b)
);

This is not a meaningful value comparison.

ReferenceEquals() is designed for object identity. When value types are passed to it, they must be boxed, resulting in separate boxed objects in this scenario, so it returns false. Microsoft explicitly documents this behavior. Microsoft Learn

Therefore:

int
 ↓
Use == / Equals()

object identity
 ↓
ReferenceEquals()

21. What happens with a Plain Struct?

Consider:

struct Point
{
    public int X;
    public int Y;
}
var p1 = new Point { X = 10, Y = 20 };
var p2 = new Point { X = 10, Y = 20 };

You can do:

Console.WriteLine(
    p1.Equals(p2)
);

and get:

True

because structs have value equality through ValueType.Equals().

However, an important modern interview detail:

p1 == p2

does not automatically work for an ordinary user-defined struct unless that struct defines the == operator. Microsoft Learn

22. What happens with a record struct?

public record struct Point(int X, int Y);

Now:

var p1 = new Point(10, 20);
var p2 = new Point(10, 20);

Console.WriteLine(p1 == p2);

returns:

True

Unlike a plain struct, record struct automatically gets the record equality operators. Microsoft Learn

23. Why is Mutable Equality Dangerous?

⭐ Senior-Level Question

Suppose:

public class Employee
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public override bool Equals(object? obj)
    {
        return obj is Employee other &&
               Id == other.Id;
    }

    public override int GetHashCode()
    {
        return Id.GetHashCode();
    }
}

Then:

var employee = new Employee { Id = 100 };

var set = new HashSet<Employee>();

set.Add(employee);

Now change:

employee.Id = 200;

The object's hash code has changed after it was inserted.

This can cause problems when looking it up in the hash set.

Interview Answer

"Fields used for equality and hashing should ideally be immutable while an object is being used as a key in a hash-based collection."

This is one reason immutable/value-oriented objects work well with equality semantics.

24. Real-World Scenario — Employee ID

Imagine your system has:

Employee ID = 101

You might create:

public readonly record struct EmployeeId(int Value);

Then:

var id1 = new EmployeeId(101);
var id2 = new EmployeeId(101);

Console.WriteLine(id1 == id2); // True

This is a good value-object scenario.

The identity of the employee entity can still be represented by:

public class Employee
{
    public EmployeeId Id { get; set; }
}

So:

Employee
   ↓
Entity / Class

EmployeeId
   ↓
Value Object / Record Struct

That's a useful domain-design example for interviews.

25. Real-World Scenario — Dictionary

Suppose:

Dictionary<Employee, string> employees;

If Employee defines equality based on:

EmployeeId

then:

GetHashCode()

must also use the same logical identity.

Otherwise, dictionary lookups can behave incorrectly.

Strong interview statement

"For hash-based collections, equality and hashing must agree: equal objects must produce equal hash codes." Microsoft Learn

26. Most Important Comparison

Memorize this:

==
↓
Operator
↓
Depends on type
Equals()
↓
Method
↓
Logical equality defined by type
ReferenceEquals()
↓
Static method
↓
Exact same object?
GetHashCode()
↓
Hash representation
↓
Dictionary / HashSet

27. Common Interview Traps

❌ "== always checks reference equality."

Wrong.

== can be overloaded and some types such as string and records use value-based equality. Microsoft Learn

❌ "Equals() always checks value equality."

Wrong.

A normal class that doesn't override Equals() uses the default object equality behavior.

❌ "ReferenceEquals() calls Equals()."

Wrong.

It directly checks object identity.

❌ "Same hash code means objects are equal."

Wrong.

Hash collisions are possible.

Same hash
   ≠
Same object/value
``` :chatgpt-content-reference{index="18"}


---

### ❌ "If I override Equals(), I don't need GetHashCode()."

Wrong.

If equality changes, hashing must be consistent with it.

---

### ❌ "Record `==` checks reference equality."

Wrong.

Records provide value-based equality.

22. Generics — Covariance & Contravariance

Generics are one of the most important C# topics for a 3+ YOE / Senior .NET interview, especially when interviewers move from basic generics into IEnumerable<T>, Func<>, Action<>, and in / out.

C# generics provide compile-time type safety and are used throughout .NET collections, LINQ, delegates, Task<T>, etc. Microsoft Learn

Part 1 — Generics Fundamentals

Q1. What are Generics in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer

Generics allow us to write reusable, type-safe code that works with different data types without duplicating the implementation.

Instead of using object and casting, we define a type parameter such as T, and the compiler ensures type safety.

Example

public class Repository<T>
{
    public void Add(T item)
    {
        // Add item
    }
}

Now:

Repository<Customer> customerRepo = new();
Repository<Order> orderRepo = new();

The same repository implementation works with different types.

Generics provide compile-time type checking and avoid unnecessary casting. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

In your .NET application, instead of creating:

CustomerRepository
OrderRepository
ProductRepository

with duplicated generic CRUD logic, you could have:

Repository<Customer>
Repository<Order>
Repository<Product>

Q2. Why are Generics better than using object?

Interview-Ready Answer

Generics provide type safety, better readability, and avoid unnecessary boxing/unboxing or casting in many scenarios.

Without Generics

public void Print(object value)
{
    Console.WriteLine(value);
}

We lose compile-time knowledge about the actual type.

With Generics

public void Print<T>(T value)
{
    Console.WriteLine(value);
}

The compiler knows the type of T.

Real-World Scenario

List<int> numbers = new();

numbers.Add(10);
// numbers.Add("Hello"); // Compile-time error

This prevents incorrect data from entering the collection.

Q3. What is a Generic Class?

Interview-Ready Answer

A generic class is a class that defines one or more type parameters, allowing the same class to work with different types.
public class Box<T>
{
    public T Value { get; set; }
}

Usage:

Box<int> intBox = new();
intBox.Value = 100;

Box<string> stringBox = new();
stringBox.Value = "Hello";

Real-World Scenario

A generic repository:

public class Repository<T>
{
    public T GetById(int id)
    {
        // database logic
        return default!;
    }
}

Q4. What is a Generic Method?

Interview-Ready Answer

A generic method defines its own type parameter and can work with different types without making the entire class generic.
public static void Print<T>(T value)
{
    Console.WriteLine(value);
}

Usage:

Print(10);
Print("Hello");
Print(10.5);

The compiler can infer the type in many cases.

Microsoft documents generic methods and generic types as reusable, type-safe constructs. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

A utility method:

public static T GetFirst<T>(List<T> items)
{
    return items[0];
}

Q5. What are Generic Constraints?

Interview-Ready Answer

Generic constraints restrict what types can be used as a generic argument. They allow the compiler to know that T has certain capabilities.

Example:

public void Print<T>(T value)
    where T : IEmployee
{
    Console.WriteLine(value.Name);
}

Because T must implement IEmployee, we can safely access Name.

Common constraints include:

where T : class
where T : struct
where T : BaseClass
where T : IInterface
where T : new()

They can also be combined. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

Suppose all entities implement:

public interface IEntity
{
    int Id { get; }
}

Then:

public class Repository<T>
    where T : IEntity
{
    public T GetById(int id)
    {
        // T is guaranteed to have Id
        ...
    }
}

Q6. What is where T : class?

Interview-Ready Answer

where T : class restricts T to a reference type.
public void Process<T>(T item)
    where T : class
{
}

Valid:

Process<Customer>();
Process<string>();

Not valid:

Process<int>();

Q7. What is where T : struct?

Interview-Ready Answer

where T : struct restricts T to a non-nullable value type.
public void Process<T>(T value)
    where T : struct
{
}

Valid:

Process<int>();
Process<DateTime>();

Q8. What is where T : new()?

Interview-Ready Answer

where T : new() means T must have an accessible parameterless constructor.

Example:

public T Create<T>()
    where T : new()
{
    return new T();
}

Usage:

Customer customer = Create<Customer>();

The new() constraint must be placed after other constraints in the constraint list. Microsoft Learn

Part 2 — Variance

Now we reach the important senior-level part.

There are three concepts:

Invariant
   ↓
Covariance
   ↓
Contravariance

Q9. What is Variance in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer

Variance describes how generic types can be converted when their underlying type arguments have an inheritance relationship.

There are three forms:

  • Covariance — out
  • Contravariance — in
  • Invariance — neither

Variance applies to generic interfaces and delegates, and it applies to reference types. Microsoft Learn

Q10. What is Invariance?

Interview-Ready Answer

A generic type is invariant when there is no implicit conversion between different constructed types, even if their type arguments have an inheritance relationship.

Suppose:

class Animal { }

class Dog : Animal { }

This does not work:

List<Dog> dogs = new();

List<Animal> animals = dogs; // ❌

Why?

Because if this were allowed:

animals.Add(new Cat());

the original List<Dog> would contain a Cat.

That would break type safety.

Real-World Scenario

List<T> is invariant.

List<Dog>
    X
List<Animal>

Even though:

Dog → Animal

the relationship does not automatically become:

List<Dog> → List<Animal>

Q11. What is Covariance?

Interview-Ready Answer

Covariance allows us to use a more derived type where a base type is expected.

It uses the out keyword.

Memory trick:

Producer → out → produces/returns data

Example:

class Animal
{
}

class Dog : Animal
{
}

IEnumerable<T> is covariant:

IEnumerable<Dog> dogs = new List<Dog>();

IEnumerable<Animal> animals = dogs;

This works because IEnumerable<out T> produces values of T; it doesn't provide an operation to add arbitrary T values. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

Suppose:

IEnumerable<Dog> dogs = GetDogs();

A method only needs to read animals:

void PrintAnimals(IEnumerable<Animal> animals)
{
    foreach (var animal in animals)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(animal);
    }
}

You can pass:

PrintAnimals(dogs);

because every Dog is an Animal.

Q12. Why is IEnumerable<T> Covariant?

Interview-Ready Answer

IEnumerable<T> is covariant because it primarily produces/returns T values rather than accepting T values for mutation.

Conceptually:

public interface IEnumerable<out T>
{
    // produces T
}

Therefore:

IEnumerable<Dog>

can be assigned to:

IEnumerable<Animal>

Microsoft specifically lists IEnumerable<T> as a covariant interface. Microsoft Learn

Q13. What is Contravariance?

Interview-Ready Answer

Contravariance allows a generic type using a base type to be assigned where a derived type is expected.

It uses the in keyword.

Memory trick:

Consumer → in → consumes/accepts data

Example:

class Animal
{
}

class Dog : Animal
{
}

Consider:

Action<Animal> animalHandler =
    animal => Console.WriteLine(animal);

We can assign it to:

Action<Dog> dogHandler = animalHandler;

Why is this safe?

Because:

Dog is an Animal

So a method capable of accepting any Animal can certainly accept a Dog.

Action<T> is contravariant. Microsoft Learn

Q14. Why is Action<T> Contravariant?

Interview-Ready Answer

Action<T> consumes a value of type T, so its type parameter is contravariant and declared with in.

Conceptually:

public delegate void Action<in T>(T obj);

Therefore:

Action<Animal> animalAction = animal =>
{
    Console.WriteLine(animal);
};

Action<Dog> dogAction = animalAction;

This is safe because animalAction can handle every Animal, including Dog.

Microsoft lists Action<T> as contravariant. Microsoft Learn

Q15. What is the easiest way to remember Covariance vs Contravariance?

Interview-Ready Answer

Remember:

OUT → Output → Producer → Covariance

IN → Input → Consumer → Contravariance

Or:

Covariance     = Derived → Base
                 out

Contravariance = Base → Derived
                 in

Example:

IEnumerable<Dog> → IEnumerable<Animal>
        out

Action<Animal> → Action<Dog>
        in

Very Important

Don't memorize only the arrows.

Think about what the generic type does:

Produces T → out
Consumes T → in

That makes the rule much easier to derive.

Q16. What is Func<T> covariance/contravariance?

This is a very common interview question.

Func can have both:

input parameters → contravariant
return type      → covariant

For example:

Func<Dog, Animal>

Conceptually:

Func<in T, out TResult>

So:

T         → in
TResult   → out

Microsoft documents Func<> as supporting both contravariant input parameters and covariant return types. Microsoft Learn

Example

Func<Animal, Dog> handler = animal => new Dog();

Here:

Animal = input  → in
Dog    = output → out

Real-World Scenario

A factory/mapper:

Func<BaseRequest, DerivedResponse>

can model a function that accepts a broad request type and produces a more specific response type.

Q17. Can we create our own Covariant Interface?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes. We use out on the generic type parameter, and the type parameter can be used in output positions.

Example:

public interface IRepository<out T>
{
    T GetById(int id);
}

Then:

IRepository<Dog> dogRepository = ...;

IRepository<Animal> animalRepository = dogRepository;

This is valid because the repository only returns T.

Important restriction

You cannot use a covariant T as a normal input parameter.

For example:

public interface IRepository<out T>
{
    void Add(T item); // ❌
}

That violates covariance rules.

Variant type parameters have restrictions on where they can be used. Microsoft Learn

Q18. Can we create our own Contravariant Interface?

Yes.

public interface IHandler<in T>
{
    void Handle(T item);
}

Now:

IHandler<Animal> animalHandler = ...;

IHandler<Dog> dogHandler = animalHandler;

This is valid because the interface consumes T.

Q19. Can a generic class be Covariant?

Interview-Ready Answer

No. C# variance annotations using in and out are supported on generic interfaces and delegates, not generic classes.

For example:

public interface IProducer<out T>
{
    T Get();
}

Valid.

But:

public class Producer<out T>
{
}

Invalid.

Microsoft explicitly restricts variant type parameters to generic interfaces and delegates. Microsoft Learn

Q20. Does Variance work with value types?

Interview-Ready Answer

No. Generic variance applies to reference types, not value types.

For example:

IEnumerable<string> strings = ...;

IEnumerable<object> objects = strings; // ✅

But variance doesn't provide the equivalent conversion for value-type arguments such as:

IEnumerable<int>

Microsoft documents this restriction explicitly. Microsoft Learn

Q21. What is the difference between in, out, and ref?

Very common trap.

KeywordPurpose
inContravariant generic parameter / readonly reference parameter
outCovariant generic parameter / output parameter
refPass variable by reference

For generics:

interface IConsumer<in T>
{
}

means contravariance.

interface IProducer<out T>
{
}

means covariance.

But:

void Process(ref int value)
{
}

has nothing to do with generic variance.

Interview Tip

Always look at the context.

in T
out T

inside a generic interface/delegate → variance

in parameter
out parameter
ref parameter

in a method → parameter passing

Q22. Give a real-world example of Covariance and Contravariance.

Interview-Ready Answer

Imagine an application processing notifications.

class Notification
{
}

class EmailNotification : Notification
{
}

Covariance — Producer

IEnumerable<EmailNotification> emails = GetEmails();

IEnumerable<Notification> notifications = emails;

We're saying:

"I have a collection producing EmailNotifications, and I only need to read Notifications."

Contravariance — Consumer

Action<Notification> processNotification =
    notification => Process(notification);

Action<EmailNotification> processEmail =
    processNotification;

We're saying:

"This handler can process any Notification, so it can definitely process an EmailNotification."

This producer/consumer distinction is the key idea behind variance.

Q23. What is the difference between Covariance and Contravariance?

CovarianceContravariance
Keywordoutin
ThinkOutputInput
RoleProducerConsumer
DirectionDerived → BaseBase → Derived
ExampleIEnumerable<Dog> → IEnumerable<Animal>Action<Animal> → Action<Dog>
Common typesIEnumerable<T>, Func<TResult>Action<T>, IComparer<T>

Examples of variant interfaces include IEnumerable<T> as covariant and IComparer<T>, IComparable<T> as contravariant. Microsoft Learn

Q24. Why is List<T> not Covariant?

This is an excellent Senior-level follow-up.

Suppose this were allowed:

List<Dog> dogs = new();

List<Animal> animals = dogs;

Then:

animals.Add(new Cat());

Now:

List<Dog>
    ↓
contains Cat ❌

That violates the type safety of List<Dog>.

Therefore List<T> is invariant.

Interview Answer

List<T> is mutable, so it both produces and consumes T. Making it covariant would allow unsafe writes. That's why it remains invariant.

Q25. Why can IEnumerable<Dog> be assigned to IEnumerable<Animal>?

Because IEnumerable<T> is designed for enumeration/reading rather than adding arbitrary elements.

IEnumerable<Dog> dogs = GetDogs();

IEnumerable<Animal> animals = dogs;

You can safely read every element as an Animal.

This is exactly the kind of conversion enabled by covariance. Microsoft Learn

Q26. What is the difference between Generics and Variance?

Interview-Ready Answer

Generics allow us to write reusable type-safe code using type parameters.

Variance is a feature of certain generic interfaces and delegates that allows compatible conversions between constructed generic types when their type arguments have an inheritance relationship.

Example:

List<T>

is generic.

IEnumerable<out T>

is generic and covariant.

Most Important Interview Questions to Prioritize

For your 3+ YOE / Senior .NET preparation, learn these in this order:

🔴 Must Know

  1. What are generics?
  1. Why use generics?
  1. Generic class vs generic method
  1. Generic constraints
  1. What is covariance?
  1. What is contravariance?
  1. What are in and out?
  1. Why is IEnumerable<T> covariant?
  1. Why is Action<T> contravariant?
  1. Why is List<T> invariant?

🟠 Strong Interview Level

  1. Func<in T, out TResult>
  1. Create your own covariant interface
  1. Create your own contravariant interface
  1. Variance with interfaces vs delegates
  1. Why variance works only with reference types
  1. Covariance vs contravariance vs invariance
  1. Generic constraints and new()

🟡 Senior Follow-ups

  1. Producer vs consumer principle
  1. Why mutable collections generally can't be covariant
  1. How variance affects API design
  1. Variance with IComparer<T>
  1. Variance with delegates
  1. Difference between generic in/out and method parameter in/out

🔥 30-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer asks:

"Explain covariance and contravariance in C#."

Say:

"Variance describes how generic types can be converted when their type parameters have an inheritance relationship. Covariance uses out and is used when a generic type produces or returns values, so a derived generic type can be used where the base generic type is expected. For example, IEnumerable<Dog> can be assigned to IEnumerable<Animal>. Contravariance uses in and is used when a generic type consumes values, so a generic type using a base type can be used where a derived type is expected. For example, Action<Animal> can be assigned to Action<Dog>. List<T> is invariant because it's mutable." Microsoft Learn

🧠 Easy Memory Trick

GENERIC VARIANCE
       │
       ├── INVARIANT
       │      └── no conversion
       │
       ├── COVARIANT
       │      └── out
       │      └── Producer
       │      └── Output
       │      └── Dog → Animal
       │
       └── CONTRAVARIANT
              └── in
              └── Consumer
              └── Input
              └── Animal → Dog

One line to remember:

out = I give you T. in = I take T.

That one distinction will help you derive most covariance/contravariance questions instead of memorizing them.

23. Delegates in C#

Delegates are a high-priority C# interview topic because they connect directly to callbacks, Func<>, Action<>, lambdas, LINQ, events, and dependency-friendly designs.

A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method with a specific parameter list and return type. It lets you pass a method as an argument and invoke it later. Microsoft Learn

1. What is a Delegate in C#?

Interview-Ready Answer

A delegate is a type-safe reference to a method. It defines the method's parameter list and return type, and it allows us to pass methods as parameters or invoke them later.

Example

public delegate int Calculate(int a, int b);

public static int Add(int a, int b)
{
    return a + b;
}

Calculate operation = Add;

int result = operation(10, 20);

Console.WriteLine(result); // 30

Here:

Calculate
   ↓
Delegate type

Add
   ↓
Method

operation
   ↓
Delegate object referencing Add

Delegates can reference compatible static or instance methods. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

Imagine your order-processing system needs different calculation strategies:

CalculateDiscount
CalculateTax
CalculateShipping

Instead of hardcoding one method, you can pass the required method through a delegate.

2. Why do we use Delegates?

Interview-Ready Answer

Delegates are useful when we want to pass behavior as a parameter, implement callbacks, support flexible strategies, or invoke methods dynamically.

Example

public void Process(int value, Func<int, bool> condition)
{
    if (condition(value))
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Valid");
    }
}

Now:

Process(10, x => x > 5);

The caller provides the behavior.

Real-World Scenario

Suppose you have:

ProcessCustomers()

Sometimes you want:

customers older than 30

and sometimes:

customers from India

Instead of creating multiple methods, you can pass the filtering logic.

This "passing behavior" capability is one of the major purposes of delegates. Microsoft Learn

3. How do you declare a custom Delegate?

Interview-Ready Answer

Use the delegate keyword:

public delegate void Notify(string message);

This delegate can reference any compatible method:

public static void SendEmail(string message)
{
    Console.WriteLine(message);
}

Notify notification = SendEmail;

notification("Order created");

The method must have a compatible signature.

Real-World Scenario

public delegate void PaymentCompleted(decimal amount);

Different payment implementations can trigger different callbacks.

4. What is the relationship between a Delegate and a Method?

Think of it this way:

Method
   ↓
actual implementation

Delegate
   ↓
type-safe reference to compatible method

For example:

public delegate int Operation(int a, int b);

public int Add(int a, int b)
{
    return a + b;
}

The delegate doesn't contain the implementation of Add; it can reference and invoke it.

5. Can a Delegate point to an Instance Method?

Yes.

public class Calculator
{
    public int Add(int a, int b)
    {
        return a + b;
    }
}

Calculator calculator = new();

Calculate operation = calculator.Add;

Console.WriteLine(operation(10, 20));

A delegate can reference both static and instance methods, provided their signatures are compatible. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

A service object can expose a method as a callback without the caller needing to know the internal implementation.

6. What is a Multicast Delegate?

Interview-Ready Answer

A multicast delegate is a delegate that contains an invocation list with multiple methods. When invoked, the methods are called in sequence.

Example:

public delegate void Notify();

public static void SendEmail()
{
    Console.WriteLine("Email sent");
}

public static void SendSms()
{
    Console.WriteLine("SMS sent");
}

Notify notification = SendEmail;

notification += SendSms;

notification();

Output:

Email sent
SMS sent

Delegates support both single-target and multicast invocation. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

When an order is completed:

OrderCompleted
      │
      ├── SendEmail()
      ├── SendSMS()
      └── UpdateAnalytics()

One delegate can invoke multiple handlers.

7. How do += and = work with Delegates?

Interview-Ready Answer

notification += SendEmail;

adds a method to the invocation list.

notification -= SendEmail;

removes it.

Example:

Notify notify = SendEmail;

notify += SendSms;
notify += LogOrder;

notify -= SendSms;

Now only:

SendEmail
LogOrder

remain in the invocation list.

8. What happens if a Multicast Delegate has a Return Value?

This is a common interview trap.

Suppose:

public delegate int Calculate();

and:

Calculate operation = Method1;
operation += Method2;

Both methods execute when the delegate is invoked.

But if the delegate returns a value:

The return value from the last method in the invocation list is returned to the caller.

Earlier return values are not automatically collected.

Example

static int Method1()
{
    return 10;
}

static int Method2()
{
    return 20;
}
Calculate operation = Method1;
operation += Method2;

int result = operation();

result will be:

20

Interview Tip

If you need results from every handler, use another approach such as collecting results explicitly.

9. What are Action, Func, and Predicate?

These are built-in delegate types provided by .NET, so you don't always need to declare your own delegate. Microsoft Learn

Action

Used when the method returns void.

Action<string> print = message =>
{
    Console.WriteLine(message);
};

Conceptually:

Input → Action → no return value

Action<T> represents a method that takes a parameter and returns void. Microsoft Learn

Func

Used when the method returns a value.

Func<int, int, int> add = (a, b) => a + b;

Important:

Func<int, int, int>
     │    │    │
     │    │    └── return type
     │    └────── input
     └─────────── input

The last generic parameter is always the return type. Microsoft Learn

Predicate

Commonly represents a method that takes one value and returns bool.

Predicate<int> isEven = x => x % 2 == 0;

10. Action vs Func vs Predicate

DelegateParametersReturn
Action0void
Action<T>1+void
Func<TResult>0TResult
Func<T, TResult>1+TResult
Predicate<T>1bool

Easy Memory Trick

Action    → performs an action → void
Func      → performs a function → returns value
Predicate → checks condition → bool

11. What is a Lambda Expression in relation to Delegates?

Interview-Ready Answer

A lambda expression is a concise way to provide a method implementation, and it can be converted to a compatible delegate type.

Example:

Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;

Here:

x => x * x

is the lambda.

It becomes the implementation for:

Func<int, int>

Real-World Scenario

LINQ heavily uses this pattern:

var adults = users.Where(x => x.Age >= 18);

The lambda provides the filtering behavior.

Delegates are one of the foundations that make this style possible. Microsoft Learn

12. Delegate vs Lambda Expression?

Interview-Ready Answer

A delegate is a type, while a lambda is an expression used to create a function implementation that can often be converted to a compatible delegate.

Example:

Func<int, int> square = x => x * x;

Here:

Func<int, int>
      ↓
Delegate type

x => x * x
      ↓
Lambda expression

Don't say:

"Lambda and delegate are the same."

They are related but not the same concept.

13. What is a Method Group?

You may see:

Func<int, int> operation = Square;

instead of:

Func<int, int> operation = x => Square(x);

Square here is a method group that can be converted to the compatible delegate.

Example:

static int Square(int x)
{
    return x * x;
}

Func<int, int> operation = Square;

C# performs the method-group conversion.

Microsoft documents this as a standard way to assign methods to delegate variables. Microsoft Learn

14. Can a Delegate point to multiple methods?

Yes.

Notify notify = SendEmail;

notify += SendSms;
notify += Log;

notify();

This creates a multicast delegate.

Think:

Delegate
   │
   ├── SendEmail
   ├── SendSms
   └── Log

15. What is a Generic Delegate?

Interview-Ready Answer

A generic delegate has one or more type parameters, allowing the same delegate definition to work with different types.

Example:

public delegate void Process<T>(T item);

Usage:

Process<int> processInt = x =>
{
    Console.WriteLine(x);
};

Process<string> processString = x =>
{
    Console.WriteLine(x);
};

Generic delegates provide reusable, strongly typed delegate definitions. Microsoft Learn

16. Can Delegates be used as Method Parameters?

Absolutely. This is one of their most important uses.

public void ProcessNumbers(
    int a,
    int b,
    Func<int, int, int> operation)
{
    int result = operation(a, b);

    Console.WriteLine(result);
}

Now:

ProcessNumbers(10, 20, (a, b) => a + b);

or:

ProcessNumbers(10, 20, (a, b) => a * b);

Same method, different behavior.

Real-World Scenario

This is essentially the Strategy pattern at a small scale:

Process()
   │
   ├── Add strategy
   ├── Multiply strategy
   └── Discount strategy

17. What is a Callback?

Interview-Ready Answer

A callback is a method that is passed to another method and called later when a particular operation completes or an event occurs. Delegates are commonly used to implement callbacks.

Example:

public void ProcessOrder(Action callback)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Processing order...");

    callback();
}

Usage:

ProcessOrder(() =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("Order completed");
});

Real-World Scenario

API call completed
       ↓
callback
       ↓
Send notification

Delegates are specifically useful for callback scenarios. Microsoft Learn

18. Delegate vs Interface — when would you use each?

Interview-Ready Answer

I would generally use a delegate when I need to pass one piece of behavior, such as a callback, predicate, or calculation. I would use an interface when I need to define a broader contract with multiple related members and potentially state/behavior across implementations.

Delegate

Func<Order, bool> filter;

Good for:

one behavior

Interface

public interface IPaymentService
{
    void Pay();
    void Refund();
}

Good for:

multiple related behaviors

Real-World Scenario

Filtering orders:

Func<Order, bool>

Payment processing:

IPaymentService

19. Delegate vs Event — what's the difference?

This is extremely important because events are built on delegates.

Delegate

A delegate can be invoked by code that has access to the delegate.

public Action? SomethingHappened;

Potentially:

SomethingHappened?.Invoke();

from outside the declaring type if publicly exposed as a delegate field/property.

Event

public event Action? SomethingHappened;

Consumers can:

publisher.SomethingHappened += Handler;
publisher.SomethingHappened -= Handler;

but they cannot normally raise the event from outside the declaring type.

Interview Answer

A delegate represents a callable method reference, while an event provides a controlled publisher-subscriber mechanism built on delegates. With an event, external subscribers can add and remove handlers, but the publisher controls when the event is raised. Microsoft Learn

We'll cover Events as the next dedicated topic in the roadmap.

20. What is Delegate Invocation?

You can invoke a delegate in several equivalent ways.

operation(10, 20);

or:

operation.Invoke(10, 20);

For nullable delegates:

operation?.Invoke(10, 20);

The last form safely does nothing if the delegate is null.

21. Can a Delegate be null?

Yes.

Action action = null;

Calling:

action();

causes a NullReferenceException.

Safer:

action?.Invoke();

22. What is the difference between delegate and Func?

Interview-Ready Answer

delegate is the C# syntax for defining a custom delegate type, while Func is a predefined generic delegate type provided by .NET.

Custom:

public delegate int Calculator(int a, int b);

Built-in:

Func<int, int, int> calculator;

Both can represent a compatible method.

When would I create a custom delegate?

When the delegate represents a domain-specific concept and a meaningful name improves readability.

For example:

public delegate void PaymentCompletedHandler(
    Payment payment);

may communicate intent better than:

Action<Payment>

23. What is Delegate Variance?

This connects directly to the previous topic: covariance and contravariance.

Delegates can support variance.

For example, Action<T> is contravariant:

Action<Animal> animalHandler =
    animal => Console.WriteLine(animal);

Action<Dog> dogHandler = animalHandler;

Because Action<in T> consumes T. Microsoft Learn

Func<> supports contravariant input parameters and a covariant return parameter.

Func<in T, out TResult>

So this topic directly connects:

Generics
   ↓
Variance
   ↓
Delegates
   ↓
Func / Action

24. Are delegates type-safe?

Yes.

Suppose:

public delegate int Calculate(int a, int b);

This won't compile:

Calculate operation = SomeMethodWithWrongSignature;

The method must have a compatible signature.

That's one of the major advantages over traditional unmanaged function pointers: delegates are object-oriented and type-safe. Microsoft Learn

25. Where do you see Delegates in real .NET development?

You should be able to mention these in an interview:

LINQ
 ├── Where()
 ├── Select()
 ├── OrderBy()
 └── Any()

Collections
 └── List.Sort()

ASP.NET / .NET
 └── callbacks / middleware patterns

Events
 └── event handlers

Async APIs
 └── callbacks in some APIs

Application code
 ├── Strategy-like behavior
 ├── filtering
 ├── validation
 └── notifications

LINQ is especially important because lambda expressions/delegates are heavily used for passing filtering, projection, and other behavior. Microsoft Learn

  1. Why do we use delegates?
  1. How do you declare a delegate?
  1. Delegate vs method
  1. Delegate vs lambda

  1. What is a callback?
  1. Delegate as method parameter
  1. Delegate vs event

  1. Generic delegates
  1. Method group conversion
